# T1DMAI

Note

Most of the code in this repo was written by AI. If you don't like that, feel free to leave.

This repo is a zoo. Here I train & test many blood glucose forecasting models (including my own) on both my own data and metabonet (public).

My model is a small transformer that forecasts blood glucose 2 hours ahead. I've made two variants: D16 DILATE and D16 MSE which use DILATE and MSE loss for training, respectively. D16 refers to the width of the model (16). They are both trained on synthetic traces, and then a LoRA adapter is added for light fine-tuning, but I also test them without the adapter.

Feast thine eyes on some of their forecasts (these have been trained on synthetic traces, then fine-tuned with a LoRA adapter on my training split):

Caution

Research and educational use only - not a medical device. T1DMAI is a research artifact. It is not clinically validated, has no regulatory clearance, and its output is a forecast of research signals, not medical advice. It must not be used to make medical, diagnostic, or treatment decisions, to calculate or adjust insulin doses, or to manage diabetes in any way. For medical guidance consult a qualified healthcare professional. The software is provided "as is", without warranty of any kind (see LICENSE ).

## 1. Background

I have type 1 diabetes and I wanna know if I can train a BG forecasting model to help me with my daily management. To this end I've made some auxiliary tools:

- T1DMSIM creates synthetic CGM traces since UVA/Padova was too slow on my laptop.

- T1DMDROID runs the models on my phone, also has some neat functionality like reading BG from multiple CGMs at once.

For evaluation, I use the recommendations by Jacobs et al., IEEE Reviews in Biomedical Engineering, 2024 [1] . It's a nice paper that you should probably read.

## 2. Main results

All models suck. XGBoost is the best one but my own model comes close. More details below:

- On my data, D16 DILATE + LoRA comes 3rd of 26 (22.8), behind XGBoost (22.2) and LightGBM (22.4). Wilcoxon puts it level with both at 60 and 90 min, behind them at 30 and 120.

- On MetaboNet, D16 DILATE + LoRA comes 9th (34.6) but has the lowest RMSE of all models at 90 min. XGBoost leads at 30, 60 and 120.

- At 60 min a 3771 parameter LoRA adapter helps both models on both datasets: 26.1 to 22.8 and 27.1 to 23.5 on my data, 36.6 to 34.6 and 36.7 to 35.1 on MetaboNet. At 120 min on MetaboNet it makes D16 DILATE worse (48.0 to 50.4).

- On MetaboNet, LoRA also fixes the bands. The 90% band holds the truth 75-78% of the time at 60 min with sim only and 81-85% with LoRA. On my data both are 83-85%.

- T1DMAI + LoRA reacts earliest on my data: 40-50 min time gain at 60 min, against 30 for XGBoost.

- It also catches the most lows on my data: 40-47% at 60 min, against 29% for XGBoost. On MetaboNet every low-RMSE model misses nearly all lows (XGBoost 0%, T1DMAI 6-8%), while linear extrapolation catches 58%.

- LightGBM matches XGBoost within 0.2 mg/dL everywhere. An LSTM with 15 hours of history comes 3rd on MetaboNet (33.6 at 60 min), against 35.9 for the 2 hour one.

- Zero-shot Chronos-2 and TimesFM 2.5 beat zero-shot Chronos-Bolt by 1.4-2.7 mg/dL at 60 min on both datasets, but trail fine-tuned Chronos-Bolt.

## 3. Models

Numbers in brackets point to References . Everything except the baselines and the foundation models was trained from scratch on each dataset's training split. T1DMAI comes in two versions: sim only is the checkpoint in models/ , and sim + LoRA adds a frozen-base rank 1 adapter [23] (3771 parameters) trained on the real training split.

More in docs/USAGE.md and ARCHITECTURE.md .

## 4. Data

My data. 115 days from T1DMDROID: days 1 to 80 for training, 81 to 115 for testing. Note that the model sees future inputs like insulin & carbs. I should probably also train the adapters while withholding those inputs.

MetaboNet [2] . Official split, 279 test people from 9 studies. Blind, because most of them use closed-loop pumps whose future insulin reacts to glucose the model hasn't seen.

## 5. Method

- LoRA checkpoints are picked by mean RMSE on the last 10 days of each subject's training data.

- All models forecast at the same moments.

- 95% intervals: bootstrap over people (MetaboNet) or days (my data).

- Significance: Wilcoxon signed-rank on paired absolute errors against the best model, Bonferroni corrected.

- Clinical error grids: DTS [20], Clarke [22], CG-EGA [21].

## 6. Results

## 7. Limitations

- My data is N=1 over 35 days.

- The test sets differ a lot (in range 89% vs 75%, CV 28% vs 40%), so don't compare numbers across them.

- Lows are rare: 292 forecasts on my data, 8347 on MetaboNet.

- T1DMAI fell back to the last reading on 0.7% of my forecasts and 0.4% on MetaboNet, including all 28 ShanghaiT1DM ones. The other models never fall back.

- The bands are raw quantiles, no conformal correction.

- The sparse GP's own uncertainty isn't shown. Its noise fit hit the bottom of its grid, giving a band about 1 mg/dL wide.

- Time gain is only computed for my data.

- Unlogged meals count as "no meal".

- CPU timings are single runs on one laptop core and varied by up to 45% between runs.

- LightGBM, LSTM (15 h), Chronos-2 and TimesFM 2.5 have no CPU timing yet.

## 10. Reproduce

python -m zoo.run MODEL --cache CACHE --template template.parquet --truth truth.parquet [--causal] python finetune.py --checkpoint CKPT --cache CACHE --lora-rank 1 --val-days 10 --select-on rmse \ [--blind | --no-blind] python export_submission.py --checkpoint CKPT --template template.parquet --cache CACHE \ --max-context 336 --fill ladder --quantiles [--future-doses zero] python leaderboard.py MANIFEST.json --out results

Chronos-2 and TimesFM 2.5 run under .venv-zoo ( requirements-zoo.txt ).

## 11. Published scores

RMSE (mg/dL) that each model's paper reports, beside the same model on my data and on MetaboNet. The papers use other people, splits, inputs and history lengths, so a gap between the two sides is not a like-for-like comparison. My data is non-blind, MetaboNet blind (§8).

RMSE in mg/dL at the single step 30 or 60 min ahead, as printed in each paper. T1DMAI has no published score.

Chronos-Bolt (Zhang et al. 2026) and N-HiTS (Potosnak et al. 2025; Sergazinov et al. 2024) are published only as RMSE averaged over every step up to the horizon, which is not the same quantity, so they have no row.

# The Discovery Exposer Kit

Most AI agent setups fail when untrusted prompt text can mint execution authority, replay receipts, or trigger tool calls nobody approved.

I'm a first-time developer. With AI, I built Discovery (v1.0–v1.1.8) to make that fail closed. Today the full build history and verification outputs are public:

• 3,315/3,315 receipt hashes verified (0 mismatches) • 3,315/3,315 event signatures verified (0 failures) • 3,060/3,060 attack-labeled cases blocked (0 executed) • 255/255 valid controls executed (0 wrongly denied)

## About this kit

This kit is the public release of Discovery v1.1.8 , together with the build history and the records of the September 5, 2026 incident. The full folder list, with file counts and dates, is in INDEX.txt .

Who I am. I'm Shawn Phillip Thompson, founder of Sentinel Risk Intelligence LLC. I spent about 30 years in OEM collision repair. Discovery is the first software I've built, and I built it with AI tools.

What SRI is. Sentinel Risk Intelligence LLC (SRI) is a Minnesota LLC formed in January 2026. It builds control and evidence tools for AI agents.

What Discovery is. It's a deterministic layer that checks each AI agent action against the authority the agent was given, before the action runs. Details are below.

What's in the kit.

- 00_Evidence/ has the screenshots and photos, chat transcripts, the SEC whistleblower chat and the IC3 complaint.

- 01_Findings/ has the findings, the verification record and the v1.1.8 evidence.

- 02_DISCOVERY_VERSIONS/ has every Discovery build, v1.0 through v1.1.8.

- 03_examples/ has an illustrative SSM sample output.

The September 5 incident. On the night of September 5, 2026, from about 11:30 PM Central, I believe my PC was accessed without my authorization while Discovery work was on it. My account records show a ChatGPT data export started September 6 at 3:41 AM Central and OpenAI sign-in codes sent at 6:35 AM. I don't recall requesting either one. These are the steps I took:

- I reported it to OpenAI on Case 14713357. Their September 9 reply said they found no suspicious logins.

- I filed an IC3 complaint on September 10.

- On September 11, I sent OpenAI a notice asking them to preserve their logs.

- On Case 17638799, I asked for a human reviewer and for the IP address, device and session records.

It has not been confirmed which files, if any, were taken or whether any data left the machine. This kit makes no claim that OpenAI used or trained on this work. OpenAI Cases 14713357 and 17638799 are open, and they are the place for those questions. The screenshots and chats in 00_Evidence/ are my own records of what I saw and reported.

What I'm asking for.

- I'm asking OpenAI to answer the two open cases, including the session and IP records I asked for.

- I'm asking readers to verify Discovery for themselves, using the steps below.

Contact. sri.execute@gmail.com

## Discovery v1.1.8

Discovery is a deterministic action-control layer for AI agents, built by Sentinel Risk Intelligence LLC. Before an agent's action runs, Discovery checks it against the authority it was actually given, and allows, holds or denies it. Every decision produces a verifiable receipt.

Built by a first-time developer, with AI.

## What Discovery does

- Deterministic decisions. The same input always gives the same result. No model sits in the decision path.

- Authority comes only from the spec. Text in a request can never grant itself authority.

- Precedence is locked. When rules conflict, the lower rank wins.

- Mutations are handled strictly. If an agent changes the amount or destination, it continues only at the authorized cap. If it changes the tool or operation, Discovery fails closed.

- Single-use commits. An approval can't be replayed.

- Signed receipts. Each decision gets an Ed25519 signature and a SHA-256 hash chain, so anyone can check that a decision happened and wasn't altered.

## How SSM fits in

SSM is SRI's reading and observation layer. Discovery decides, SSM reads. After a decision, SSM records what happened. It has no decision authority and can't allow, deny or change anything. SSM code is not part of this release. See 03_examples/SSM_SAMPLE_OUTPUT.md for illustrative example records only.

## Verify this release

What the included suites prove and don't prove is listed honestly in 01_Findings/VERIFICATION.md .

## Where to find the builds and version history

- Every Discovery build, v1.0 through v1.1.8, is in 02_DISCOVERY_VERSIONS/ , one numbered folder per version.

- The current build is 02_DISCOVERY_VERSIONS/11_v1.1.8/ , and its evidence is in 12_v1.1.8_evidence/ .

- The full version list is in VERSION_HISTORY.md , and the findings are in 01_Findings/ .

## How to use

- Clone or download this repository.

- Verify the files: sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt (on Windows, certutil -hashfile <file> SHA256 ).

- Unzip 02_DISCOVERY_VERSIONS/11_v1.1.8/V1_1_8_AUDIT_PACKAGE.zip .

# 🦅 RAVEN Recon

Scope-aware reconnaissance and AI-assisted security-testing workbench — for bug-bounty hunters and penetration testers. Runs on Windows and Kali Linux as a desktop app, a local web UI, or in the terminal.

> ⚠️ Authorised testing only. Use RAVEN Recon only on systems you own or have written permission to test. Read RESPONSIBLE_USE.md first. العربية: README.ar.md

## Contents

- What it does

- Download and install — Windows · Kali / Debian / Ubuntu · Verify your download

- Three ways to run it

- Step-by-step guide

- AI: Claude, your own local model, skills

- Safety model

- Your data and privacy

- Build from source and run the tests

- Troubleshooting

- Project layout

- Contributing

- Licence and copyright

## Download and install

### Windows

Option A — ready-to-run app (recommended):

- Download RAVEN-Recon-windows-x64.zip from the Releases page .

- Verify it , unzip it, and run RAVEN.exe . (Windows 10/11 with the Edge WebView2 runtime, which is built into Windows 11.)

Option B — from source (needs Python 3.11+ — or winget install -e --id Python.Python.3.12 — and Git ), in PowerShell:

git clone https: // github.com / 9illcodelli6 - cpp69cve / raven - recon.git cd raven - recon powershell - ExecutionPolicy Bypass - File .\install.ps1

This creates a private Python environment, a Start Menu entry , and the commands raven-recon , raven-recon-web and raven-sec (open a new terminal afterwards). Uninstall: .\install.ps1 -Uninstall (your data is kept).

### Kali / Debian / Ubuntu

Option A — ready-to-run app:

# download RAVEN-Recon-linux-x64.tar.gz and SHA256SUMS.txt from the Releases page, then: sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt --ignore-missing tar -xzf RAVEN-Recon-linux-x64.tar.gz sudo apt install -y gir1.2-webkit2-4.1 bubblewrap # own window + command sandbox ./RAVEN/RAVEN

Option B — from source (recommended on Kali):

git clone https://github.com/9illcodelli6-cpp69cve/raven-recon.git cd raven-recon ./install.sh

The installer asks before running sudo apt install for the few system packages it needs ( python3-venv python3-gi gir1.2-webkit2-4.1 bubblewrap ), creates .venv , adds RAVEN Recon to the applications menu and installs the raven-recon and raven-sec commands in ~/.local/bin . Uninstall: ./install.sh --uninstall (your data is kept).

### Verify your download

Official builds exist only on this repository's Releases page. Each release has SHA256SUMS.txt and a GitHub build-provenance attestation proving the file was built by this repository's workflow:

sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt --ignore-missing gh attestation verify RAVEN-Recon-linux-x64.tar.gz --repo 9illcodelli6-cpp69cve/raven-recon

Windows: Get-FileHash .\RAVEN-Recon-windows-x64.zip -Algorithm SHA256 and compare with SHA256SUMS.txt . Copies from anywhere else ("PRO", "cracked", re-uploads) are not official and may be malicious.

The web UI listens on the loopback interface only and every API call needs a per-session token, so other machines on your network cannot reach it.

- Create a workspace — RAVEN OS sidebar → Workspace (or in the Recon Workbench: workspace menu → new workspace ). Enter the program name and exactly the scope the program allows : in-scope hosts or wildcards ( *.example.com ), exclusions, and ports. Leave allow private addresses off unless it is your own lab.

- Set your identity — Workbench → Identity : the User-Agent and the researcher header your program asks for (for example X-HackerOne-Research: <your handle> ).

- Run a collection — Workbench → Run collection : certificate-transparency names, HTTP probes on every scoped port, and endpoint discovery. Watch progress in the terminal panel; stop any time.

- Review the surface — Surface (hosts ranked by review priority), Endpoints , Graph , Changes (what is new since the last run), Runs . A score is a review priority, never a vulnerability verdict.

- Test by hand — open a request in Repeater , fuzz a parameter in Intruder (with a baseline to spot anomalies), compare two accounts in the Access-control lab , check a reflection in the XSS lab , decode tokens in Decoder . Everything is in HTTP history .

- Use the AI agent (optional) — add your Claude key (see below), open AI Agent , pick Claude Opus 5.5 , describe the task (e.g. "Check /api/orders/{id} for IDOR using my two test accounts" ). Read each proposed request or command and Approve or Deny it.

- Record and report — the agent and the labs create candidate findings; review them in Findings , then Export workspace report (Markdown) and write your own report.

- Stop button — Emergency Stop halts every job, request, agent run and command at once; Resume re-enables them.

- Appearance — Settings → Appearance : Full (animated artwork background), Static (same artwork, no animation — lighter on older machines) or Off (plain dark). Systems set to reduce motion get Static automatically.

RAVEN works fully without AI. For AI features choose one:

Claude (recommended, best results). Create an API key at console.anthropic.com (set a monthly spend limit there), then RAVEN → Settings → Claude (Anthropic API) → paste the key → Save & test .

- The key is stored encrypted in your data folder and never shown again; it is never passed to commands RAVEN runs.

- Used by AI Chat , the AI Agent page and raven-sec .

- Each agent run has a budget (default $3) and a turn limit (default 40) — change them in Settings. The estimated cost is shown next to every run.

- You pay Anthropic for your own usage and must follow Anthropic's Usage Policy.

Your own local model (free, offline). Install Ollama , pull a model (for example ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b ), then Settings → Optional external provider (Ollama) → enable it and enter the model name. It powers AI Chat ; the agent requires Claude. Details and the advanced built-in RAVEN-Sec model: docs/LOCAL_AI.md .

Skills — testing playbooks the agent loads when relevant ( raven/skills/ ):

Terminal: raven-sec (chat), raven-sec -q "question" , raven-sec agent "objective" --scope app.example.com (asks y/N before every action; --scope host:port for other ports, --allow-private for your own lab only).

- Scope enforcement on every outgoing request (canonical URL, IDNA-correct hostnames, resolved address pinned, private/loopback blocked unless enabled, no redirects followed).

- Human approval for every target request, recon job and command the AI agent proposes; approvals are bound to the exact action shown.

- Offline sandbox (bubblewrap, Linux) for agent commands: no network, no home directory.

- Emergency Stop , per-workspace request budgets and rate limits, per-run AI budget.

- Local API on 127.0.0.1 only, per-session token, Origin and Host checks.

- No offensive extras: no denial-of-service, malware, persistence, EDR/AV evasion or credential stuffing. AI output is advisory — verify before you report.

- Data lives on your machine: ~/.local/share/raven-recon (Linux) or %LOCALAPPDATA%\RAVEN-Recon (Windows). Override with RAVEN_DATA_DIR .

- RAVEN contacts only: the targets you approve, crt.sh for certificate transparency, allow-listed trusted research sources (OWASP, MITRE, NVD, GitHub advisories) when you or the agent search, and Anthropic's API if you enabled Claude.

- No telemetry.

# ClickHouse Loom

Shared memory, document search and code intelligence for AI agents. For Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and your own agents.

English · 简体中文 · 日本語 · 한국어 · Português (Brasil) · Español

What Loom is for · Benchmarks · Get started · Capabilities · Integrations · Documentation

Loom is an open-source, self-hosted MCP server that gives your agents long-term, shared memory: what one agent learns in a session, the next agent or tool can find. In an authenticated team deployment, each agent uses a token scoped to namespaces and read or write roles. Check shared memory and denied access .

Agents connect through MCP, HTTP, Python or TypeScript. Self-host with Docker or on Kubernetes with the Helm chart ; agent context and index data live in ClickHouse , and a deployment can choose Postgres at first boot for live memory and knowledge state. The dashboard brings memories, repositories, tasks and runs into one place.

## What Loom is for

- Long-term memory shared across your coding agents , with plugins that load context at session start and capture the session as it runs. Agent memory · Connect a coding agent

- Memory for an agent application , per user, from the Python or TypeScript SDK. Your first agent

- A multi-user MCP memory server with namespaces, roles and tokens. Multi-user mode · Namespaces and sharing

- A code index of your repositories that coding agents query for definitions, callers and change impact. Code index · Language support and limits

- Memories linked to the code they are about , which follow it through refactors, are flagged when it changes and appear when an agent reads or edits it. Memory linked to code

- Lower model cost for coding agents , as measured below. Coding-agent cost

- Document search with citations (RAG) , including PDF, .docx and .pptx files the extractor service converts. Document search

- Shared context for multi-agent workflows : shared memory, task inboxes and decisions. Multi-agent

- Memory, recall, audit and erasure for autonomous agents. Autonomous agents

- A record of agent work , with searchable conversations (when recording is on), session briefs to resume from, runs with their goals, outcomes and model costs when supplied, and PR and tracker history. Runs and PR history

Memory for a software factory. Loom gives implementation and review agents shared lessons, issue context and source provenance across sessions. Scope each principal's access with tokens, await required writes and task handoffs in your application, and recheck code-linked lessons against the current source before review. The same service supports multi-agent workflows and autonomous bots; your orchestration runs the agents, tests and approvals. Offering a tool does not guarantee the model uses it. Multi-agent workflow · Autonomous-agent memory

Every use case, and when another tool fits better: use cases .

Read Choosing memory for a software factory for memory architecture choices, data ownership and operating responsibilities.

Loom is not an in-process library for one agent's short-lived memory, nor an agent framework. When Loom does not fit

## Measured results

Both coding setups use Claude Code ( claude-sonnet-5 ) on the ClickHouse codebase; cost is the whole session's model bill, excluding Loom's server-side model calls, hosting and indexing. Answer quality measures coverage of a verified answer's key points, with a contradiction penalty. File localization counts whether the right file is among the up to three files the agent is asked to name at the end of its answer.

The memory row compares retrieved memories with full conversation history using the same gpt-5 reader. Token savings exclude memory construction; the 94% vs 90% accuracy difference is descriptive, not statistically established.

Separately, Loom's memory.ask configuration scored 96.6% answer accuracy on all 500 LongMemEval-S questions. This is a product evaluation with its own configured answer models, not the fixed-reader comparison above.

Results are specific to the tested workloads.

Protocols and reproducible artifacts · detailed results · evaluate on your workload

## Get started

### 1. Choose your Docker setup

- Personal use—the default: no login, localhost-only access and a dev/local namespace. One person can connect multiple agents.

- Team use: authenticated accounts and namespace access controls. Start in multi-user mode from the first boot .

Both modes support the same Loom features, including configured LLMs and embeddings. Single-user is not a reduced-feature edition. You can also switch an existing installation without deleting its data ; grant new accounts access to the existing namespaces.

To try it with nothing installed, open it in a codespace:

( what it runs and who can reach it )

For the default personal installation, with Docker installed (on Windows, in a WSL 2 terminal where docker works: Docker Desktop with its WSL integration on, or Docker Engine installed in the distribution):

curl -fsSL https://github.com/ClickHouse/loom/releases/latest/download/install.sh -o loom-install.sh && sh loom-install.sh && rm loom-install.sh

Run it from your home directory, or another directory only you can write to . The installer starts Loom and ClickHouse, applies migrations and prints the dashboard URL: http://localhost:7777/ ; on a new install it then checks that a memory saves and reads back. On a terminal it also offers to connect the coding agents it finds (Claude Code, Codex, VS Code) and, on a new install, opens the dashboard. The image includes the server, workers, dashboard and Python, TypeScript and Go compiler indexers, plus the C++ one on amd64 ; TypeScript dependencies are prepared automatically. Quickstart and pinned releases

The installation lives in ~/.loom ( LOOM_INSTALL_DIR chooses another directory): the Compose file and the startup settings in ~/.loom/.env . Running the install command again upgrades in place and keeps your .env settings.

Keep single-user mode localhost-only. For shared access, follow the team deployment guide , including TLS.

### 2. Configure models and API keys

The stock installation boots without keys or network. Storage, the dashboard, structural code indexing and semantic search work, on a small local embedding model the image carries; the fake LLM gives no AI-generated answers.

Open Settings → Models & keys , choose both providers and models, enter their keys, then click Test & apply . No Docker restart is needed; changing the embedding space rebuilds the existing index. The dashboard's embedding choices are hosted providers: to keep local and add an LLM, set the LLM lines in ~/.loom/.env instead ( Models and keys ).

One OpenAI API key can serve both roles. Claude needs a separate embedding provider. OpenAI, Gemini and OpenAI-compatible embedding endpoints are supported. Your agent's CLI login or subscription does not supply Loom's provider keys.

Prefer environment configuration? Edit ~/.loom/.env , then recreate the server:

docker compose --project-directory " $HOME /.loom " up -d --force-recreate loom

A key alone does not change the pinned models (the local embedder and the fake LLM); set the provider and model too. Saved dashboard settings take precedence over .env . Follow models and API keys for provider recipes and health checks.

Everything else is in one file. loom.example.yaml lists every setting with its default and what it does, by area: the ClickHouse connection, timeouts and budgets, rate limits, workers, and the *_enabled switches that turn features on and off. Set any of them as LOOM_<NAME> in ~/.loom/.env and recreate the server; a deployment that mounts a config file can set them in a copy of this file instead ( how settings are read ). One marked live also changes while Loom runs: loom settings set <name> <value> , or Admin → Deployment settings. loom settings list --changed shows what differs from the defaults and where each value came from ( runtime settings ).

### 3. Connect your agents

If the installer connected your agent, skip the commands below. On the machine running a personal installation, the plugins need no token:

# Claude Code claude plugin marketplace add ClickHouse/loom claude plugin install loom@loom # Codex codex plugin marketplace add ClickHouse/loom codex plugin add loom@loom

Start a new session; the first one connects to http://localhost:7777 . In Codex, run codex interactively once and approve the plugin's hooks; until then only the tools work. Tell the agent something worth keeping, then ask about it in the next session.

Cursor lists Loom as a plugin and an MCP server . For a team marketplace on a Teams or Enterprise plan, a team admin can also import this repository; its Cursor plugin installs the MCP entry and Loom's skills. On the machine running a personal installation, the button below adds the local MCP entry , which needs no token:

For VS Code agent mode on the machine running a personal installation, the buttons below add the local MCP entry , which needs no token:

For a team server, pass --config server_url=… --config token=… to Claude Code, or point Codex at it as described in connect a coding agent . Create tokens in Settings → Tokens . Cursor and other MCP clients, and the SDK , are covered there too.

## Why Loom

- Memory that carries forward. Share decisions and findings across agents and sessions. Each fact records who wrote it, version history and conflict review make corrections traceable, and a namespace can be rolled back to any point in time. Memory

- Code intelligence with evidence. Find definitions, callers, change impact and relevant tests; connect code to commits, pull requests and issues. Use source locations, completeness signals and per-tier freshness to check a result. Code index

- Grounded retrieval. Search permitted memories, documents, conversations and tracker records. Answers cite their sources; low-confidence retrieval can abstain. Retrieval

- Multi-agent handoffs. Assign work through durable task inboxes with leases, retries, review rules and outcomes. Your agents execute the workflow; Loom preserves the handoffs. Task queues

- Control over agent data. Manage namespace access, provenance, retention, audit records and verified erasure. Context remains queryable in ClickHouse. Security

## Integrations

Langfuse and ClickStack are optional integrations, not bundled services in the Docker stack.

## Benchmark details

### Detailed retrieval, reader and code-search results

These measure different tasks, not one aggregate score. SWE-bench measures file localization, not issue resolution. The results ledger includes scoring definitions, small-sample evaluations, weaker and negative findings, and the full protocols, models and artifacts.

For shared agent context, code intelligence and permissioned retrieval, start with the documentation . For deployment requirements, see the prerequisites .

# go-migrate

Run versioned SQL migrations from a standalone CLI, or embed the runner in a Go application. go-migrate supports PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite, SQL Server, Oracle Database and IBM Db2 LUW. Preview the SQL, then require its plan ID at deployment to check the plan, database and schema under the migration lock.

go install github.com/go-gen-ecosystem/go-migrate/cmd/gomigrate@latest

## Why go-migrate

The table compares built-in capabilities in three pinned releases. A dash means we found no built-in equivalent for that row.

For transactional SQL migrations on PostgreSQL, SQLite and SQL Server, go-migrate and goose can commit the change and its history row in the same transaction. golang-migrate records a dirty version, executes the migration, then marks the version clean separately. Its force V command lets an operator set the version and clear dirty state after checking the database. go-migrate execution · golang-migrate execution and recovery · goose transactional SQL

Packaging and feature comparisons use the tagged source and build configuration. golang-migrate release drivers · goose SQL annotations · goose SQLite driver · goose release build

### SQLite allocations per 100 migrations

Each operation constructs a library runner and applies 100 migrations to a fresh SQLite database. Each migration creates a table and inserts one row. All three use the same SQL bodies and pure-Go driver ( modernc.org/sqlite v1.62.0 ), with WAL and synchronous=OFF . The table shows medians of six samples per configuration on Linux/amd64, Go 1.26.11, Intel Core Ultra 9 285HX. B/op is cumulative Go heap allocation per batch. Benchmark source

At defaults, go-migrate allocated the fewest bytes and goose made the fewest allocations. The golang-migrate result was sensitive to its 100,000-byte buffer per migration. The fourth row changes only that setting. Larger SQL files, remote sources and durable storage are different workloads. golang-migrate buffer implementation

Each column lists bytes allocated per batch for the six samples, in execution order.

Start in a disposable checkout of v1.0.1 . Go 1.26.11 needs to refresh the tagged benchmark module's go.mod and go.sum , which is why the command uses -mod=mod .

cd benchmarks/compare GOWORK=off CGO_ENABLED=0 GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.11 go test -mod=mod -run ' ^$ ' -bench ' ^BenchmarkUp100_ ' -benchmem -count=6 .

For the fourth row, add these lines at the start of BenchmarkUp100_GolangMigrate in that checkout and repeat the command with -bench '^BenchmarkUp100_GolangMigrate$' .

old := gm . DefaultBufferSize gm . DefaultBufferSize = 4096 defer func () { gm . DefaultBufferSize = old }()

## Quick start

gomigrate init # .gomigrate.yaml + migrations/ gomigrate create add_users # migrations/20261116120000_add_users.sql gomigrate lint # risky SQL? (no database needed) gomigrate up --sql # dry run: the exact SQL that would run, and its plan ID gomigrate up --expect-plan < id > # apply exactly the reviewed plan, or fail with plan_changed gomigrate status # table; -o json for scripts gomigrate down # roll back the last one (--steps, --to, --to-tag, --all)

-- +migrate Up CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY , email VARCHAR ( 255 ) NOT NULL UNIQUE); -- +migrate Down DROP TABLE users;

## Library

//go:embed migrations var migrations embed. FS dir , _ := fs . Sub ( migrations , "migrations" ) m , err := migrate . New ( db , "postgres" , migrate . WithFS ( dir )) // malformed files fail here, not mid-run if err != nil { return err } _ , err = m . Up ( ctx )

- Migrator methods: apply and roll back: Up , UpTo , Down(ctx, migrate.DownTarget{Steps: 1}) (or To: "3" , or Tag: "v1" ), Redo ; read-only: Plan , PlanDown , PlanRepair , PlanID , Statements , Callbacks , Status , Validate , Lint , Migrations ; history administration: Repair(ctx, migrate.RepairTarget{Migration: "3", Action: migrate.RepairClearFailed}) , MarkApplied , Baseline , Tag . To accept deliberate checksum drift, use migrate.RepairAcceptChecksum for that version. Bare Repair(ctx) returns ErrInvalidArgument and changes nothing.

- apply and roll back: Up , UpTo , Down(ctx, migrate.DownTarget{Steps: 1}) (or To: "3" , or Tag: "v1" ), Redo ;

- read-only: Plan , PlanDown , PlanRepair , PlanID , Statements , Callbacks , Status , Validate , Lint , Migrations ;

- history administration: Repair(ctx, migrate.RepairTarget{Migration: "3", Action: migrate.RepairClearFailed}) , MarkApplied , Baseline , Tag . To accept deliberate checksum drift, use migrate.RepairAcceptChecksum for that version. Bare Repair(ctx) returns ErrInvalidArgument and changes nothing.

- Approved plans: m.Up(ctx, migrate.ExpectPlan(id)) runs only if the plan, computed again under the lock, still has the ID that was reviewed; otherwise it fails with ErrPlanChanged and runs nothing.

- Options: WithFS , WithGoMigrations , WithTable , WithLockWait ; WithLogger ( halolog ); WithPlaceholders , WithContexts , WithLabels , WithBaselineOnMigrate ; WithAllowOutOfOrder , WithAllowMissing , WithHooks , WithInstalledBy .

- WithFS , WithGoMigrations , WithTable , WithLockWait ;

- WithLogger ( halolog );

- WithPlaceholders , WithContexts , WithLabels , WithBaselineOnMigrate ;

- WithAllowOutOfOrder , WithAllowMissing , WithHooks , WithInstalledBy .

- Without a database: migrate.Lint(dialect, opts...) analyzes migrations with no connection.

- Errors: every error works with errors.Is , and migrate.ErrorCodes(err) gives stable codes.

- Concurrency: a Migrator is immutable after New and safe for concurrent use.

## Migration files

Directives:

-- +migrate Up notransaction -- e.g. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY -- +migrate Context dev,test -- run only with --context dev or test -- +migrate Labels billing -- run only with --label billing -- +migrate DBMS postgres -- run only on PostgreSQL -- +migrate RunAlways -- repeatable: run on every up -- +migrate Precondition onFail=MARK_RAN expect=0 SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name = 'legacy' -- +migrate Lint ignore=drop-table -- accept a reviewed lint finding -- +migrate StatementBegin / StatementEnd -- keep a block as one statement

Supporting rules:

- Placeholders: ${name} is replaced from --placeholder name=value or the placeholders: config. Built-ins are ${migrate:dialect} , ${migrate:table} and ${migrate:user} .

- Versions compare numerically: 9 < 10 , 1.9 < 1.10 , 001 == 1 == 1.0 .

- SQL checksums cover the Up section. They normalize line endings, a leading BOM and insignificant whitespace outside literals, and preserve statement-block boundaries.

- Preconditions: HALT fails the run, MARK_RAN records the migration without running it, and CONTINUE leaves it pending. Plans flag such migrations as conditional .

- Callbacks appear in --sql plans (they run even when nothing is pending), are covered by the plan ID and are linted.

## SQL Server

Use sqlserver as the dialect or a sqlserver:// URL in GOMIGRATE_DSN . A library caller opens its *sql.DB using the sqlserver driver registered by github.com/microsoft/go-mssqldb . The CLI includes that driver and remains CGO-free. Choose the target database with the URL's database parameter or the YAML database.name field. The CLI enables TLS and verifies the server certificate by default. Supply driver TLS options via the URL or database.params . A disposable local fixture with a self-signed certificate can set trustservercertificate=true .

Each migration direction runs as a T-SQL batch by default. Put GO on its own line to begin a new batch. A trailing -- comment is allowed. GO inside a quoted identifier, string, or block comment stays in the SQL. Use separate batches when a statement such as CREATE PROCEDURE must be first in its batch. GO N repetition and SQLCMD commands such as :r are outside the supported script format. StatementBegin / StatementEnd can also set explicit batch boundaries. The text dry run prints GO between batches and the JSON plan lists the exact payload of each batch.

SQL Server 2022 is the conformance target. The migration login needs access to the configured history schema and permission to create and modify history and application objects there. An unqualified history table uses the login's default schema. See the SQL Server example .

## Oracle Database

Use the oracle dialect or an oracle://user:password@host:port/service URL in GOMIGRATE_DSN . The YAML database.name field identifies the Oracle service. The CLI bundles Oracle's native-Go oracledb driver and uses password authentication. The driver requires Go 1.26.9 and keeps the CLI CGO-free. Library callers can register and open oracledb themselves through database/sql . The driver is distributed under the Universal Permissive License 1.0 .

The CLI selects TCPS on port 2484 by default and requests certificate-chain and server-identity verification. Set wallet_location or ssl_server_cert_dn as needed through the URL or database.params . An isolated Oracle Free test instance can use protocol=tcp to connect on port 1521. The conformance fixture uses password authentication over TCP on a private network. It targets Oracle AI Database 26ai Free and connects to the FREEPDB1 service.

A history table with no explicit schema uses the session's initial current schema. The tool folds ordinary configured identifiers to uppercase as Oracle does for unquoted names. The migration user needs permission to create and modify its history and application objects and an EXECUTE grant on SYS.DBMS_LOCK . Oracle releases the migration lock when the physical session ends. Use a driver configuration that fails the run on session loss.

Ordinary SQL uses semicolon separators. Wrap Oracle PL/SQL blocks and stored routines in -- +migrate StatementBegin and -- +migrate StatementEnd . Keep the final END; and omit the SQL*Plus slash command. Oracle q'[...]' and nq'[...]' literals can contain semicolons and newlines. See the Oracle example .

## IBM Db2 LUW

Use the db2 dialect or a db2://user:password@host:port/database URL in GOMIGRATE_DSN . The CLI bundles the independent, MIT-licensed go-db2 driver and remains CGO-free. Library callers can register the db2 driver and supply a database/sql pool. The conformance target is IBM Db2 Community Edition 12.1.5.0 on Linux x86-64 with the default database collation.

The CLI enables certificate-verified TLS and defaults to port 50001. Provide the instance's TLS listener port and ssl_ca if you use a private CA ( tls and ssl_ca can also be set in database.params ). An isolated fixture can opt in to unencrypted TCP with tls=false&allow_plaintext_auth=true . The CLI supports username and password authentication.

Db2 history identifiers use uppercase names for ordinary unquoted identifiers. An unqualified history table uses the initial current schema. The migration login needs permission to create and modify its history and application objects and EXECUTE on the SYSIBMADM.DBMS_LOCK module. Use Db2 LUW 12.1.3 or newer with the Db2 native DBMS_LOCK module installed. Regular schema migrations run in a transaction. Use notransaction for statements that cannot run in one. Wrap Db2 SQL PL routines or compound statements in StatementBegin and StatementEnd . Keep the semicolons inside the block and omit CLP terminators such as @ . See the Db2 example .

## Safety model

- Locking: a cross-process lock scoped to the configured migration history. PostgreSQL and MySQL: pg_advisory_lock / GET_LOCK , which the server releases if the process dies. SQL Server: a session-owned sp_getapplock per database. Distinct history tables in the same database share that lock so aliases of a table under a case-insensitive or accent-insensitive collation cannot bypass it. Oracle: an exclusive DBMS_LOCK session lock per schema and history table that survives Oracle DDL commits. Db2: a numeric SYSIBMADM.DBMS_LOCK session lock derived from the schema and history table. Db2 keeps the lock across commits and releases it when the session ends. Histor

# Modern Web Guidance

Modern Web Guidance is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform.

Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community.

Documentation · Eval Dashboard · Source Code · Report an Issue

## Quickstart

npx modern-web-guidance@latest install

This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See Alternative Installation Methods below.

#### Try it out (without installing)

# Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search " animate a dialog modal backdrop " # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve " animate-to-from-top-layer " # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan .

## Why?

Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions.

Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code.

Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap. Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on:

- Modern Browser APIs : Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse.

- Performance & Accessibility : Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances.

- Responsible Fallbacks : Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries.

## What's Included?

We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are designed to be token-efficient ; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know.

### Core Disciplines

#### 🎨 User Experience

Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color ).

#### 📐 CSS Layout

Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid , modern color spaces like oklch , text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming).

#### ⚡ Performance

Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield ).

#### 📝 Forms & UI

Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields).

#### ♿ Accessibility

Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability).

#### 🤖 Built-in AI

Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs).

View an example: the navigation-drawer guide .

#### The full list

### CSS & Layout (140 features)

### HTML & DOM (36 features)

### JavaScript & APIs (74 features)

### accessibility

- accessible-error-announcement : Synchronize programmatic accessibility states (like aria-invalid) with the visual :user-invalid state to ensure screen reader users receive error feedback only after interaction, mirroring the visual experience.

- accessible-generated-content : Use CSS generated content ( ::before / ::after ) in ways that stay accessible, including alternative text for decorative content.

- respect-os-text-scale : Respect the operating system's text scale preference for a page so font sizes, layout, and rem-based measurements follow the user's accessibility settings.

### built-in-ai

- language-detection : Detect the language of user-generated content or already present site content.

- language-model : Run on-device natural language inference in the browser using the Prompt API, with streaming output, structured JSON responses, and multi-turn session management.

- summarizer : Summarize text content using the on-device Summarizer API.

- translator : Translate text between languages using the on-device Translator API.

### css

- animate-to-intrinsic-sizes : Smoothly animate interactive components (like accordions, menus, and expanding cards) to and from their natural dimensions.

- atrule-support-conditionals : Conditionally apply certain CSS rules or declarations only if a certain at-rule is supported by the browser.

- calculate-with-intrinsic-sizes : Calculate the size of an element based on its intrinsic size, while ensuring it fits within given design constraints.

- child-state-based-styling : Build a component that changes its styling based on the state of one of its child elements. For example, a component that renders in light or dark mode based on whether a theme toggle is checked (or not).

- content-based-styling : Build a component that changes its layout based on whether it contains specific child elements (or not). For example, if the component contains an image, use a multi-column layout, otherwise default to a single-column layout.

- css : Action-oriented guidelines for modern CSS architecture, including the cascade, selectors, scoping, nesting, and design tokens. Use this guide when authoring styles or managing design systems.

- css-layout : Modern CSS layouts such as flexbox, grid, subgrid, container queries, anchor positioning, and intrinsic sizing. Use this skill when architecting responsive UI components or page layouts.

- design-token-reactivity : Define higher-order design tokens, like density modes (compact, comfortable, spacious) or themes and have descendant components react to changes directly and in component-appropriate ways.

- dynamic-sibling-styling : Create dynamic visual spectrums or layout arrangements that automatically adapt to the number of elements in a group.

- fluid-scaling : Scale items like font size, spacing, and media sizes smoothly based on the parent container's size rather than using fixed breakpoints

- individual-transform-properties : Animate or override individual CSS transform properties (e.g. translate, rotate, scale) independently of other transform properties on a single element.

- overflow-clipping-control : Adjust the visible clipping boundary of an element to align with the content edge, padding edge, or border edge—or a specified offset from any of these—offering finer-grained control over how content is clipped.

- reduce-style-repetition : Reduce excessive style repetition by encapsulating complex or dynamic styling logic into reusable functions (such as a function that computes a gradient based on a set of input parameters).

- responsive-design : Build UI that adapts to container and viewport size, including container queries, dynamic viewport units, aspect ratios, and responsive typography.

- selector-atrule-combinations : Target elements based on the intersection or union of selectors and conditional @-rules while minimizing repetition.

- size-aware-styling : Build a component whose styles can be conditionally dependent on its own width or height, rather than the width or height of the viewport. For example a card component that can change its layouts depending on how large it is, or a call-to-action button that can conditionally display helper text based on its width.

- style-parent-with-has : Style parent elements of a form field (e.g. labels or fieldsets) when the field is invalid.

- usage-aware-component-variations : Build components that adapt visual logic based on semantic context using CSS container style queries.

### forms

- animated-select-picker : Create a custom select component whose dropdown is animated. For example, the menu fades or slides into view, or the options animate upon selection.

- autofill-address-form : Build an address form with correct autocomplete attributes and autofill support.

- autofill-highlight-inputs : Customize the styling of form fields that have been autofilled and not edited by the user

- autofill-payment-form : Build a payment form that collects card details with correct autocomplete values and autofill support.

- autofill-sign-in-form : Build a sign-in form with correct autocomplete values and autofill support.

- autofill-sign-up-form : Build a sign-up form with correct autocomplete values and autofill support.

- brand-consistent-forms : Match checkboxes, radio buttons, range sliders, and progress bars to your site's color palette without replacing them with custom components.

- branded-select-styling : Create custom select elements whose button, picker, arrow icon, and checkmark all seamlessly match your brand or design system's typography, colors, spacing, and border treatments.

- custom-select-picker-layouts : Create custom select pickers whose options are positioned in unique or interesting ways, rather than the traditional stacked list of options.

- form-fields-automatically-fit-contents : Allow form fields to grow and shrink to fit the user input, e.g. as the user types or selects a different option. Apply maximum and minimum size limits to create dynamic and responsive form fields that conform with the page design.

- ime-safe-enter-submit : Implement Enter-to-submit in textareas and single-line inputs (chat, search, inline rename) safely for IME (Input Method Editor) users to prevent submitting incomplete text.

- required-field-feedback : Provide error message for required form fields that were skipped or left empty only after user interaction, to avoid preemptive errors and ensure feedback is timely and contextually relevant to the user's flow.

- rich-media-picker : Create a custom select component whose options can contain complex HTML formatting (e.g. images, icons, and other rich formatting) rather than just plain text.

- select-menu-interaction : Validate that a non-default option has been chosen in a select menu only after the user has interacted with the control.

- slider : Style a native range slider with custom track, thumb, fill, and focus states while preserving native functionality and accessibility.

- sms-otp-form : Verify user phone numbers and one-time passcodes delivered over SMS with automatic code extraction and accessible form input.

- switch : Build an accessible switch with the native HTML switch attribute, falling back to a styled checkbox when not supported.

- validate-input-after-interaction : Show form field validation feedback (e.g. password complexity or email format requirements) only after the user has finished their initial interaction, avoiding premature errors on page load or while the user is typing.

### html

- accessible-web-components : Make custom elements accessible by default, setting roles and ARIA state via the ElementInternals ARIA mixin, managing focus with delegatesFocus, and keeping ARIA relationships within a single shadow root.

- custom-elements : Define, register, and manage the lifecycle of autonomous custom elements, covering constructor rules, lifecycle callbacks, upgrade timing, attribute/property reflection, and naming conventions.

- form-associated-custom-elements : Make a custom control participate natively in forms with formAssociated and ElementInternals, submitting its own value, integrating with constraint validation, and reacting to reset, disable, and state-restore.

- prerendering-custom-elements : Server-render a custom element, then hydrate it in place without re-rendering or a flash of unstyled content.

- shadow-dom : Encapsulate a component's DOM and styles with Shadow DOM, construct the tree efficiently with HTML templates, and project consumer content with slots.

- styling-web-components : Style across the shadow boundary with :host selectors, inherited and custom properties for theming, ::slotted and ::part, and cascade layers and container queries inside compone

# GURU

GURU is an Android app that ships a Linux shell and 390 tools, so a language model can work in it and act on your phone and your network.

You bring the model: Ollama on your own hardware, or your own key for Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or xAI. It runs commands, calls tools, reads what comes back and keeps going until the job is done. No root, no adb for normal use, no account. Free, AGPL-3.0, sideloaded APK.

Public beta. One maintainer, a lot of it AI-written, nobody outside has audited it. If all you want is a shell, use Termux.

## What it does

You give the model a job. It picks a tool and calls it. GURU checks the call against the permissions you've granted, runs it and hands the result back. The model reads the result and picks the next call. That repeats until the job's done or it hits something it can't do.

A failed step goes back as the actual error. If a command isn't found, the model can run apt and try again. If a permission is missing, the tool says which one, why it matters and how to grant it.

Termux gives you a shell and you type into it. GURU puts a model on the other end.

## The rooms

## The agents

An agent is a name, a set of written instructions and the tools it may use. You run one yourself, or GURU calls one mid-conversation and manages it while it works on its own context, then reports back.

Twenty ship with the app. Each can be edited, switched off or deleted.

Build your own with a name, instructions and any tool the picker offers. An agent with no tools still reasons. The picker shows exactly what it holds and offers nothing else, and one press grants all of them or none. Publish it to Ottio free or at a price, and you keep the majority of every sale.

## What's in the box

The tools sit behind a permission layer built on 167 declared Android permissions. Declaring isn't holding, so you grant what you want. The accessibility service, the notification listener and screen capture each have to be switched on by you in Settings. GURU can't do that for itself.

Every write is followed by a read, and the device's answer is compared against what was written. A transport saying it worked is not evidence.

## Where your data goes

Your prompts, the conversation and any image you attach go to the model endpoint you chose and nowhere else. Point it at Ollama on your LAN and none of it leaves your network.

Public traffic goes over Tor by default. LAN and loopback go direct. If Tor has no circuit, GURU waits up to 30 seconds for one, then fails the request. It never falls back to a direct connection on its own. Anything carrying a credential goes over Tor regardless. /clearnet overrides the default and /tor locks it on.

API keys sit in the Android Keystore, one AES-256-GCM key per service, non-exportable. Memory is encrypted at rest with Argon2id and XChaCha20-Poly1305. With a cloud model, whatever it recalls goes into the prompt and leaves the phone. Cloud backup is off.

Prompts, skills, tool definitions, agent templates and canvas packs come from api.unuslumen.com , so a new capability reaches you the day it's built with no APK update. The fetch is a plain GET with no login, no cookie and no install ID, and it goes over Tor. The server is closed source and stateless. What it serves isn't secret, because all of it lands on your phone and you can read it in the app. If the server's down GURU still boots, and you write your own prompts.

The same content is mirrored to GuruProduction/GURU-content whenever it is published, so the public record follows the app.

## Otio

Three layers, and only the first is live.

The creator market. You sell what you build: agents today, and skills, tools, masks, games, websites, apps and books as the machinery takes them. It ships as the agent market because agents are what exist so far.

The data marketplace. GURU stops other apps farming your data and absorbs that traffic itself. You see your captured data, categorised, and decide what to sell. The buyers are the companies already buying it today, straight off you instead of off big tech. It gets switched on when there are enough backers to do it properly.

The social network. A decentralised social layer inside the app, for you and your GURUs. Least specified of the three, because it comes last.

Identity is a wallet, not an account: no sign-up, no login, no email capture, no profile the server can attach to a person. Unus Lumen holds the money and pays creators out. 80 percent to the maker, 20 percent plus payment costs to Unus Lumen. Payments are not switched on yet, and a priced agent says so rather than giving itself away.

## Limits

I am one man. I don't have a computer science background and I'm not claiming to be technical. I'm completely self taught and I use language models to do 90% of the coding work. I know exactly what I want the app to do and I direct the workload across multiple agentic CLI sessions, burning about 8 billion tokens a week.

The project hasn't had a professional security audit, there are bugs I haven't come across and none that have been reported to me yet, and I have to spread my time very thin.

So the app is good. It's usable and very powerful already, but it's in its infancy, so please bear with me. Thank you for your support.

## Install

GURU isn't on the Play Store and won't be. Take the signed APK from Releases and allow unknown sources when Android asks. It's 743 MB because the userland, the Python runtime, the reverse-engineering toolchain and the native binaries are inside it, so nothing gets fetched later. Android 8.0 or later.

Check it before you install. The SHA-256 is on the release page.

sha256sum GURU.apk apksigner verify --print-certs GURU.apk

Every release is signed with one key. The certificate SHA-256 should be:

3E:58:42:37:B1:41:8E:12:01:C6:A4:ED:7C:07:B5:8A:F7:B7:C5:A1:FB:E2:E6:BE:F7:6B:03:A2:BA:E8:CD:3C

Build from source with cd GURUbeta-FULL && ./gradlew assembleDebug . You need JDK 17 and the Android SDK. CONTRIBUTING.md has the rest.

### Connect a model

First launch asks where your model lives. After that it doesn't ask again.

No model runs on the phone and nothing goes through Unus Lumen. I don't see your prompts and I don't take a cut of your tokens. A loop burns a lot of tokens, so watch the bill on cloud models. Small models lose the thread on long jobs.

GURU adds no content filter of its own. A cloud provider applies its own rules. A local model does whatever its weights do. The prompts are readable in the app, so check.

## Why

I got sick of being data farmed and told no by products that charge extortionate amounts for a worse experience. I wanted full control of my own phone and network with a good model behind it. So I built it.

I'm Steven, Unus Lumen, Bristol. One person, no funding, no team. Break it and tell me what's wrong. Open an issue or send a PR. Security problems go through SECURITY.md , privately.

## Docs

Architecture · Contributing · Security · Privacy policy · Notice · A note from Steven

## Licence

AGPL-3.0 for the app. The GURU name and branding are trademarks of Unus Lumen Ltd, so a fork renames. NOTICE.md lists every bundled component and its licence.

Website · YouTube · X · TikTok · Instagram · Kick · steven@unuslumen.com

### Tune your agent's harness: tools, prompts, skills, model and hyperparams

A real production agent, after tuning: 2.5x fewer failures, 6x cheaper, 2x lower latency. Measured on held-out data, on a smaller model. It's a multi-turn agent with over 200 tools.

Better models move the frontier. A tuned harness gets you above it.

## What it tunes

Most optimizers tune the prompt. Harness Tuner tunes everything around the model.

- Tools. The biggest win we see. Your tools probably wrap APIs written for code, not for agents. It rewrites them for the agent: smaller responses, better descriptions, no repeated calls. When a script should do the job, it writes a new code tool.

- Prompts and skills. It cuts contradictions, adds the requirements nobody wrote down, and moves long instructions into skills that load only when needed.

- Model and settings. It tunes thinking level, temperature and the rest. It keeps your model by default. Allow other models at start-up, or optimize for speed or cost, and it also searches models and providers.

- RAG, fine-tunes and sub-agents. It attaches, swaps or drops the ones in your project.

It tries different methods, not just different words: one big prompt or skills, RAG or a skill, many small tools or one general one.

## How it works

- You set the goal and steer. Optimize for quality, cost or speed. When it cuts cost or latency, it holds quality. Tell it what to focus on and what not to touch, in plain English.

- Many goals, not one number. Bring all your evals. It tracks every one.

- Fix one thing at a time. Each experiment runs only the evals it targets, so trying an idea is cheap. Before anything is promoted, it's checked against every eval. Nothing regresses quietly.

- A graph, not a line. Experiments branch from any earlier version, often from several parents, and the winners merge back.

- Train, val and test, enforced in code. Agents only ever see train. Val decides promotions. Test is never read, so the number you report is one it never optimized against.

- Several winners, your pick. It finds the best quality, the cheapest at good quality, a balanced option and the fastest. Compare them side by side in Kiln .

- Runs on the coding agent you already use: Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode, on your existing subscription.

- Works with Kiln . Our free app tracks every experiment and shows the trade-offs side by side.

## Optimize the demo project

Copies a small moderation task, which ships with the tuner, into a new folder, adds it to Kiln, and tunes it: 624 labelled forum posts, and an eval. The baseline prompt doesn't know the forum's house rules, so there's plenty to find and fix.

> Requires adding an OpenRouter API key to Kiln. The harness-tuner run will cost about $2.

uv tool install harness-tuner harness-tuner --demo

## Quickstart

uv tool install harness-tuner harness-tuner

It walks you through the rest: starting Kiln (or getting it from kiln.tech ), then picking the project and task to tune. Your agent needs to be a task in Kiln, with evals. Kiln can walk you through creating both.

It works in waves until the budget or the clock runs out, wraps up, then writes a report and prints where it is. Details: docs/your-own-task.md .

## What you need

- Kiln , on the same machine. The CLI walks you through installing and starting it.

- An agent, with evals. Kiln can walk you through creating both.

- A coding agent you already use: Claude Code (the default), Codex or OpenCode. The tuner's agents run on your subscription.

- Your model provider keys, stored in Kiln. Used for running the agent being tuned, and evals.

- uv , to install it.

Missing something? docs/install.md has a check and a fix for each requirement.

Harness Tuner is free and open source, but it needs LLM API calls. See docs/costs.md for details.

## Works with Kiln and Seahaven

Tuning an agent takes more than a loop. Kiln and Seahaven have the rest:

- Evals that say what good looks like, as many as your product needs.

- Synthetic users that hold multi-turn conversations, the same for every candidate.

- Synthetic worlds for agents that change data. Every run gets a fresh copy of the world, and evals grade what the agent actually did, not what it said it did.

## FAQ

Prompt optimizers tune the prompts inside a program. Harness Tuner tunes the whole agent you already have: its tools, skills, prompts, model and settings, against every eval you care about.

In a way, that's what it does, with the rigor and scale built in:

- a code loop runs the process, so it can't get off track

- real experiments, each one tracked

- batches of experiments planned and run in parallel

- many evals, each tracked on its own

- cost control: experiments run only the evals they target, winners merge, and ideas that aren't working stop early

- val and test sets withheld from the agents

- skills that guide your coding agent through each step

A tuned harness is easier to deploy (no GPUs, off-the-shelf models), easier to update when new product requirements come up, quicker to move to the latest model releases, and cheaper. Kiln supports fine-tuning too, and the tuner can use your fine-tuned models in advanced cases.

A model router picks a model for each request, based on how hard it guesses the request is. Harness Tuner makes the task easier for the model, by giving your agent the tools and instructions it needs. That often lets every request go to a cheaper model, and it improves quality in ways a bigger model doesn't.

It doesn't touch your original tools. It writes wrappers: small code tools that call your existing tools and reshape what goes in and out. A wrapper can trim a response to the fields that matter, loop over a set of results, fold many calls into one, or do the math so the model doesn't have to. Your tools keep their current signature, so nothing outside Kiln changes.

Kiln builds you evals that use synthetic users. Each eval item sets a persona, a goal and a number of turns, and a model plays the user. The simulated user is the same for every candidate, so comparisons are fair, and its cost is tracked separately from your agent's.

Experiments call your agent's tools, so they need an environment where those tools can run. The best option is a synthetic world for your evals, built with Kiln Seahaven . It gives you a safe, reproducible and highly parallel place to run them.

The tuner's agents only ever see the train split. Val is used only to decide which candidates get promoted. Test is never read by the tuner: you run it for your final report, so the number you quote is one it never optimized against. This is enforced in code, not asked for in a prompt.

Run the tuner again and pick the new model at start-up (or allow any model). It checks the new model against every eval, re-tunes the harness for it if needed, and builds on everything it learned in earlier runs. Upgrading becomes a routine run, not a project.

Harness Tuner runs on Kiln , our free app. Kiln provides:

- Evals: creating and running them ( Kiln evals ).

- Experiment tracking: the provenance of every experiment: what it changed, and which experiments it came from.

- Views of the results: a Compare view to compare experiments on evals, cost and speed, and an Experiment Graph view to see how the tuning progressed.

- Harness history: every experiment's harness is kept, for future experiments and comparisons.

It depends on the scope of the project. A small agent with a small eval can cost a few dollars. A large agent with hundreds of tools can cost several hundred. You set a budget for the model calls through Kiln (your agent CLI's own usage is not counted) and a time limit, and it stops starting new work when either runs out.

Harness Tuner does several things to keep costs down:

- Targeted experiments: each experiment runs only the evals it's trying to improve, and stops early when an idea isn't working.

- No wasted runs: if your evals can't detect a real win, it says so before spending anything.

- Subscription agents: the tuner's own agents run on your existing Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode subscription. It uses some of your quota, but that's usually much cheaper than per-token billing.

Evals need direct API access and can't run on a coding agent subscription, so their tokens bill to your provider keys in Kiln. Details: docs/costs.md .

## Docs

- How it works : the whole loop, with a diagram.

- Install : every requirement, with a check and a fix for each.

- Concepts : waves, experiments, splits and the promotion gate. Read it before your first run's report.

- Your own task : what your task needs, and how the first run starts.

- CLI reference : every command and flag.

- Objectives and models : what to optimize, and which models it may use.

- Costs : estimate a run before you start it.

- Limitations : what it doesn't do. Read it before planning a long run.

- Architecture : the wave loop, the gate, measurement, memory and the sandbox.

- Agents : the ten agent roles and what each one does.

- Agent CLIs : how it runs on Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode.

## Contributing

See CONTRIBUTING.md .

## License

Harness Tuner is MIT licensed .

The Kiln name and logos are trademarks of Chesterfield Laboratories Inc.

# Select

Run your company with AI agents that earn their autonomy.

Agents of any kind — developers, marketers, support, sales — work in an organization you design. Every result is checked by code against a delivery contract, and an agent stops needing your approval only once its verified record shows it can — per task type, revocable at any time.

> Status: 0.2. Accounts, guided setup, local IMAP/SMTP mail tests, routines and the verification loop are covered by end-to-end tests. Docker images build and the Compose stack starts successfully in Ubuntu GitHub Actions CI. Real model API calls have not been verified yet: see Limits .

## Why Select

Multi-agent orchestrators let you decide in advance what agents may do alone. Select replaces that guess with evidence:

- Delivery contracts. Each task type has a YAML contract. The system runs its checks itself and keeps a receipt — contract version and hash, every check, the evidence. A model never declares that a check passed.

- Autonomy earned per agent and task type. Supervised → sampled → autonomous after a streak of verified successes; back to supervised at the first blocking failure or human correction.

- Limits the score never overrides. Payments, contracts, taxes and hiring are always supervised, in code.

- An honest counter. The share of work finished without a person is always shown next to the rate of errors people found afterwards.

- No invented numbers. Every value carries its source; a quantity that is not in the customer's e-mail fails verification.

Both diagrams are SVG and can be reviewed or edited directly in the repository.

## What it does

These four come from the end-to-end test run against local IMAP and SMTP test servers ( E2E_SCREENSHOTS_DIR ); the others are the demo company. All are real captures.

## Explore the interface

These are real Playwright screenshots of Select running locally with fictional demo data . No external model provider or mailbox is connected in this capture session.

## Quickstart

Requirements: Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS) or Docker Engine with Compose (Linux).

git clone https://github.com/Kirby54/Select.git select cd select ./start.sh # Windows: .\start.ps1

The script writes .env with random secrets (keep a copy), starts the containers and opens http://localhost:3000 , where the first visit creates your account. Without the script: cp .env.example .env , set the secrets, docker compose up --build .

No API key yet? Open the demo company from the account menu and press Run demo week .

Five-minute guide: docs/getting-started.md . Development setup without Docker: docs/installation.md .

## How autonomy works

Default promotion thresholds are 20 and 50 verified successes in a row — starting hypotheses to calibrate, not proven values . An e-mail to an address that never wrote to you always goes to a person. Details: docs/autonomy.md .

## A contract

id : support_reply version : 1 title : Support reply risk : medium required : [to, subject, body] checks : - id : recipient_from_message rule : provenance # the address must be the one that wrote to us params : { fields: [to] } - id : no_unauthorised_promises rule : forbidden_phrases params : { field: body, phrases: ["refund", "discount", "guarantee"] } approval : mode : by_autonomy external_action : send_email

More in docs/verification.md .

## Architecture

Next.js 16 web app → FastAPI API → PostgreSQL 16, with a worker on a durable PostgreSQL job queue that runs agents, reads mailboxes, sends approved e-mail and fires routines. select-verify is a separate Python library with no database or network access. See docs/architecture.md and the interface's design system .

## Security

Agents never hold a permission to send, pay or sign; the server applies the approval rules and sends. External content is treated as data and checked against stored sources. Passwords use Argon2id; sessions live in an HttpOnly cookie with an anti-forgery header; provider keys and mailbox passwords are encrypted. Read docs/security.md and docs/deployment.md before opening Select to a network.

## Tests

make test # Python verifier/API tests on PostgreSQL plus frontend unit tests make e2e # Playwright UI scenarios against a running stack

e2e/complete.spec.ts (4 more scenarios) runs on a password-mode stack with the local mail servers of scripts/dev-mail.py : first owner, guided setup, a real IMAP mailbox, an e-mail triaged, routed, quoted, approved and sent once over SMTP (the .eml file is checked), a weekly routine seen from a New York browser on Paris time, and an invited colleague joining.

## Verify a real model (optional)

The CI tests use network doubles, not real provider keys. Before connecting production data, use the explicit live-provider probe with your own test credentials . It sends a harmless fixed JSON-generation prompt and reports whether the chosen model returns the expected result. It never stores the key or accesses company data. Real-provider compatibility is not yet certified by the maintainers.

## Benchmarks

None published yet. The protocol ( autonomy-bench : same tasks and models, autonomy rate and undetected-error rate side by side, compared with a single agent and with Paperclip) is in bench/README.md . Until it runs, Select makes no comparative claim. Feature parity is tracked honestly in docs/parity.md .

## Limits

- Provider calls have not been exercised against real paid-model APIs (no keys in CI). An Ollama-compatible localhost HTTP stub is used to test the full worker, deterministic verification and approval pipeline; it does not execute a real model.

- Docker : GitHub Actions builds both images, starts PostgreSQL, API, worker and web with Compose, and reaches the API health endpoint through the web proxy on Ubuntu. The start.sh script itself was tested with a stand-in Docker CLI; real macOS/Windows installations and start.ps1 have not been exercised in CI.

- Mailboxes were tested against local IMAP and SMTP servers, not yet at a real provider. No OAuth: Microsoft 365 and Outlook.com cannot connect yet; Gmail needs an app password.

- Agents write text and structured results through model APIs. Code-change proposals can be checked for basic diff structure and sent to mandatory human review, but no repository code is edited, executed or pushed by Select. There is no isolated Claude Code or Codex runtime yet. See review-only code proposals .

- Attachments are not read; quotes are sent as e-mail text, without a PDF.

- No e-invoice : the invoice draft is not an XRechnung or ZUGFeRD file and is never presented as compliant. Businesses exempt from VAT ( franchise en base ) are not handled properly yet.

- No single sign-on, two-factor authentication, plugins or sandboxed code execution.

## Documentation

Five minutes · Installation · Provider probe · Configuration · Mail · Agents · Autonomy · Verification · Workflows and routines · Architecture · Deployment · Security · Troubleshooting · Design system · Français

## Contributing

Start with CONTRIBUTING.md . Good first contributions: a new contract for a task type you know, or a new deterministic rule — each with one accepted and one rejected example.

## Roadmap

- Verify with real model keys and real mailboxes; keep Docker startup, recovery and tests green across supported environments.

- Coding-agent runtimes: run Claude Code or Codex in a code workspace, verify with the project's tests, approve the exact diff.

- Run without Docker (embedded database), like a one-command install.

- Quote PDFs, attachments, OAuth mailboxes, VAT-exempt businesses.

- Run autonomy-bench and publish the raw results.

## Licence

The application ( apps/ ) is licensed under AGPL-3.0-only ( LICENSE ). The select-verify library is licensed under Apache-2.0 ( packages/select-verify/LICENSE ) so that other tools can adopt delivery contracts freely.

## Support

Questions and ideas: GitHub Discussions. Bugs: GitHub Issues. Vulnerabilities: privately, see SECURITY.md .
