# ludo: the Ludo AI command line

Generate game assets with Ludo AI from your terminal or from a coding agent: sprites and spritesheet animations, images, 3D models (with rigging and animation), video, sound effects, music and voices.

npm install -g @ludoai/cli # or run without installing: npx @ludoai/cli ... ludo login # log in with your browser (you can create an account there) # no account yet? ludo signup --email you@example.com --plan pro (see "Signing up from the terminal") ludo image create --prompt " a knight with a red cape " --image-type sprite

## Why a CLI

- Local files just work. Pass a path to any image, audio, video or model flag and the CLI uploads it for you. No base64, no hosting.

- Results land on disk. Generations wait for the job to finish and save every result file to ./ludo-output (or --out <dir> ), named after the operation and job (or --name sfx_pump for sfx_pump.mp3 ; nothing is ever overwritten). Result URLs expire after 7 days; the files do not.

- Always current. Commands, flags, enums, defaults and prices are built from the live API spec, so new models and features show up without updating the CLI.

- Cheap for agents. An agent learns only the commands it needs, through --help , instead of loading every tool schema up front.

## Usage

ludo <group> <command> [flags] ludo <group> <command> --help

The table is a snapshot: ludo --help always shows the current list. Every command also answers to its API operation id ( ludo createImage ... ), the same names the API docs and the MCP server use.

### Examples

# Animate a sprite from a local file; the spritesheet, video and frames are saved to ./sprites ludo sprite animate --initial-image knight.png --motion-prompt " walk cycle " --out sprites # Cut out a background ludo image remove-background --image photo.jpg # Image to 3D, then rig it ludo model create --image chest.png ludo model rig --model ludo-output/create3DModel-1a2b3c4d.glb # Music ludo audio music --description " calm piano melody for a title screen " --duration 30 # Ask Ludo's docs before using a feature ludo docs search --query " which animation model should I use for pixel art? "

### Flags

- API fields become kebab-case flags: image_type is --image-type . Booleans are switches ( --crop , --no-crop ). Array fields repeat ( --images a.png --images b.png ).

- --input body.json (or --input - for stdin) supplies the whole request body; flags override it.

- --no-wait submits the job and prints {id, status} ; ludo jobs wait <id> picks it up later.

- --json prints JSON even on a terminal. It is the default when stdout is not a terminal.

- --timeout <s> stops waiting (the job keeps running), --quiet silences progress on stderr.

- --open opens the result in its default app (Aseprite, say), --play plays generated audio, --copy puts the saved file paths on the clipboard.

- WebP results are also saved as PNG, side by side (engines and most tools want PNG). --image-format png keeps the PNG only and --image-format webp the WebP only ( "image_format" in .ludo.json sets it for a project). A spritesheet's grid is stored in its PNG and --engine files are made from it, so keep the PNG for sheets.

- --engine godot also writes a Godot 4 SpriteFrames resource ( .tres ) next to a spritesheet: drop it on an AnimatedSprite2D . Inside a Godot project it uses a res:// path.

- --engine texturepacker writes a TexturePacker JSON atlas ( .json ) next to a spritesheet, with the animation named after the file. PixiJS: const sheet = await Assets.load("knight-walk.json") , then new AnimatedSprite(sheet.animations["knight-walk"]) . Phaser: this.load.aseprite("knight", "knight-walk.png", "knight-walk.json") , then this.anims.createFromAseprite("knight") ( load.atlas gives the frames alone).

- --engine unity writes the sheet's .png.meta , which imports it sliced into one sprite per frame, and an .anim clip that plays them on a SpriteRenderer . Export into your project's Assets/ folder (or copy the PNG, .meta and .anim there together). A .meta already there keeps its guid, so scenes and prefabs that use the sprites still find them.

### In the terminal

At a terminal, results show up right there, spritesheets as a looping animation. Terminals that draw real images (iTerm2, Kitty, Ghostty, WezTerm) show the actual picture. Elsewhere (including inside tmux) the preview is skipped with a note, and --open opens the result full size instead. ludo preview <file> shows any saved image again (Ludo spritesheets remember their grid; for other sheets pass --grid 8x4 --fps 12 ). A spinner shows the job's status while you wait, and each result suggests a next step.

None of this reaches scripts or AI agents: it is drawn on stderr and only when both outputs are a terminal. --plain , NO_COLOR or LUDO_PREVIEW=0 turn it off.

### Output

In JSON mode a generation prints:

{ "job_id" : " … " , "status" : " succeeded " , "task_type" : " animateSprite " , "credits_charged" : 9 , "result" : { "spritesheet_url" : " https://… " , "video_url" : " https://… " }, "files" : [{ "url" : " https://… " , "path" : " ludo-output/animateSprite-1a2b3c4d-1.png " , "absolute_path" : " /home/you/game/ludo-output/animateSprite-1a2b3c4d-1.png " }] }

Inline base64 in a result (such as a spritesheet's generated sound effect) is saved to a file and replaced by its path.

### Exit codes

## Free tools

ludo toolbox holds tools that run on your machine: offline, with no account, no API key and no credits. They work on any spritesheet or sound, not only Ludo's.

# Cut a spritesheet into one PNG per frame. The grid comes from --grid, from the sheet's Ludo # stamp, or is detected; when detection is not sure it stops and asks for --grid. ludo toolbox sprite slice knight-walk.png # Put frames back together into a sheet that remembers its grid (ludo preview plays it) ludo toolbox sprite join ludo-output/knight-walk/ --cols 4 --fps 12 # Edit the frames of a sheet: drop frame 7, hold frame 4 for three frames, play as a ping-pong ludo toolbox sprite frames knight-walk.png --drop 7 --hold 4x3 --pingpong # How well it loops, 0 to 1: how alike the last frame and the first are (0.85 and up is clean, # under 0.7 a seam you see). It approximates the loop_score Ludo's API returns, offline. It only # measures; Ludo's sheets come cut to their loop, and `ludo sprite edit --edit-mode fix_loop` # repairs one that does not loop. ludo toolbox sprite loop knight-walk.png # Several takes of one animation (like --n 4): which loops cleanest, the cleanest first. ludo toolbox sprite loop walk-1.png walk-2.png walk-3.png walk-4.png # Image edits. On a sheet (its Ludo stamp, or --grid) every frame gets the same edit, so the # frames stay aligned. ludo toolbox image trim knight-walk.png # cut the empty border, one box for all frames ludo toolbox image pad trimmed.png --restore # put back what trim cut ludo toolbox image pad hero.png --to 128x128 --anchor bottom ludo toolbox image extrude tiles.png --by 2 --grid 8x8 ludo toolbox image scale hero.png --by 4 # nearest neighbour; --by 1/4 scales down ludo toolbox image scale hero.png --by 1.5 --filter lanczos # any factor; Pillow's filters ludo toolbox image flip knight-walk.png # face the other way; --vertical for upside down ludo toolbox image rotate hero.png --by 90 ludo toolbox image outline hero.png --color " #1a1c2c " # 1 px, no corners; --shape square, --width 2 ludo toolbox image shadow hero.png --offset 2,2 --opacity 40 ludo toolbox image convert hero.png --to webp # lossless WebP # Palettes: list and save one (.hex, .gpl, .pal, .txt, .png), map onto a Lospec palette or # another sprite's colours, or swap colours (a red enemy becomes a blue one). ludo toolbox image palette hero.png --save hero.gpl ludo toolbox image recolor knight-walk.png --palette pico-8.hex ludo toolbox image recolor slime.png --swap " #3fa34d,#2a6e33 " --to " #3b6fd1,#24478a " # Tilesets: one PNG per tile, or the files Tiled (--tiled), Godot and Unity read. repeat lays a # tile out 3x3 and says whether its edges meet without a seam. ludo toolbox image tiles terrain.png --size 16x16 --spacing 1 --tiled --engine godot ludo toolbox image repeat grass.png # An animated GIF for sharing: one palette for every frame (the sheet's own colours when it has # 256 or fewer), 1-bit transparency (--alpha-threshold, --matte for soft edges), loops forever # unless --once. --scale 4 enlarges small pixel art. ludo toolbox sprite gif knight-walk.png --fps 12 --scale 4 # Several animations of one character at one size and ground line, in one frame size: the web # app's Export Pack. Nudge one by file name, label or position; pack.json re-runs it exactly. ludo toolbox sprite pack idle.png walk.png jump.png --name knight --engine texturepacker ludo toolbox sprite pack --manifest ludo-output/knight/pack.json --size walk=1.1 --ground jump=3 # Animations played one after another, each placed so it continues from the last frame of the one # before (the web's image matching, run locally; --align ground lines up the feet instead): the web app's Export Sequence. # The output gives each transition's offset; sequence.json re-runs it, and you can edit them there. ludo toolbox sprite sequence idle.png jump.png land.png --name knight-jump --frame-size 256x256 ludo toolbox sprite sequence idle.png jump.png --mode separate --engine godot # A GIF or animated WebP reads as a sheet of its frames, so every sprite and image tool takes one. ludo toolbox sprite slice dance.gif # Video (needs ffmpeg): a clip to a sheet, and a sheet to WebM or MOV with transparency, or MP4. # ffmpeg is found on the PATH or where brew, winget, scoop and choco put it; LUDO_FFMPEG names another. # A sheet holds 64 megapixels: without --width, a longer clip's frames are shrunk to fit. ludo toolbox sprite from-video knight-walk.mp4 --fps 12 ludo toolbox sprite video knight-walk.png --format webm --loops 3 # Sound. WAV and MP3 are read in-process; OGG, FLAC and the rest, and writing OGG or MP3, need # ffmpeg. Loudness is LUFS (ITU-R BS.1770). ludo toolbox audio info zap.mp3 # length, loudness, true peak, silence, loop seam; music: tempo ludo toolbox audio trim zap.mp3 # silence off both ends (Ludo's come trimmed) ludo toolbox audio convert theme.mp3 --to ogg # Ogg Vorbis for Godot and Unity; --mono, --bits # What is in a 3D model: meshes, triangles, size, textures, skeleton and animations; for a rigged # one which way it faces, and per clip whether it returns to its first pose and a walk's speed. ludo toolbox model info knight.glb # Setting a character up: where its feet and pivot are, its colliders, and one pixels per unit for # all its sheets (and which sheet is drawn at another size). They only report. ludo toolbox sprite metrics knight-walk.png --overlay # bounds, ground line, feet pivot; a picture to check ludo toolbox sprite collide knight-walk.png --ppu 280 # box and capsule for Godot, Unity, Phaser, Box2D ludo toolbox sprite compare knight_ * .png --reference knight_walk.png=1.8m ludo toolbox image contact icons/ * .png # one labelled picture of many images # A folder at a glance: what each asset is, what the game still lacks (with the Ludo command that # makes it) and loaders for Phaser or Pixi. ludo toolbox asset manifest assets/ --emit phaser # Engine files for a sheet you already have. Any toolbox tool that writes a sheet takes --engine # too, and a trimmed or extruded sheet exports each frame's original size and offset. ludo toolbox sprite export knight-walk.png --engine texturepacker ludo toolbox sprite export knight-walk.png --engine godot ludo toolbox sprite export knight-walk.png --engine unity --pivot feet --ppu 280

Files are saved under ./ludo-output (or --out <dir> ) and never overwrite anything.

## Projects

ludo init sets a folder up as a project. It writes .ludo.json and adds instructions for coding agents (a section in AGENTS.md , a Cursor rule when .cursor exists, the Claude Code skill when the project uses Claude Code). Every command run anywhere

# agent-access-review User access reviews for AI agents. It finds every agent and MCP server an organization runs, works out what each one can read, write, execute and send, tests that access against 12 controls, and produces the packet an auditor expects: a reviewer sign-off sheet, hashed evidence, and OSCAL assessment results mapped to NIST 800-53, SOC 2, NIST AI RMF and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. > In one sentence: the quarterly "who has access to what?" review that companies already run for employees, applied to AI agents. > Real-world case study: what you get by copying the MCP configs from official READMEs : 8 of 9 unpinned, 7 of 9 with unreviewed write/send/execute access, and an exfiltration path once they're combined. ## Quick start (2 minutes) You need Python 3.11+. No cloud account, API keys or network access. pip install agent-access-review agent-access-review demo demo reviews five example agents and writes the packet to review-demo/ . Open review-demo/access-review.md , or just read the sample report here without installing anything. Then review your own setup: Secrets in your configs are masked before anything is written, so the output is safe to share. ## Problem Every SOX and SOC 2 program runs quarterly user access reviews: list who has access to what, have an owner confirm it's still needed, revoke the rest, keep the evidence. AI agents now hold the same kind of access (API tokens, database connections, shell access, mailboxes), and almost nobody reviews them: - No owner, no approval. A developer adds an MCP server to their Claude Desktop or Cursor config and the agent instantly has their GitHub token and home directory. No ticket, no approver, and it never appears in an access review. - Over-broad by default. Setup guides tell people to grant the whole home directory, the full-control repo scope, or tenant-wide *.All Microsoft Graph permissions. - Secrets in plain text. MCP configs routinely hold raw tokens and database passwords. - A new attack path. An agent that can read sensitive data, read content an attacker wrote (a GitHub issue, an email, a web page), and send data out can be prompt-injected into leaking that data. No traditional access control looks at that combination. Agents are non-human identities. They need the same joiner/mover/leaver and recertification controls as people, plus a few that are specific to AI. ## What it checks Each control is defined once in controls.yaml and cross-walked to every framework, so one test produces evidence for all of them. The mappings are my own judgment and should be checked against official crosswalks before being relied on in a real audit. ## The AI-specific risk: exfiltration paths (AAR-09) Traditional access reviews look at one permission at a time. For AI agents, the danger is a combination : an agent that can read sensitive data, reads content an outsider wrote, and can send data out. Each leg is harmless alone. Together, one prompt injection hidden in an email, ticket, issue or web page can instruct the agent to leak the data. A human approval step on any leg breaks the chain. flowchart TB subgraph BAD["❌ finance-ops-agent: flagged AAR-09"] direction LR U1["📨 Untrusted input

These carry no owner or approval, which is exactly why they're the shadow-AI problem. Agent manifests ( agents.yaml ): a governed record for LangChain, CrewAI or custom agents, with owner, approval, tools, scopes, credentials and last-used dates. - MCP configs (Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code .vscode/mcp.json ): local npx / uvx / docker servers and remote HTTP servers. These carry no owner or approval, which is exactly why they're the shadow-AI problem. - Agent manifests ( agents.yaml ): a governed record for LangChain, CrewAI or custom agents, with owner, approval, tools, scopes, credentials and last-used dates. - Classify. An MCP config only says which server runs, not what it can do. The capability catalog turns a server name into a grant: actions, data classification, whether it ingests untrusted content and whether it can send data out. Unknown servers are flagged (AAR-12), never assumed safe. - Redact, then hash. Secrets are masked during parsing, before anything is stored, so evidence can be shared with auditors. Each agent's inventory and redacted source record are hashed with SHA-256 over canonical JSON, so any later edit to the evidence is detectable. - Review. Every tool grant gets a recommended decision ( Keep / Modify / Revoke / Investigate ) and an empty column for the reviewer, the same shape as a user access review spreadsheet. - Export. OSCAL 1.1.2 assessment results: one observation per agent pointing at its evidence file and hash, and one finding per NIST 800-53 control objective. ### The review cycle It's the same quarterly user access review that SOX and SOC 2 auditors already test for people, run on agents: flowchart LR D["1 · Discover

every 90 days"] Q -.-> D classDef step fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0284c7,color:#0c4a6e classDef decision fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,color:#78350f classDef fix fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#dc2626,color:#7f1d1d classDef done fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,color:#14532d class D,C,T,Q step class R decision class F fix class E done ## Sample run The bundled examples are a developer's Claude Desktop config, a VS Code MCP config and three governed agents. The full output is committed in sample-output/ : the reviewer packet , the decision sheet , hashed evidence and OSCAL . $ agent-access-review demo AGENT TOOLS HIGH MED LOW support-copilot 2 0 0 0 finance-ops-agent 4 4 3 0 devops-agent 2 6 1 1 claude-desktop-config 6 12 5 1 vscode-mcp 3 6 2 3 5 agents · 17 tool grants · 44 findings %%{init: {"themeVariables": {"pie1": "#dc2626", "pie2": "#f59e0b", "pie3": "#16a34a", "pieSectionTextColor": "#ffffff", "pieStrokeColor": "#ffffff"}}}%% pie showData title Findings by severity "High" : 28 "Medium" : 11 "Low" : 5 Some of what it finds: - finance-ops-agent reads vendor bills in NetSuite (restricted data), reads an inbox vendors can email (untrusted input) and can send email (egress), with no human approval. That's an AAR-09 exfiltration path : one crafted invoice email could get the agent to mail out vendor banking details. Its approval is also 216 days old, and its OCR tool hasn't been used in 164 days, so it's marked Revoke . - claude-desktop-config gives an agent the whole /Users/dev home directory, an unsandboxed terminal, a GitHub token and a database password in plain text, and runs four unpinned packages. - support-copilot passes every check: it writes to tickets, but a human approves before anything is sent. CI regenerates sample-output/ on every push and fails if it differs from what's committed, so the sample always matches the current code. ## How to read the results Recommended decision (one per tool grant, in the packet and the CSV): Severity: high means fix before the agent's next use (an unowned agent, plaintext secrets, an exfiltration path). Medium means fix within the review cycle (stale approval, unpinned package). Low means a gap in evidence rather than a risk (no usage logs, no rotation date). The reviewer fills in the empty Reviewer decision column and the sign-off table. The completed packet plus the hashed evidence files are the audit evidence for the review. ## Run it Install from a release (shown in the Quick start ), or work from source (dependencies are pinned exactly in requirements.txt ): git clone https://github.com/Mihirajmera/agent-access-review.git cd agent-access-review python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate pip install -r requirements.txt python -m agent_access_review demo # writes review-demo/ pytest -q scan options: --out DIR (default review/ ), --as-of YYYY-MM-DD (date used for recertification, rotation and dormancy), --fail-on high|medium|low (exit 1 if a finding is at or above that severity). agent-access-review --help lists examples. ### As a CI gate Keep your MCP configs and agents.yaml in the repo, and block pull requests that give an agent unpinned, archived, vulnerable or over-privileged access: # .github/workflows/agent-access.yml on : pull_request permissions : contents : read jobs : review : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v4 - uses : Mihirajmera/agent-access-review@v0.5.0 # or a commit SHA with : paths : .mcp.json .vscode/mcp.json agents.yaml # files or folders; default "." fail-on : high # high | medium | low | never The review packet goes into the job summary, and the step fails on findings at or above fail-on . A repo with no configs gets a notice instead of a failure. The report output holds the packet's path, so you can upload the folder (default agent-access-review/ ) as an artifact. Pin to a release tag or a commit SHA, not main , so a new version can't change your gate without review. That's control AAR-10 applied to this tool itself. Without the action, pip install agent-access-review and agent-access-review scan … --fail-on high do the same. ## Design decisions - Agents are identities, not apps. The review is modeled on ITGC user access reviews (owner, approval, recertification, dormancy, credential hygiene) because that's the control framework auditors already test. AI-specific risks are added on top, not instead. - AAR-09 looks at combinations, not single permissions. Each leg of an exfiltration path is harmless alone. Th [truncated]

# Mintigate demo (offline)

Offline demonstration — simulated agent, simplified demo runtime. Proprietary Mintigate Runtime not executed.

This folder is a small, deterministic demonstration that you can read in full and run on your own computer. A simulated agent proposes three fixed changes to a synthetic two-file fixture. A simplified demo runtime decides on each change in a temporary copy of the fixture, and an independent check confirms what happened.

## What it shows

Each decision is recorded with the SHA-256 of the target before and after, in a report.

## What you need

- This folder, as received.

- Node.js 18 or later. Nothing else: no package to install, no Git, no Claude Code, no SDK, no network access, no account and no model call.

## Run it

Open a terminal in this folder (on Windows, PowerShell or Windows Terminal) and run:

node mintigate-demo.mjs

The demo takes no option. There is no live mode.

## Exit codes

## What it writes

- Each run creates a new folder .output/run-<date>-<random>/ in this folder. Earlier runs are never changed.

- The fixture is copied into workspace/ inside that new folder, and the changes are made there only. The shipped fixture/ folder is never written.

- At the end of the run, even after an error, the demo removes the files and folders of that workspace/ one by one. It removes nothing else.

- What remains is one report: .output/run-<date>-<random>/report.json . It holds the decisions, the audit records, the hashes, the checks, the negative controls, the clean-up count and the hashes of the demo files that were used. It contains no absolute path of your computer.

Nothing is written outside .output/ , and no setting of your computer is changed. To remove everything, delete this folder.

## How the checks work

smoke-test.mjs does not use demo-runtime.mjs to judge the outcome. It copies the fixture, reads the files itself, computes their hashes and compares them with the expectations in scenarios.json :

- the decision of each scenario;

- for the applied change: exactly the expected line changed, and nothing else;

- for the other two: the target is unchanged, or was not created;

- the hashes in each audit record match the files;

- every protected file and every file outside the scope is unchanged, no file was created or deleted, the shipped fixture is unchanged, and the temporary copy was removed.

It then runs negative controls: deliberately wrong expectations or observations, such as expecting the refused change to be applied or pretending that the protected file changed. Each one must make a named check fail. If a contradiction went unnoticed, the run ends with code 1.

## Files

## Limits

- The agent is simulated: its three proposals are fixed in scenarios.json . No model is called.

- The runtime is a simplified demo runtime of a few rules: a folder or file scope, a list of protected files, and exact text replacements. It is not the proprietary Mintigate Runtime, which this demo does not contain or execute.

- The demo works only on its own synthetic fixture. It does not run on your repository, does not watch or intercept your tools, and has no approval command.

- It is not a benchmark and measures no performance.

## Licence

The MIT licence in LICENSE applies to the files of this kit only.

### Try a deliberate mismatch

In a separate copy of the demo, open scenarios.json . For protected-file-change , change expect.decision from PENDING_APPROVAL to APPLIED , then run:

The demo should exit with code 1: the protected change still requires approval, and the independent check rejects your altered expectation. Inspect the generated report.json to see the decision, failed checks, and file hashes.

You control this local demo and can change its policies or code. It illustrates governance rules; it does not protect against its own administrator.

## Beyond the demo

This demo illustrates scoped changes, human approval boundaries, and audit records using a deterministic agent and a simplified runtime.

Mintigate is being developed to help developers govern real agent workflows. This demo does not execute its proprietary Runtime or connect to a live model.

Explore the project, current evaluation results, and limitations: https://mintigate.com

# Laplace’s Scissors

English · 한국어

Source · Issues · Discussions

Rotate an LLM’s output matrix to compute edits while preserving protected answers.

Rust · Triton · CUDA / HIP · Readout rotation

Quick start · Commands · Implementation and tests · Math and design

Laplace’s Scissors computes rotation edits for an LLM’s original output matrix. probe constructs numerical inputs from model weights and traces directions with weak output discrimination, cancellation across layers, and the associated weight coordinates. diagnose uses cases with expected answer strings to find plane or joint rotations that repair failed answers while protecting successful ones. Each objective and protection condition is checked with actual GPU outputs. Scaling analysis applies the same edit policy across checkpoints to measure deviations from a reference curve and the amount recovered.

flowchart LR A[Original checkpoint] --> B[Observe hidden states] B --> C[Protected readout rotation] C --> D[GPU validation] D --> E[Accepted proposal] E --> F[Generate or export]

## Commands

## Quick start

### Environment

Prepare a Rust toolchain, a Python environment that can import Triton 3.8, and a CUDA or HIP driver. Python provides the Triton compilation bridge. Rust handles model loading, tokenization, execution, edit computation, and result storage.

export LAPLACE_CACHE= " ${XDG_CACHE_HOME :- $HOME / .cache} /laplaces-scissors " export LAPLACE_PYTHON=python3 cargo build --release

.cargo/config.toml places Cargo build artifacts outside the project. LAPLACE_CACHE stores models, kernels, and run results. Select the backend and device index with LAPLACE_BACKEND=auto|cuda|hip and LAPLACE_DEVICE . Set LAPLACE_DRIVER_LIBRARY for the driver library path, or ROCM_PATH / HIP_PATH for the ROCm SDK. The HIP backend also checks the selected Python environment for the rocm-sdk-core package. Device names and execution targets come from the driver.

### Fetch a model and prepare inputs

cargo run --release -- fetch Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B cargo run --release -- inspect Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --out " $LAPLACE_CACHE /graph.json " cargo run --release -- cases --count 12 --seed 7 --out " $LAPLACE_CACHE /cases.jsonl "

Model inputs accept organization/model , organization/model@revision , a Hugging Face model URL, or a local safetensors model directory. Hub inputs are pinned to a commit SHA, with SHA256 recorded for each file. Use --revision to select a revision and HF_TOKEN for authentication.

Check an answer from the original model:

cargo run --release -- generate Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \ --prompt ' What is 2 + 2? Reply with the number only. '

### Case format

Write custom cases as JSONL. expected is the zero-based index of the correct entry in choices . The choices specify the expected answer; the model generates an answer string for prompt . See the example below and the example JSONL .

{ "id" : " sum " , "prompt" : " What is 2 + 2? Reply with the number only. " , "choices" :[ " 3 " , " 4 " , " 5 " ], "expected" : 1 , "oracle" :{ "sum" : 4 }}

The original chat template builds the prompt, whose token prefix stays fixed. The expected answer is encoded separately and followed by EOS to form the target token sequence. The answer body must survive a tokenizer round trip exactly. When the original generation ends with EOS and exactly matches the expected string, every prefix of that generation is protected. For failed cases, each target answer token and EOS must score above every competing token in the vocabulary.

## Compute and apply edits

Numerical probes · Answer repair · Checkpoint export · Scaling analysis

### Numerical probes · probe

probe takes model weights and an execution graph. Seeded selections of embedding rows form numerical prefixes, a reference vector, and an orthonormal basis. Two vectors with the same norm as the reference vector are injected directly at the decoder input. Responses are compared with Jeffreys divergence, the symmetric KL divergence between output distributions. A weak direction has low output discrimination between equal-sized injections under the recorded numerical input distribution. Model acquisition for this command loads safetensors and configuration files.

cargo run --release -- probe Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \ --directions 12 --prefix-length 3 --seed 7 --probe-angle 0.05 \ --max-angle-degrees 3 --coordinates 12 --intervention-fraction 0.1 \ --out " $LAPLACE_CACHE /runs/probe " cargo run --release -- probe Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \ --inputs " $LAPLACE_CACHE /runs/probe/inputs.json " \ --proposal " $LAPLACE_CACHE /runs/probe/proposal.json " \ --out " $LAPLACE_CACHE /runs/probe-replay "

--directions sets the maximum dimension of the search basis constructed from weights. The actual dimension follows the hidden width and the rank of embedding differences. --prefix-length sets the number of numerical vectors before the injection position. --probe-angle is the spherical angle used to construct the two inputs, in radians. The minimum eigenvector of a small response Gram matrix proposes a direction; measurements through the actual decoder compare its divergence with that of the existing basis directions.

Residual branches from the selected pair of runs provide signed layer contributions. The branch with the largest negative contribution supplies --coordinates weight coordinates and attention-head totals. --intervention-fraction controls diagnostic interventions that change each selected coordinate’s magnitude in both directions. Each intervention reruns from the fixed numerical prefix. Signed contributions and measured intervention effects are recorded separately. --coordinates 0 performs layer tracing; --intervention-fraction 0 performs divergence tracing and protected rotation.

The edit is a readout rotation that protects the original output matrix’s row Gram matrix, the midpoint of the two hidden states, and reference and control states. --max-angle-degrees , --max-edit-norm , and --tolerance set bounds on angle, weight change, and protected-output error. Among three candidates within the angle bound, the program saves an edit that increases measured divergence and satisfies the protection tolerance. Candidates apply actual GPU rotation and readout to observed hidden states. --inputs loads saved inputs; protected_hidden can hold additional protected vectors from the same model. Adding --proposal reruns the saved input pair through the full decoder.

Probe outputs are manifest.json , inputs.json , trace.json , transport.json , report.json , status.json , and an accepted proposal.json . Replay also records replay-frames.json . Results include input and model hashes, actual hardware and precision, divergence, layers and weight coordinates, preservation errors, numerical residuals, and execution counts by stage. Proposal version 3 stores the divergence objective and injection-input hash. Reapplication verifies weight and execution-configuration hashes.

### Answer repair · diagnose

cargo run --release -- diagnose Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \ --cases " $LAPLACE_CACHE /cases.jsonl " \ --max-planes 8 --max-angle-degrees 120 --margin 0.05 \ --max-new-tokens 64 --context 2048 --time-budget 20m \ --out " $LAPLACE_CACHE /runs/rotation " cargo run --release -- generate Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \ --prompt ' What is 2 + 2? Reply with the number only. ' \ --proposal " $LAPLACE_CACHE /runs/rotation/proposal.json "

--max-planes sets the number of rotation planes to investigate. --max-angle-degrees bounds the rotation angle, and --margin sets the minimum logit gap between each target token and every competitor. --tolerance bounds each protected-output change divided by 1 + |original logit| ; its default is 0.00002 . The inequalities include a numerical allowance derived from this tolerance and the observed logit magnitude. For each plane, merged forbidden intervals yield the angle with the smallest weight change. Candidates are checked with actual GPU readout in order of weight change.

After checking plane candidates, a joint response computation adjusts multiple targets together. --joint-steps sets the number of adjustment steps and defaults to 12; setting it to 0 runs the plane candidates. --joint-rank sets the maximum joint rotation basis dimension and defaults to 64. --max-angle-degrees also bounds the joint rotation’s largest principal angle. --max-edit-norm bounds the Frobenius norm of the output-weight change. Acceptance requires the full-vocabulary margin, protected-output tolerance, target answer and EOS, and preservation of originally successful generation paths.

Joint search computes and shares the output basis and cost Gram matrix once. When twice the response count is smaller than the rotation dimension, it solves the Cayley system in that smaller space. Candidate scores use the compressed output basis on the GPU. After search, a rotation completion minimizes weight change while preserving observations. The original GPU readout checks that the completion stays within angle and cost bounds and preserves every prefix’s token choice, satisfied margins, and protected-output tolerance. completion in candidates.json records costs before and after completion and whether it was applied. computation in report.json records compressed-output and original-validation call counts and timings by computation stage.

--max-new-tokens bounds generated tokens, including EOS. --context must accommodate the prompt plus that generation allowance. Omitting --cases generates symbolic problems using --count and --seed . Diagnosis uses the original template with thinking disabled. generate --thinking selects the thinking format.

The time budget starts with model loading after file acquisition and covers computation and attribution. The output directory contains manifest.json , status.json , baseline.json , candidates.json , report.json , and accepted proposal.json and attribution.json files. Reports record the model revision, input token paths, weight dtypes, hardware, measured validation values, and square-root and readout call counts. Status values are complete for completion, partial for budget expiration, and failed for execution errors.

A proposal contains either orthonormal plane vectors and a half-angle coordinate, or an orthonormal joint basis and a small orthogonal matrix. At runtime, the final hidden vector is rotated before multiplication by the original output matrix. In models with shared embeddings, rotation applies at readout calls. Reapplying an answer-repair proposal checks hashes for weights, configuration, and tokenizer files, plus the output-operation contract. generate --proposal reads proposal versions 1, 2, and 3.

#### Output-row attribution

--attribution-rows sets the number of output rows to report and defaults to 6. For each row, results include high-contribution coordinates, the loss after reverting that row’s edit, the total contribution sum, and integration error. Contributions follow the specified straight-line readout intervention path and retain negative values. Setting the option to 0 saves the generation proposal and validation results.

### Checkpoint export · export

export saves a new checkpoint with the proposal applied to the output matrix. It preserves original tensors and writes the edited lm_head.weight in FP32. It unties embedding and readout weights and saves configuration, execution graph, and shard index files. The output matrix uses CPU F64 block multiplication; original-model loading and contract checks use the shared model runtime. Run the exported model using its directory path.

cargo run --release -- export Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B \ --proposal " $LAPLACE_CACHE /edits/proposal.json " \ --out " $LAPLACE_CACHE /exports/qwen3-1.7b-edited " cargo run --release -- generate " $LAPLACE_CACHE /exports/qwen3-1.7b-edited " \ --prompt ' What is 2 + 2? Reply with the number only. '

materialization.json records the original revision and hashes, applied proposal, measured weight-change norm, and FP32 storage rounding e

# Infinix — Local Autonomous Agent for Windows and Linux

> ⚠️ Project Status: ABANDONED / BASE FOR COMMUNITY. This project is no longer actively maintained by the original creator. The codebase is released as an open-source foundation for anyone to fork, improve, modify, or build upon. The only requirement: your derivative work must also remain free and open-source (GPL-3.0).

> Original Creator: Moonyeep - Built with Manus AI, based on ZeroScript architecture

Infinix is a local autonomous AI agent for Windows and Linux, controlled through supported browser-based AI chats. Its local bridge provides endpoint diagnostics, workspace tools, browser automation, shell access under a selectable capability profile, and hierarchical multi-agent delegation. No separate model API key is required for browser providers.

## 📢 About This Project

This project was created by Moonyeep using Manus AI , built upon the ZeroScript architecture. The original creator has abandoned this project and is releasing it as an open-source base for the community.

Why release this?

- The project works but needs significant improvements

- Looking for capable developers to take this base and make it better

- Fork it, modify it, rebuild it - do whatever you want

- Only requirement: Your derivative work must remain FREE and OPEN-SOURCE (GPL-3.0)

- No commercial use without keeping it open-source

Roblox Studio is an optional integration. When enabled, Infinix can also control Studio through its MCP server; the general local agent does not require Roblox Studio.

Eight AI providers are supported: DeepSeek (chat.deepseek.com, recommended), ChatGPT (chatgpt.com), Google Gemini (gemini.google.com), Kimi (kimi.ai, Moonshot AI), GLM (chat.z.ai, Z.ai), Qwen (chat.qwen.ai), Arena (arena.ai, a multi-model playground) and Meta AI (meta.ai). On ChatGPT, screenshots and image input are turned off on purpose: the free tier limits files and images on a separate quota from messages, so vision would only work part of the day. Gemini and Kimi can be unstable: Gemini tends to stop using the Roblox tools in long sessions, and Kimi sometimes uses its own native tools instead of the Roblox commands. On Arena, use Direct mode (Infinix only supports Direct; it blocks Start in Battle / Side-by-Side / Agent modes). DeepSeek is the recommended provider.

> 💬 Discord community: Join here for help and discussions.

> Also known as: Free Claude Code alternative, Free Codex alternative, OpenClaw without API key, Infinix Roblox, Infinix free download, Roblox ChatGPT agent, Roblox DeepSeek agent, Roblox Gemini agent, Roblox Kimi agent, Roblox GLM agent, Roblox Qwen agent, Roblox Arena agent, Roblox Meta AI agent, Roblox Studio AI automation, Luau AI, MCP Roblox, lemonade alternative free, lemonade.gg alternative, free Roblox AI agent, free lemonade roblox alternative

## ⚠️ Infinix is Free Beware of Paid Copycats

Infinix is 100% free and open-source. It always has been, and it always will be. There is no official paid version, no subscription, and no sign-in required to use the extension.

If you come across a site or extension using the Infinix name that asks for payment or account creation, it is not this project. The only official links are the ones listed at the top of this README.

## How it works

AI chat in browser <-> Infinix Extension <-> local Bridge -> endpoint/workspace tools and optional MCP integrations (including Roblox Studio)

The extension runs inside a supported chat page and connects to the local bridge on the same PC. The bridge provides enabled local diagnostics, workspace and process tools; the extension provides browser automation. Roblox Studio is optional and its tools appear only when that integration is enabled.

## Multi-agent teams

The supervisor can delegate bounded tasks to providers authorized at startup. Each worker runs in an inactive tab in a minimized dedicated Infinix team window with a separate per-tab ToolRegistry, so provider pages do not take focus or remain visibly open. Workers use the Basic profile and read-only diagnostics/workspace tools, including source search and Git inspection; they do not inherit terminal access, browser control, file writes, remediation, or the supervisor's Amplo permissions. Delegating children requires explicit allow_children and is bounded by the session concurrency setting and a three-level depth limit. Spawn slots are reserved before asynchronous tab creation, preventing parallel requests from exceeding the configured limit. Worker startup can take up to two minutes before a handshake timeout, and status remains starting until the provider is ready. Tool results are returned through the same result envelope as other extension tools so the supervisor receives the assigned task ID, rather than an empty {} response. Supervisor/worker messages are routed through the local bridge with direct-parent/child checks; message retries are idempotent only when the original sender and content match. agent.team.status preserves its direct-child response by default and can optionally return include_descendants=true with a bounded hierarchy and state counts. Hidden tabs continue to run where the browser allows it, but browser or OS suspension can pause them.

Reliability requirements for slow provider startup, hidden-tab execution and bridge-mediated team messaging are tracked in MULTIAGENT_RELIABILITY_REQUIREMENTS.md ; some items still require implementation.

## Software development workflow

For repository work, the local agent can load root AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md guidance and common project manifests with workspace.context , search literal source text with workspace.search , and inspect local changes using git.status and bounded git.diff . File reads support bounded line ranges. The recommended flow is to inspect repository guidance and existing changes first, search call sites before editing, make focused changes, add targeted tests, run relevant checks, and review the resulting diff. These additions provide repository context and code navigation; worker agents remain read-only and should return findings/evidence to the supervisor.

Core regression tests: python3 -m unittest discover -q . Extension tests: run node over each zeroscript-extension/test-*.js file from the repository root.

## Reusable skills

The package includes 12 task skills for endpoint diagnostics, incident response, browser automation, software development, testing, study, secure downloads, Linux privileged operations, research, data analysis, administrative assistance and multi-agent delegation. See skills/INDEX.md . The agent should load only the relevant skill and references; these guides do not grant permissions or override the active profile.

## Setup

Linux is supported with Chrome/Chromium or Edge and the start_agent.sh launcher. The launcher automatically prepares Python dependencies; see INSTALL_LINUX.md.

On Linux, the Amplo session can use the terminal.run_as_admin tool when sudo is available. If needed, the OS desktop opens its askpass authentication dialog. Enter the password there—not in the chat. It is passed directly to sudo, never to the model or Infinix logs, and is not stored by Infinix; the system may cache sudo authorization until its normal timeout.

📺 Setup tutorial on YouTube covers every step below.

### 1. Download the zip and install the extension

Download the latest zip from the Releases page and extract it. The zip contains both the Bridge and the extension folder.

On Linux, Chrome/Chromium and Edge are supported. To load the extension:

- Go to edge://extensions (Edge) or chrome://extensions (Chrome)

- Enable Developer mode (top right toggle)

- Click Load unpacked

- Select the zeroscript-extension folder from the extracted zip

### 2. (Optional) Connect Roblox Studio

Open Studio and load a Place, then enable MCP (first time only):

- Click Assistant AI in the top bar

- Click ... (top right of the Assistant panel)

- Click Manage MCP Servers

- Click Enable Studio as MCP Server

Not sure where to find these options? The video tutorial shows exactly where to click.

### 3. Run the Bridge

Windows: double-click start.bat inside the extracted folder.

macOS: double-click MacOS_Start.command inside the extracted folder. The first time, macOS will show a security warning ("could not verify... free of malware") - this is normal for any script downloaded outside the App Store, click Done, then go to System Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll to the bottom, and click Open Anyway. You only need to do this once.

Linux: open a terminal in the extracted project folder and run chmod +x start_agent.sh (if needed), then ./start_agent.sh . It creates a local virtual environment, installs websockets, and downloads Python 3.12 into your user directories if the system only has an older Python (e.g. Ubuntu 20.04). It does not use sudo or change system packages. See INSTALL_LINUX.md.

Keep the terminal/window open while using Infinix. The General Agent does not require Roblox Studio; enable the Studio MCP server only when you want Roblox-specific tools.

### 4. Start a session

Go to https://chat.deepseek.com (recommended), https://chatgpt.com , https://gemini.google.com , https://www.kimi.ai , https://chat.z.ai , https://chat.qwen.ai , https://arena.ai or https://www.meta.ai and open a new chat. The Infinix bar appears above the input box. Click Start session. Type what you want to build.

Only works on chat.deepseek.com, chatgpt.com, gemini.google.com, kimi.ai, chat.z.ai, chat.qwen.ai, arena.ai and meta.ai - it will not work on any other site. On Arena, keep the mode dropdown on Direct - Infinix blocks Start in Battle / Side-by-Side / Agent modes (it only drives a single Direct reply). Gemini and Kimi can be unstable (model behavior, not the extension): Gemini may stop using the Roblox tools after a while, and Kimi may use its own native tools instead. If the AI starts answering in plain text instead of acting, remind it to use the commands or start a new session.

### 5. Watch the setup tutorial

Watch the setup tutorial on YouTube

## What the AI can do

- Read and edit scripts

- Run Luau code directly in Studio

- Inspect the game tree and instances

- Generate meshes, materials, and models

- Browse and insert from the Creator Store

- Control play-testing

- Remember your project across sessions (persistent project memory saved inside your place)

## New in 1.6.24

Autonomous Amplo session restored: the profile still shows two warnings at startup; after confirming both, diagnostics, scans, repairs, terminal commands, and authorized account actions run without per-action approval. Basic/Development keep their own prompts. The bridge does not bypass or auto-accept UAC/sudo.

## New in 1.6.23

- Local endpoint diagnostics: added bounded read-only tools for OS/architecture, processes, services, addresses/listeners, security status, recent events, startup entries and installed tools on Windows/Linux.

- Windows account incident snapshot: inventories local users, members of the built-in Administrators group, user profiles, CMD policy and command-redirection indicators without changing them; specifically helps distinguish an account from its Windows profile.

- Session-wide autonomy: after the two startup confirmations for the Amplo profile, diagnostics, scans, repairs, terminal commands and account-disable actions run without per-action approval. Basic/Development retain their configured prompts. A fixed Windows action can disable one confirmed local account by exact SID, refusing the current account, built-in -500, and the last verifiable enabled local administrator; it does not delete profiles or end existing sessions. The bridge never auto-elevates through UAC or sudo.

- Linux shell support: terminal.run now offers Bash/sh/zsh and installed PowerShell Core as the bridge user. Windows keeps CMD/PowerShell; command execution still follows the existing permission profile.

### The CLI-first AI coding agent runtime.

Pipe it, schedule it, embed it. One binary, any model, MCP-native — built for autonomous work, not just chat.

Website · Docs · Tap Registry · Benchmarks · Issues

Octomind is a CLI-first AI coding agent runtime. It gives an LLM real access to your repo — reading and writing files, running shells, searching code, delegating to sub-agents — through MCP tools. The same session engine works interactively , piped through stdin , as a background daemon , over WebSocket , or as an ACP sub-agent inside another agent's stack.

# Interactive octomind run developer:general # Piped — CI, scripts, automation echo " Explain the auth module " | octomind run developer:general --format plain # Daemon — keep it alive, talk to it from another terminal echo " watch the build " | octomind run --name watcher --daemon --format jsonl octomind send --name watcher " run the test suite "

## Why Octomind?

Most coding agents assume a human is watching the screen. Octomind is built for the work that keeps going after you leave.

- Policy as code, not approval popups. Deterministic guardrails — pre-call guards, post-result hooks, post-turn validators — live in TOML and scripts, so they work in CI, daemons, and scheduled runs.

- Proven on real PRs. It solved 24 of 25 held-out tasks at lower cost than the closest competitor. See the benchmarks .

- Ready-made specialists. octomind run developer:general pulls a packaged agent (prompt, model, MCP servers, tool permissions) from a tap . Publish your own with one repo.

- Sessions that stay sharp. Adaptive compression keeps long tasks moving while retaining task knowledge and the live exchange.

- Any model, any budget. Use Octomind Cloud or your own key (OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Ollama, and more), pick a model per role, and set spend thresholds per request and per session. A request over its threshold stops; at the session threshold a terminal session asks y/N before continuing, while a non-interactive octomind run stops with exit code 75.

- One config. Models, tools, roles, guardrails, budgets: all TOML, no framework code.

## Quick Start

1. Install (macOS, Linux):

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/muvon/octomind/master/install.sh | bash

On Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https: // raw.githubusercontent.com / muvon / octomind / master / install.ps1 | iex

On macOS, you can also install with Homebrew:

brew install muvon/tap/octomind

2. Get model access. The fastest path is Octomind Cloud, which includes models and needs no configuration:

octomind login

Prefer your own provider key? Skip login and export one (also OPENAI_API_KEY , ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , DEEPSEEK_API_KEY ), then follow Model access to point the config at it:

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY= " your_key "

3. Run a specialist in your project:

cd ~ /your/project octomind run developer:general

You're now in a session with an agent that can read your code, run commands, and edit files. The interface is a plain line prompt with markdown rendering — no TUI to learn, so it works over SSH, in tmux , and in CI logs. The first time you run a specialist, it may install its tools and ask for credentials.

> developer:general comes from the default tap muvon/tap , not your local config. Plain octomind run starts the config's default role, assistant:concierge .

Try the recorded bug-fix demo : two failing tests, an agent fix, and an independent test rerun.

## Benchmarks

Measured on octobench against 25 tasks harvested from merged pull requests across Python, PHP, Rust, C++, and JavaScript. Each agent works in the pre-fix repo; held-out tests from the merged fix decide pass or fail. These are the published July 30, 2026 results, not a measurement of this checkout.

- The harness matters. opencode used the same model and endpoint; octomind solved 24 vs 19 at roughly half the cost. All four agents ran stock invocations with no tuning, so this measures the whole harness, not individual features.

- Worst-case pricing, still ahead. glm-5.2 ran without prompt caching while Opus billed ~97% of context re-reads at cache rates — and octomind still led on solves, cost, and wall time.

- Reproducible. Per-case table, artifacts, and reproduction guide: BENCHMARK.md . Background: blog post .

## Guardrails: Policy as Code

Drop a .agents/guardrails.toml in your repo. The runtime enforces it deterministically, with no code to compile and no plugin to install.

# Pre-call deny — block a class of calls before they execute [[ guard ]] match = " shell(command=^rm \\ s+-rf?) " message = " rm -rf blocked. " # Conditional rule — only fires after the agent ran git status this session [[ guard ]] match = " shell(command=git push) " when = [ " +shell(command=git status) " ] message = " Review changes before pushing. "

Hook and validator script examples: Guardrails guide .

## Five Ways to Run It

The same session engine, exposed however your workflow needs it.

Need machine-readable results? Pass --schema schema.json to constrain the final response to a JSON Schema (requires a model with structured-output support). See Structured output .

## Features

### Specialists

octomind run developer:general # general dev, language skills auto-activate octomind run doctor:blood # blood-test interpretation specialist octomind run lawyer:sg # legal specialist

Running a specialist fetches its manifest from the tap registry, installs any required binaries, resolves credentials, starts the right MCP servers, and then opens the session.

Build and register your own:

octomind tap init yourteam/my-tap # scaffold, validate, git-init, and register locally octomind tap yourteam/my-tap # on another machine, after publishing to GitHub

The octomind- prefix is added automatically: yourteam/my-tap maps to the repository yourteam/octomind-my-tap .

## Installation

The install script detects your OS and architecture (Linux and macOS on x86_64/aarch64) and installs to ~/.local/bin/ . Pass --install-dir <DIR> or set OCTOMIND_INSTALL_DIR to override. On Windows (x86_64/aarch64), install.ps1 installs to %LOCALAPPDATA%\octomind\bin and adds it to your user PATH ; it honors OCTOMIND_INSTALL_DIR and OCTOMIND_VERSION too. install.sh still works from Git Bash or MSYS2.

Command not found? Add the install directory to your PATH :

export PATH= " $HOME /.local/bin: $PATH "

Building from source requires protoc ; see Building from source for per-OS prerequisites.

Verify:

octomind --version octomind config # generate the default config octomind run # start your first session

Shell completions: octomind completion <bash|zsh|fish|elvish|powershell> .

### Model access

Octomind Cloud — octomind login (device-code sign-in, like gh auth login ) stores a gateway key locally. The default config already uses octohub:auto . Learn more .

Bring your own key — set the provider's environment variable ( OPENROUTER_API_KEY , OPENAI_API_KEY , ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , DEEPSEEK_API_KEY , …) and point the model tables at it. The supervisor and compression profiles also default to octohub:auto , so update all three:

[ model ] name = " openrouter:google/gemini-2.5-flash " [ supervisor . model ] name = " openrouter:google/gemini-2.5-flash " [ compression . model ] name = " openrouter:google/gemini-2.5-flash "

Provider details and per-role overrides: Providers & models .

## Configuration

Config lives at ~/.local/share/octomind/config/config.toml on macOS and Linux, and under %LOCALAPPDATA%/octomind/config/ on Windows. Set OCTOMIND_DATA_DIR to override the data root.

octomind config --show # view current config octomind config --validate # validate config

Override any value for a single run with -c :

octomind run -c supervisor.enabled=false

Full reference: Configuration reference · Environment variables .

### Session commands

Full list: Session commands .

### Telemetry

Octomind reports anonymous usage: which commands, tools, and models are used, plus timings, token counts, and error kinds. It never sends your code, prompts, file paths, tool arguments, or environment values. Opt out in any of three ways:

export DO_NOT_TRACK=1 # the cross-tool standard, honored first export OCTOMIND_TELEMETRY=0 # for subsequent commands in this shell # or set `telemetry = false` in config.toml

Exact field list: Telemetry .

## Documentation

Full index: doc/README.md · Hosted: octomind.run/docs .

## Contributing

The most impactful contribution isn't code — it's specialist agents. A cardiologist publishing doctor:medications . A tax attorney publishing lawyer:us . A security researcher publishing security:owasp . One TOML file, and everyone facing that problem gets a specialist-grade AI.

- How to write a tap agent

- Open issues

Code contributions are welcome too. Set up the hooks and run the gate before you push:

pip install pre-commit && pre-commit install make dev # fmt + clippy + test

Commits follow Conventional Commits . Full guide, architecture overview, and code conventions: CONTRIBUTING.md · internals: Architecture .

Community participation follows our Code of Conduct . Report vulnerabilities privately using the security policy .

## License

Apache License 2.0 — see LICENSE .

https://github.com/Ninnix/lokey.markdown:
Lokey is an Android keyboard with local word prediction, dictation and translation. The models run on your phone. Writing a message does not require an account, a subscription or a connection to an inference service.

The keyboard is native Kotlin and Android Canvas, with a C11 bridge to the inference runtimes. It supports 39 languages , eleven keyboard families, and a few small models chosen for work that belongs on a phone.

## Screenshots

## What you can do

- Get up to three complete-word suggestions, ranked from model probabilities.

- Hold Enter to dictate; slide up to keep recording or left to cancel.

- Translate into another app's text field with LFM or Qwen, using the same text model that supplies prediction and autocorrection.

- Use native script layouts, accent menus and bundled input converters.

- Change key colors, save designs, create layouts, and choose recorded switch sounds and haptic feedback.

- Keep copied text in a local clipboard, with pinning and deletion controls.

Swipe typing, adaptive letters and autocorrection are optional and start off. Keyboard height starts at 100%. Settings you have already chosen are preserved.

## Start here

Lokey requires Android 9 or later and an ARM64 device . Download the signed APK from Releases , open Lokey, and follow setup to enable and select the keyboard. Choose your language and download the models you want. Ordinary keyboard input works without downloading a model.

The interface follows Android's language setting. Android 13 and later also provide a separate app-language setting. Keyboard layout and model language remain separate choices. See supported languages .

## Models

Lokey uses one active text model for prediction, autocorrection and translation, and one speech model for dictation. An LFM-only installation uses LFM for all three text functions; Qwen is not required. Automatic chooses this pair for your language and hardware. Supported Qualcomm Hexagon devices can use the NPU; CPU execution remains available. Model files are downloaded separately from the app.

MODELS.md explains selection, formats, memory reuse and limits.

## Build

Use JDK 17 or later, Android SDK 37, NDK 28.2.13676358 and CMake 3.31.6.

./gradlew :app:assembleDebug

The APK is written to app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk . The build guide covers runtime checkouts and optional Hexagon support. The release guide covers signing and distribution.

## Privacy

Prediction, translation and speech recognition run locally. The app has no advertising or analytics SDK. Clipboard history, settings, custom designs and speed-test records use Android's private app storage.

Model downloads contact Hugging Face and its delivery providers, which receive network request information such as your IP address. Text and microphone audio are not part of those requests. Opening an external link or sharing a result uses the app you choose.

Read the privacy policy and the developer Data Safety disclosure .

## Status and documentation

Lokey is beta software. Device checks cover the OnePlus 15 and POCO F3; performance and model quality vary with the phone and language. Interface translations still need full native-speaker review.

- Keyboard use and customization

- Supported languages

- Language and keyboard mapping

- Models and inference

- Building , testing , and releasing

# BRACE

BRACE provides small, domain-specific verifiers for developers who need checked computations and repair previews. Each domain declares its supported inputs, acceptance rules and work limits. It returns a checked result or an explicit refusal. Direct code handles work the contract already determines; the integer harness also accepts proposals from an AI or another program.

At an input of 2, 2 + 2 and 2 × 2 both give 4 . In the PAT example, a mislabeled lesson proposes addition when the instruction calls for multiplication. A check on the final number alone would pass. BRACE records different-operation and withholds the answer. Run the PAT example

## Available now

The first five commands run offline with Python 3.12 or later and the standard library. No model download or account is required. Research replays also document their own assumptions and budgets; they are not a general reasoning guarantee.

The new connector command independently checks which mapping was selected , then binds that choice to the exact source and target before building and auditing the complete patch. A correct conversion alone cannot establish that the right mapping was chosen. The example suite produces 14 checked mappings, two verified no-matches and two refusals. It applies no changes.

Connector contract and runnable CLI · How bounded domains fit together

## Propose, repair, accept and reuse

The composition example supplies a wrong identity plan for four squaring examples. A full check rejects it; bounded deterministic repair finds square on the second check. A separate host action accepts that checked draft as Fold . After accepting Nudge as add1 , the host can request do Nudge then Fold , check the ordered plan and explicitly save it as Lift .

Reopening independently rechecks all saved lessons. Reusing Lift on fresh examples requires another check; reversing the named order is withheld without changing the lessons. The one-command demo also rehearses rollback and a bounded clarification. It uses disposable synthetic storage and no model calls.

A checked lesson means the plan matches its supplied observations. Reuse requires new expected outputs; it does not establish an unrestricted learned rule or certify unknown predictions. The host owns acceptance, observations and storage. The CLI accepts structured events, not unrestricted chat.

To inspect captured outcomes, the optional receipt inspector finds the latest two records matching an exact action, status and decision. It returns original request/receipt text with source identity and event positions. Scan is the default; cache and index options are explicit. Unsupported captures receive a structured refusal. This is a read-only evidence viewer, not another checker or a lesson-acceptance path.

## From conversation to checked arithmetic

A caller says, “The counter reads 13. Bump it up by 4, then triple the new reading.” Reverse those last two operations and the answer changes from 51 to 43 . Qwen 2.5 0.5B submitted the same calculation both times. BRACE verified the submitted arithmetic both times. What evidence would justify accepting the model’s interpretation?

In an initial trial, Qwen alone answered 1 of 8 clear requests correctly. Having Qwen translate the request and handing off the arithmetic raised that to 4 of 8 . The backend answered 8 of 8 when given the intended inputs. On a fresh set, a stricter reader prevented all 11 wrong or unwarranted releases, but it also withheld all eight clear requests. You can reproduce both results and try confirming or correcting a handoff yourself. Run the handoff experiment

An exploratory replay on those same 16 conversations suggested interrupting only on an explicit conflict. On a subsequent, preregistered test of 32 new conversations , the verifier could not resolve any of them. It sent no conflict notices. The reminder alone and the conflict-only policy both got 8 of 16 clear requests right and released 20 wrong or unwarranted numbers overall. See the prospective test and replay

A follow-up rule asked which operation came first in the original bonus example, then missed all eight fresh cases with the same ambiguity. A separate probe showed why the handoff matters. The reader dropped one of two requested additions, and BRACE correctly checked the shortened calculation. See the missing-order trial and counterexample

## Where BRACE fits

- Require a check before using an answer. Route the task through run_bound and let the host application release the value only when outcome.status == "checked" . The application must own that release path. The proposer adapter runs as trusted Python code.

- Offer a check when an AI asks for one. Expose the same call as a tool. The caller can inspect the receipts, revise a rejected step and submit it again under the host's retry policy. Skipping the call produces no BRACE verdict.

The integer API supports adding an integer and then multiplying by an integer. It can do the arithmetic directly. Plugging in your own proposer lets you measure which steps it gets wrong and whether a retry helps. BRACE checks the operation and five witness values, and the second step must cite the receipt for the accepted first step. The connector profile uses a direct selector because it outperformed the model in the bounded comparison. These are separate domain APIs; a new task type needs its own contract and checker.

The connector experiment asks whether the caller requested the action that passed the technical check. Its offline replay includes a valid patch preview for a request the caller explicitly excluded. You can reproduce the failure and inspect the evidence. Try the connector replay

## Run the harness

From this directory, use Python 3.12 or later. The built-in demo and tests run offline using the standard library.

python -B demo.py --json python -B -m unittest -q test_harness

The demo runs Start with 3. Add 1, then double the result. It tries a wrong operation first at each step. Four checks yield the final value 8 . Changing Start to Begin returns unsupported-input . The suite covers 18 cases. Demo · Tests

Both operands may be negative. For Start with 6. Add -11, then multiply by -3. , the checked values are -5 after addition and 15 after multiplication.

## Write a proposer

Extract the release and put your script beside harness.py . Import Candidate , Reply , encoded , and run_bound from harness . Call run_bound(instruction.encode("utf-8"), adapter) . The host calls your trusted synchronous Python function adapter(ticket, view) for each step.

Return Reply(ticket.ticket_id, (Candidate(encoded(payload)),)) to submit one candidate. Build payload as a Python dictionary with exactly these nine keys.

Candidate IDs accept 1–64 ASCII letters, digits, underscores, periods, or hyphens. Coefficients, witness outputs, and results must be integers with absolute value at most 10**15 . The returned outcome exposes outcome.status , outcome.value , and outcome.receipts . Each receipt has a step , verdict , and value . A successful two-step run has status checked and a checked receipt for each step.

## Try PAT as a proposer

Download and unzip BRACE-Harness and PAT into the same parent directory. From inside BRACE-Harness-main , run these commands with Python 3.12 or later. If your PAT directory has another name, pass its path to --pat .

python -m pip install " numpy>=1.24 " python -B examples/pat/demo.py --pat ../PAT-main

Each case starts with its own in-memory PAT lessons. In the first case PAT recalls “multiplying” as multiplication and BRACE releases 4 . In the second case that word was deliberately labeled addition. At an input of 2, both adding 2 and multiplying by 2 give 4. BRACE returns different-operation and withholds the answer. On one retry, the adapter excludes addition only at the rejected step. PAT recalls “doubling,” BRACE rechecks both steps and releases 4 . The original lesson is still available afterward.

In the third case PAT recalls multiplication correctly, and the demo deliberately changes the reported result from 4 to 5 . BRACE returns wrong-result and withholds the answer. On one retry, the adapter takes the rejected draft and recalculates 2 × 2 from its original coefficients and the checked input. BRACE releases 4 . The demo compares both submitted drafts and verifies that the lesson, operation, operand and five witness values match. The new run has its own run ID and first-step receipt.

The fourth case gives the whole request one retry. PAT recalls “adding” as multiplication, so step one proposes 1 × 1 = 1 . BRACE returns different-operation and stops before step two. On retry, PAT recalls an alternative lesson, “sum,” and BRACE checks 1 + 1 = 2 . Step two now runs for the first time. It proposes multiplication but reports 5 for 2 × 2 . BRACE returns wrong-result . The retry is spent, so the final answer is withheld.

The example submits one candidate per step. The correct case spends two checks, each single-fault case spends four, and the two-fault case spends three. After NumPy and both repositories are available, the example runs offline. Adapter · Runnable example

## Research examples

- Learning a domain from observations. BRACE learned local action meanings and requested measurements to test them. With the same finite rule family and 38 readings, choosing inputs where rules disagreed yielded 114 correct fresh answers versus 55 from the next integer. Two errors remained when the true rule was absent, and selection required more internal computation. Domain induction and transfer · Missing-setting repair · Choosing the next observation

- Repeated additions. A consecutive-integer detector flagged 22 of 24 fresh cases involving possible repeated additions and 6 of 8 outside controls. A later reader linked both amounts to their event text on 4 of 18 relevant requests, including a penalty that had been copied into a second record. Repeat detection · Event attachment and replay

- Bracket geometry. Two measured marks admit two possible tip positions, 96 drawing units apart. Reveal the third mark to distinguish them. Open the viewer locally or run python -I -S -B preview/verify.py to check the coordinates. Bracket viewer

- Task handoff. The experimental reader completed 25 of 36 connector requests. It still checked a URL that the user mentioned only as an example. The trial includes all wordings and an offline replay. Delivery experiment

- Which request did the caller mean? When one API error fits three routes and a tool can only check two, it can ask which action the caller meant. Compare two readers on “this request,” “another request,” and replies that mention multiple actions. Run python -I -S -B research/connector-clarification/comparison.py . Connector clarification example
