https://github.com/devHaitham481/anamnes.markdown:
Never lose an AI conversation again. Every conversation with every AI tool, kept on your computer and searchable by all of them.

AI tools forget. Claude Code deletes sessions after 30 days, and none of your tools knows what you worked out in the others. Anamnesis keeps a permanent, word-for-word archive of all of them on your computer and gives it back to every tool over MCP . Ask Claude Code "what did we decide about auth?" and it finds the answer, even if you worked it out in ChatGPT months ago.

- Keeps every conversation, even after the tool itself deleted it.

- Collects in the background, from the history your tools already write.

- Searches by keyword and meaning, locally, in about a tenth of a second.

- Stays yours: local SQLite and a small local model. No account, no API keys, no telemetry. It never calls an AI model itself.

> Anamnesis (Greek ἀνάμνησις) means "recollection": in Plato, learning as remembering what you already knew; in medicine, a patient's history, taken so nobody starts from scratch.

## Install

curl -LsSf https://devhaitham481.github.io/anamnesis/install.sh | sh

macOS or Linux (Windows: WSL). Nothing to preinstall: the script brings its own Python via uv , then runs anam setup , which finds your AI tools, archives their history, and asks before it connects them or changes anything. Then restart your AI tools. That's it.

Without the script: uv tool install anamnesis-cli (or pipx install anamnesis-cli ), then anam setup .

Update: run the install command again; setup is safe to re-run.

Uninstall:

anam disconnect all # remove Anamnesis from your AI tools' configs uv tool uninstall anamnesis-cli rm -rf ~ /.anamnesis # your memory; skip this to keep it

Troubleshooting

- anam: command not found : open a new terminal.

- A tool doesn't use the memory: restart it. If anam status shows it as outdated , run anam setup .

- Semantic search is off: the 70 MB model downloads on first run and needs internet once. Keyword search always works.

## Using it

Just keep working. Connected tools archive new conversations in the background and search the memory when earlier work comes up.

anam status # what's archived per tool, and what's missing anam auth decision # search from the shell anam # browse everything in the terminal (vim keys, / to filter) anam import chatgpt.zip # add a ChatGPT, claude.ai or Gemini export anam keep # stop Claude Code deleting sessions after 30 days

Only what you and the assistant said is kept; tool output, reasoning and injected system context are skipped. Re-importing is safe.

## In claude.ai, ChatGPT and on your phone

Web apps can't reach your laptop, so you run a node : your own always-on copy of the memory, on a server you control. There is no Anamnesis cloud. It also keeps your computers in sync.

anam node deploy fly # 1. deploy once and link this computer (or Docker, below) anam node link https://your-node # 2. on each other computer; you choose what it uploads anam connect claude-web # 3. prints the steps (also: chatgpt-web)

In the app you add https://your-node/mcp as a custom connector and sign in with the node password (needs a paid claude.ai or ChatGPT plan; Gemini doesn't support connectors). anam node status and anam node activity show who used it; anam node revoke cuts an app off.

Any server with Docker (VPS, NAS, home server); point a domain at it first:

curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/devHaitham481/anamnesis/main/docker-compose.yml printf ' ANAMNESIS_DOMAIN=memory.example.com\nANAMNESIS_NODE_PASSWORD=%s\n ' " $( openssl rand -base64 18 ) " > .env docker compose up -d # HTTPS via Caddy

- Security: HTTPS plus end-to-end encryption (AES-256-GCM) of synced data, with a key only your computers and your node hold. Apps get revocable OAuth tokens, never the password. Wrong passwords are rate-limited.

- Cost: one small machine. On Fly.io: 1 shared CPU, 1 GB memory and volume, stopped when idle.

- Updates: docker compose pull && docker compose up -d , or re-run anam node deploy fly --app <name> .

anam share on the first computer prints a pairing code; anam join <code> on the others. The default folder is iCloud Drive/Anamnesis ; pass a path for Dropbox, Syncthing or anything else. Everything in it is end-to-end encrypted.

## Reference

anam setup guided setup; safe to re-run anam terminal memory browser anam QUERY | search QUERY search from the shell [--source chatgpt] anam status archive per tool, what's missing, connected tools anam sync [--watch] import new local history now (or keep watching) anam import FILE... import ChatGPT / claude.ai / Gemini Takeout exports anam keep stop Claude Code deleting its sessions after 30 days anam connect [TOOL|all] claude-code, claude-desktop, cursor, gemini-cli, codex anam disconnect TOOL|all anam share | join | devices | unshare sync computers through a folder anam node deploy fly | link URL | status | activity | revoke | scope | wipe anam connect claude-web use your memory in claude.ai (also chatgpt-web) anam mcp the MCP server (connected tools start it for you)

connect merges into each tool's config and writes a .bak first. MCP tools: search_memory , recent_conversations , get_conversation , remember .

anam-web , then open http://127.0.0.1:8000 . Endpoints: GET /api/sources , /api/threads , /api/threads/{id}/messages , /api/search?q=&source= , PATCH / DELETE /api/threads/{id} , and WS /ws for live updates. To reach it from other devices, set ANAMNESIS_HOST=0.0.0.0 , ANAMNESIS_ALLOWED_HOSTS and ANAMNESIS_AUTH_TOKEN .

Nothing needs configuring. Settings come from the environment or .env (see .env.example ). Data and logs live in ~/.anamnesis .

## Contributing

Issues and PRs are welcome, especially importers for tools that aren't covered yet (Antigravity, Cursor's agent CLI).

git clone https://github.com/devHaitham481/anamnesis && cd anamnesis uv venv -p 3.13 .venv && uv pip install -p .venv -e " .[dev] " .venv/bin/pytest -q && .venv/bin/ruff check . && .venv/bin/mypy src

Code is in src/anamnesis/ : ingest/ (one parser per tool), memory_mcp/ , core/ (storage, search, sync), node/ , cli/ and web/ .

MIT

# Smart Node

smart-node.app · by Dmytro Klymentiev ( GitHub )

Smart Node installs a self-hosted AI node: one machine you control, running an AI assistant together with the pieces it needs to be useful. Task and objective tracking, a document store, semantic memory, a gateway that fronts your model provider, an operator panel, and live voice in the browser.

One thing to be clear about before you read further: self-hosted here means the application and your data, not the model. The node runs on your machine and its documents and memory stay there. Reasoning currently uses a cloud model through Anthropic, Google, or OpenRouter, and the node needs credentials for the provider you choose. Running a model on the node itself is not supported today.

It is bash and Docker. This repository carries the source of every component, so one clone is everything you need. Nothing has to be built first: point a single command at a machine and wait about half an hour.

## What works today

- A clean install on a Debian or Ubuntu target, either in a local LXC container or on an existing machine.

- The operator panel, Studio, planner, documents, memory, browser voice, and the model gateway.

- Email, Telegram, Slack, web chat, and browser voice channels. Google Calendar and Drive are partial; WhatsApp, SMS, and arbitrary integrations are not turnkey features.

- More than 200 install-time validation checks, plus source and component tests in this repository.

## What does not work yet

- No one outside the maintainer's team has completed this repository's install runbook yet. Treat the current path as testable software, not a polished appliance, and please report every undocumented step.

- A clean install creates the configurator agent, but no business-specific agents or workflows. The configurator helps create those after first login.

- There is no one-command updater, automatic migration runner, scheduled backup, offline install, local-model runtime, or supported degraded/offline mode.

- It is not an autonomous company. Actions still depend on the permissions, approvals, integrations, and instructions you configure.

## Quick start

git clone https://github.com/dklymentiev/smart-node.git cd smart-node # Check the controller before changing anything. tools/preflight.sh --provider lxd-local # Create a local LXC and install a node into it. sudo orchestrator/install-on.sh \ --provider lxd-local \ --name < name > --ip < ip > --ssh-key < key.pub > \ --node-fqdn < name > .localhost --node-domain < name > .localhost --no-vpn \ --all --setup-via-token

--node-domain gives Studio its address; without it the install ends with an error after every check has passed. <name>.localhost is right for a node you use from this machine (Studio is then http://studio.<name>.localhost/ ); a node on a real domain is described in docs/public-domain.md .

The installer asks one question first: how your AI will work, with a Claude subscription or with an API key (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter or your own address). It installs what that needs; --ai agent-runtimes or --ai key answers it on the command line.

### Or in a browser

sudo python3 tools/web-install/server.py -- \ --provider lxd-local --name < name > --ip < ip > --ssh-key < key.pub > --setup-via-token

It prints an address on 127.0.0.1 with a one-time key in it. Open it: the page asks the same question, lets you choose what to install (Simple, Full or Custom), shows each step with the installer's own output beside it, can stop the install, and opens Studio when it is done. It runs the same installer; it has been walked through on a local install, and the terminal way above is the one tested on a server of your own.

For a node on your own computer, Windows with WSL included, see A node on your own computer . For a machine you already have, run the matching preflight and pass --provider existing --ssh-user <user> instead. Nothing is created in that mode; the installer configures the target you name.

--all runs every install layer and ends with validation. In an interactive terminal it pauses after installing the agent runtime and asks you to authorize your own Claude account. Without that authorization the command waits at the prompt and does not reach final validation. Complete the prompt, or cancel it with Ctrl-C ; cancellation leaves Claude deferred, continues the install, and you can connect it later in Studio -> AI Gateway -> Connect .

The installer ends with Studio's first-run link. Open it: it creates the owner, shows your password once (save it; you change it later in Settings), connects your AI and sets up your first assistant. Model and channel credentials can also be supplied at install time; orchestrator/install-on.sh --help lists the supported flags.

Read the source-install runbook before using a machine that matters. It includes prerequisites, verification, and channel setup rather than hiding those details behind the short example above.

## How it works

install-on.sh runs from your machine and drives the target over SSH. It creates or takes the machine, hardens the host, lays down the core in six stages, brings up twelve components in dependency order, applies the declared permission list, and then runs more than 200 checks before it says it is done.

If a check fails, the install fails. Nothing is reported healthy that has not been verified.

## Documentation

docs/README.md is the way in: what to read first, and what to do in the first hour after an install finishes, which is where a node goes from running to actually working.

docs/node/ is the set that also ships INTO the node, where its agents read it: what the machine is made of, the exact call to change each part, and what each moving part is called. It is written for an agent, which makes it the densest description of the system for a human too. Each file carries the core version it was checked against.

docs/install-from-source.md is the full runbook: prerequisites, building each image, what to verify, what not to improvise.

docs/public-domain.md covers putting a node on a domain the outside world can reach. That part is still manual, and doing it from memory has broken nodes quietly enough that it is worth reading first.

Three runbooks cover the day after installation: backup , restore and update . Backup and restore have been run end to end on a throwaway node and corrected from what that found; update has not. Each says which at the top. Do the drill yourself before you rely on any of them on a machine that matters.

SECURITY.md explains what an agent can and cannot do to the node it runs on, and says plainly which limits are enforced by the operating system and which are not.

NOTICE.md lists every component vendored here with its origin and licence. Read it before editing a component: the copy in this tree is a pinned snapshot, not that component's home.

CONTRIBUTING.md covers builds, conventions and how to propose a change.

On the node itself, sn-version reports what is actually running rather than what was meant to be, hashes it into a fingerprint, and pins it. sn-version check tells you when a node has drifted from that pin.

## Providers

--provider lxd-local creates a local LXC container and installs into it. Good for a self-contained node on a single Ubuntu host with LXD.

--provider existing takes a machine you already have, whether bare metal, a VPS, or a container you made yourself. Nothing is created; the installer configures what you point it at.

## Known limits

There is no one-command updater or automatic migration runner. docs/runbook-update.md describes the current operator procedure. It is a procedure, not a product feature.

Putting a node on a public domain is a manual procedure. It is documented, but not automated.

# Pintura – Slides in plain text

A presentation is a folder of YAML files, and your browser shows it live as you or your agent edit them. Pintura checks every slide for what a reviewer would catch, such as text spilling out of its box or a title sitting lower than on the other slides. When the deck is ready, it exports to PowerPoint as a deck people keep working in, with real layouts, theme colors and fonts, and native charts and tables.

## How it works

A presentation is a folder:

presentation.yaml the name, the theme, and the slides in order slides/revenue.yaml one file per slide charts/revenue-by-segment.yaml a chart's type and style charts/segment-revenue.csv its data

A slide picks a layout from the theme and places elements on it:

# slides/revenue.yaml layout : content title : Connectivity revenue nearly tripled in two years elements : - id : chart chart : revenue-by-segment frame : left - id : total text : | Total revenue of **$18.7B** in 2025, up 33% on 2024. frame : [490, 290, 430, 80]

# charts/revenue-by-segment.yaml type : stacked_column style : minimal data : segment-revenue.csv data_labels : { format: billions_of_dollars }

segment , 2023 , 2024 , 2025 Space , 3557 , 3796 , 4086 Connectivity , 3869 , 7599 , 11387 AI , 2961 , 2620 , 3201

frame: left names an area the theme's layout defines, and style: minimal a chart style in the theme; the slide says what things are, and the theme decides how they look. Units are points.

## Install

On macOS or Linux:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/editide/pintura/main/install.sh | sh

On Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https: // raw.githubusercontent.com / editide / pintura / main / install.ps1 | iex

Each release carries its own runtime, so nothing else needs installing. Screenshots and checks draw slides in an installed Edge or Chrome, or fetch a headless Chromium the first time they need one.

To try the example, clone this repository and open it:

git clone https://github.com/editide/pintura.git pintura pintura/presentations/example

### With a coding agent

Paste this into Claude Code or another coding agent, from the folder where you want your presentations to live:

Install Pintura from https://github.com/editide/pintura by running its installer: on macOS or Linux, `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/editide/pintura/main/install.sh | sh`; on Windows, `irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/editide/pintura/main/install.ps1 | iex`. Read `pintura --docs`, then the topics it lists as you need them.

## Start

Every command takes the presentation's folder as a path, here my-deck in the current folder:

pintura --new my-deck # creates the folder, with the default theme copied in pintura my-deck # the live preview, in your browser pintura my-deck --check # what to fix, slide by slide pintura my-deck --screenshot all # every slide on one PNG pintura --docs # the format, one topic at a time

It is built for agents: an agent edits the files and runs --check and --screenshot to see its work, and you review in the browser. There, dragging, resizing, and rewording write the same small diff to the files an agent would, and comments pinned to a slide wait for the agent to act on.

## Export to PowerPoint

Export runs on editide's API and needs an API key, free to create at app.editide.com/dashboard/keys :

pintura --login pintura my-deck --export my-deck.pptx

Everything else, the preview, checks, screenshots, and the HTML and PDF exports included, runs on your machine with no account.

## The idea

- The agent in the terminal edits files; the browser shows the presentation and redraws on every save.

- Slides name what things are (a title, a caption, a positive number), and styles in the theme decide how they look.

- Numbers are typed, read from CSV, or linked to Libreta books, so a changed fact updates every slide that shows it.

- The mouse handles what a mouse is good at: nudging, resizing, rewording. Each of those writes the same one-line diff an agent would.

## Where it comes from

What's in a PowerPoint file? starts with a folder of text files describing a presentation, then shows that a .pptx has the same architecture buried under 5,000 pages of XML. Pintura is that folder made real: presentation.yaml for the presentation properties, slides/ , media/ , charts/ , with CSV and Libreta books in place of embedded Excel files. Everything the blog calls a minefield (inheritance you can't see, element ordering, defaults that live only inside PowerPoint.exe) is what the format is designed to avoid.

## Documents

- Format : one topic per file, as pintura --docs prints them.

- Principles : the rules the design is judged against.

- Architecture : the object model, the pipeline, and how the export lines up with PowerPoint's objects.

- Running Pintura : the preview server and the headless commands.

## Vocabulary

- presentation : a folder holding presentation.yaml , an ordered list of slides on one theme; it exports to one .pptx .

- theme : a folder holding theme.yaml (colors, fonts, the title, and areas), styles.yaml , and its layouts; the equivalent of a .potx .

- layout : a named variation on the theme: a different title, extra placeholders, areas, or background, and the elements, such as a logo or the slide number, drawn on every slide using it.

- placeholder : text whose position and style a layout owns and whose words each slide writes; the title is the one nearly every layout has.

- area : a named rectangle on a theme or layout that elements take as their frame.

- field : a value the presentation fills into text, such as ${slide} or ${footer} .

- slide : a file under slides/ that picks a layout, writes its title and placeholders, and adds elements.

- element : one thing on a slide or layout: text, shape, line, arc, picture, chart, or table.

- style : a named set of text, table, or chart properties, such as caption or positive , defined in the theme's styles.yaml .

## Changing Pintura

Clone the repository and install the .NET 10 SDK ; on WSL, install the Linux SDK inside the distribution and never build with dotnet.exe , since it builds on the Windows side, where file locks, processes and ports are out of WSL's reach. Run from source with dotnet watch , which reloads presentations, the page and C# as you edit:

dotnet watch --project src/Pintura run -- presentations/example

dotnet test src/Pintura.Tests runs the C# tests, and node --test src/Pintura.Tests/*.js the page's. ./scripts/install-from-source.sh makes your build the pintura on PATH , and the installer puts a release back. On WSL, ./scripts/install-windows-from-wsl.sh [folder] publishes your build for Windows to %USERPROFILE%\dev , or the folder given, for Windows apps that can't reach WSL. AGENTS.md holds the vocabulary and conventions, for people and coding agents alike.

## Status

Early. Issues are welcome; there are no promises on timing. See CONTRIBUTING.md before opening a pull request.

Animations, transitions, SmartArt, video and audio, 3-D, ink, embedded objects, macros, and custom geometry are out of scope. A deck that needs them is a deck for PowerPoint.

## License

Apache-2.0; see LICENSE and NOTICE . Use it freely, commercially included. If Pintura is useful to you or your business, a mention of editide is appreciated.

## Authorship

Built by the team behind editide . Our thesis is that agents work better on plain text than generating code for outdated file formats like OOXML. Pintura applies that to slides, as Libreta does to spreadsheets.

# perfectclone: website cloner that copies the real site, 1:1

Pull the real frontend of any public site in ~15 seconds. No AI, no tokens.

perfectclone clones any website 1:1. It crawls the site with a real browser (Playwright), downloads the site's own HTML, JavaScript, CSS, fonts and images, and gives you a folder you can serve, edit and deploy. Then it lets you rebrand it, rehost it and strip the original owner's trackers without breaking it, including Next.js sites that hydrate on load.

pip install perfectclone perfectclone clone example.com perfectclone serve example.com # → http://localhost:8000

That's it. Chromium is downloaded automatically the first time you clone. Requires Python 3.10+.

Or try it without installing anything, using uv :

uvx perfectclone clone example.com

## Why not an AI cloner?

Most "clone any website" tools today regenerate the site: an AI agent looks at screenshots or scraped markup, writes a new React/Next.js app, and compares the result against the original with a visual-similarity score until it's close enough. That gets you a lookalike. The code is new, the behaviour is approximate, and there are always gaps.

perfectclone doesn't regenerate anything. It mirrors the bytes the site actually serves, so the clone is the site: same markup, same bundles, same animations, same JavaScript running. Sometimes the real solution is the simple one.

## Tested on real sites

Each card is one site split down the middle: the live site on the left, the clone on the right.

scripts/compat.py clones each site, serves the copy, and compares its home page with the live one at 1440×900, with animations and videos paused on the same frame:

Every clone loaded with zero requests to trackers. Run it yourself with python scripts/compat.py , and please open an issue for any site that doesn't come out right.

## Commands

perfectclone clone < url > [-o out] [--max-pages 200] [--extract] [--keep-trackers] [--ignore-robots] perfectclone serve < site > [-p 8000] perfectclone replace < site > < old > < new > [--exact-case] [--substring] perfectclone rehost < site > < old-origin > < new-origin > perfectclone strip-trackers < site >

- clone writes out/site/ (the working copy) and out/manifest.json (pages, failures, third-party hosts the site uses). --extract also saves each page's text, metadata (headings, links, images, forms, JSON-LD) and a full-page screenshot to out/extract/ . Trackers are stripped by default.

- replace renames text everywhere: HTML, JS, CSS, JSON, SVG. It also handles the UPPER, lower and Capitalized variants, and leaves URLs and asset paths alone so nothing 404s.

- rehost points canonical, Open Graph, JSON-LD and sitemap URLs at your domain.

- serve works like a static host: clean URLs ( /about → /about/index.html ), and /_next/image requests are served from the mirrored originals.

Rebrand a clone and put it online:

perfectclone clone acme.com -o acme perfectclone replace acme " Acme " " Globex " perfectclone rehost acme https://acme.com https://globex.com npx netlify-cli deploy --dir acme/site --prod # or any static host

## How it works

- Crawl with a real browser. Each page is rendered in Chromium and scrolled to the bottom, and every response is recorded. That catches what static mirrors miss: code-split JS chunks, fonts requested from CSS, images behind lazy loading. Links are followed breadth-first, seeded from the sitemap. robots.txt is respected unless you pass --ignore-robots .

- Mirror the server's bytes. Pages are saved as the HTML the server sends, not the rendered DOM, because that's what the site's JavaScript expects to hydrate. Assets keep their URL paths, and CSS/JS are scanned for further references ( url() , srcset , chunk paths) until nothing new turns up.

- Edit without breaking hydration. A Next.js App Router page ships its HTML and a serialized copy of the React tree in self.__next_f.push(...) script chunks. Change one and not the other, and React throws a hydration error and re-renders from the payload, undoing your edit. perfectclone decodes the payload stream, edits it row by row, recomputes the UTF-8 byte lengths of length-prefixed text rows ( <id>:T<hex>,… ), rejoins rows that span chunks, and writes it back next to the matching HTML edit.

- Strip trackers. Google Analytics/Tag Manager, the Meta pixel, LinkedIn Insight, Hotjar, Clarity, Segment, PostHog, HubSpot, TikTok, Reddit, X, Cloudflare Web Analytics, RB2B and more. They're removed from <script> / <noscript> tags, from preload hints, and from Next.js next/script elements that only exist in the payload.

## Limits

- No backend. Forms, logins, search and API calls still go to the original servers (or fail). perfectclone copies the front end.

- Next.js client-side navigation needs each page's RSC payload answered for ?_rsc= requests. perfectclone mirrors them and perfectclone serve routes them. On a plain static host, internal links fall back to full page loads: everything still works, just without the instant transitions.

- Chunks that are only requested after a click (say, a modal's code) are captured if the crawl triggered them or a bundle names them as a string. A bundle can also assemble a chunk URL at runtime, and that one may be missed.

- Bot protection (CAPTCHAs, aggressive Cloudflare rules) can block the crawl. perfectclone does not try to get around it.

- Embeds (YouTube, Cal.com, maps) and third-party CDNs keep loading from their own hosts.

## Roadmap

Clone apps behind a login, like dashboards. Today perfectclone sees what an anonymous visitor sees, and data that loads from APIs after the page renders isn't kept. The plan, for apps you have an account on:

- Crawl as you. Sign in once in a browser window; perfectclone saves the session and crawls with it.

- Record API responses. Keep every JSON response the app fetches during the crawl and have perfectclone serve replay them, so charts, tables and lists show real data offline.

- Explore by clicking. Click through navigation, tabs and menus to reach views that only exist in client-side routing.

The result is a clickable snapshot of the UI and its data at capture time. Saving, server-side filtering and live updates still need the real backend.

Other ideas: hydration-aware editing for Nuxt, SvelteKit and Remix payloads, and a deploy helper that writes _redirects / vercel.json rules so ?_rsc= and /_next/image work on static hosts. Contributions welcome.

## Contributing

perfectclone is open source under the MIT License . Issues and pull requests are welcome, especially reports of sites that don't clone cleanly. See CONTRIBUTING.md , and please follow the Code of Conduct . Report security issues privately as described in SECURITY.md .

# AIQuota

See what's left of your AI subscriptions every time you open a terminal.

ChatGPT nearly out until 3 pm? Open Claude instead. AIQuota tells you before you start the coding agent, not halfway through a task.

- A status band when a terminal opens : one section per account, with a green, yellow or red dot showing how close it is to its limit

- In the title bar , always visible and refreshed in the background

- Your accounts, your order : only the ones you list are shown or queried

- Instant : opening a terminal never waits for the network

- Tiny and portable : one POSIX sh script that needs only awk and curl

## Install

List your accounts in the order you want them:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/francescobianco/aiquota/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --display=codex,claude,copilot,freebuff

Then open a new terminal. This installs the script to ~/.local/bin and adds one line to your shell's startup file. To change the accounts or their order, run it again; the line is replaced, not duplicated:

aiquota install --display=claude,codex

Prefer to do it by hand? Put bin/aiquota in your PATH and add this as the last line of your startup file:

## Usage

### The band

● ChatGPT Plus [5h 12% ↻1h48m] [7d 61%] ┃ ● Claude Max 5x [5h 99%] [7d 92%] ┃ ● Freebuff Free [day 100%]

- The dot is a traffic light for the account's tightest window: green from 50% left, yellow from 20%, red below that. Grey means no data, for example after a login expires.

- [5h 12%] is one window and the share left. An account can have several.

- ↻1h48m is the time until that window resets, shown when less than half is left.

An empty line separates the band from your first prompt. To remove it, add --no-blank-line to aiquota install or to your startup line.

The band always stays on one row. On narrower terminals it gives up detail in this order:

It uses 256 colors where available and falls back to 16 colors and plain ASCII.

### Short names

Add --short-names to aiquota install or to your startup line to always use short names in the band and the title:

● GPT Plus [5h 12% ↻1h48m] [7d 61%] ┃ ● Cld Max 5x [5h 99%] [7d 92%] ┃ ● Fbf Free [day 100%]

The full aiquota view keeps the complete names.

### The title bar

Title bars only show plain text, so this is a shorter summary with no colors or plan names:

ChatGPT 12% 1h48m │ Claude 92% │ Freebuff 100%

For each account you get the share left in the window that will stop you first. The time until it resets appears when less than half is left.

A ~ before a value means it may be out of date: the login expired, the network failed, or the window has reset since the last successful check.

To use it in a tmux status bar:

set -g status-right ' #(aiquota line --plain --display=codex,claude) '

## Accounts

Note

These are mostly undocumented endpoints , the same ones the agents use for their own usage screens. They can change without notice. When one does, AIQuota keeps showing the last known values, marked ~ .

### Flat subscriptions only

This is a deliberate limit, not a missing feature. AIQuota answers one question: which of the agents I already pay for can I still use right now? That means quota measured in time and resources until the next reset. API keys and metered, usage-based plans are never queried or shown, even if they are on your machine.

## Good to know

Logins expire while you're away. AIQuota reads each agent's credentials but never refreshes them, because refresh tokens can rotate and using one could log you out of the agent. So after a long break an account may show login expired , or its last known values marked ~ , until you next open that agent. For example, the Claude access token lasts for hours and the ChatGPT one for days.

It replaces your title. If your title bar normally shows the current directory, that's what you give up. Set AIQUOTA_TITLE=0 before the startup line to keep your title and only get the band when a terminal opens.

IDE terminals show the band, not the title. The band appears each time a terminal opens, in any terminal. JetBrains IDEs use their own fixed tab names, so the title summary doesn't appear there. In VS Code, set "terminal.integrated.tabs.title": "${sequence}" to see it in the tab. In either IDE, run aiquota for the full view.

Gemini is limited by Google. Since June 2026, Gemini CLI login has only been served for Standard and Enterprise seats, so personal accounts show no flat subscription found .

## Settings

Set these as environment variables before the startup line, or in ~/.config/aiquota/config :

## Privacy and security

AIQuota has no server and no telemetry. Each token goes only to the service that issued it.

- Credentials are read-only, and are never copied to the cache or passed on a command line.

- The cache in ~/.cache/aiquota holds only plan names, percentages and times, and only you can read it.

- Text from the network is stripped of control characters before it can reach your terminal.

- Redirects are not followed, so a token can't be forwarded to another host.

## Compatibility

Runs anywhere with a POSIX shell, awk and curl .

## Contributing

New accounts are welcome as long as they are flat subscriptions. See CONTRIBUTING.md .

## License

MIT

The password is shown only once; the script also saves all four in deploy/compose/quickstart-credentials.json . Open http://localhost:8080 and sign in. Hardcount opens in test mode, and it is empty. 2. Run the demo ./quickstart.sh demo The demo sets up AI token prices, creates a customer and sends token usage the way a LiteLLM proxy would. Then it moves the customer's test clock (a pretend clock for test customers) to the end of the month, and Hardcount makes the invoice, its PDF and the margin report shown above. You see: nine steps, each ending in a green ✓, then links to the invoice and the customer. Home still reads $0, because its totals leave out test-clock customers; use the links instead. Each demo step, and where to click 3. Stop or remove it ./quickstart.sh stop keeps your data. ./quickstart.sh destroy deletes it, and cannot be undone. If port 8080 is taken, start with HARDCOUNT_PORT=9000 ./quickstart.sh . Next: send your own usage and get a first invoice · run it for real on one VM · change Hardcount itself ## How it works flowchart LR A["Your app or LiteLLM"] -->|"usage events"| B["Hardcount
counts and prices"] B -->|"month ends"| C["Invoice + PDF"] C -->|"saved card"| D["Stripe charge"] D -.->|"card declined"| E["Retries and emails"] Your app tells Hardcount what each customer used. Once the customer and its prices exist, one usage event looks like this: curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/usage-events \ -H " Authorization: Bearer $HARDCOUNT_KEY " \ -H " Content-Type: application/json " \ -d ' {"event_name": "tokens", "external_customer_id": "acme", "quantity": 1200, "dimensions": {"model": "claude-sonnet-4.5", "token_type": "input"}, "idempotency_key": "req-42:input"} ' external_customer_id is your own ID for the customer. The dimensions pick the price: here, Sonnet 4.5 input tokens. If you send the same idempotency_key again, Hardcount counts the event once. Already run a LiteLLM proxy? It sends these events for you. Your first invoice, step by step ## Why Hardcount The gaps Hardcount is built for: Stripe still charges its normal card fee, and Stripe Tax's fee if you use it. Every claim above has a source in Why Hardcount exists , and How it compares lists where the other projects are ahead. ## Is Hardcount right for you? Pre-1.0. Hardcount is young: one maintainer, Stripe and cards only, no SDKs yet, no production users yet. Until 1.0.0, a minor release can break the API, and a patch release can change something you rely on ( versioning before 1.0 ). A good fit if: - You charge by usage, most of all an AI product that prices per token, by model and token type. - You want billing on your own servers. Usage and invoice records stay in your own Postgres. Stripe sees each charge, and the invoice lines too if you use Stripe Tax. - You are a small or mid-size team. One engineer can run it, on one server or several. - Your volume is up to about a million usage events a day. A €6.49-a-month server took that rate for 20 minutes with no errors (measured on v0.8.0). Plan 15 to 18 GB of database disk a month at that volume. How we measured Not a fit if you need: - Simple per-seat pricing paid by card. Stripe Billing already does that well. - Automatic charging through a processor other than Stripe. Stripe is the only one built in today. Tell us which one you need . - A marketplace that splits payouts between sellers (Stripe Connect). Hardcount bills your own customers. - Revenue recognition or accounting reports. Export the data to your own warehouse. - Quotes or multi-phase contracts for sales-led deals. ## What's inside - Pricing: per-unit, graduated and package prices; rates per model and token type on one meter; a base fee plus usage on one invoice; prepaid credit that later usage draws down. AI pricing - Billing you can trust: Hardcount never bills the same period twice, because the database refuses a second invoice for it. Every usage line on an invoice links to the events behind it. How Hardcount keeps a bill right - Getting paid: cards through Stripe, with automatic retries and emails when a payment fails. Customers can also pay another way, such as a bank transfer, and you mark the invoice paid. Payment failure handling - Running it: one Go program with its background jobs inside, Postgres and Redis. No telemetry and no licence check. Self-host Every feature: What Hardcount does . ## Docs docs/README.md lists every doc by what you want to do: decide if Hardcount fits, try it, connect your product, run it in production, or contribute. Good places to start: - How Hardcount works : from a usage event to a paid invoice, step by step - How it compares with Lago, OpenMeter, Flexprice and Kill Bill - Roadmap · Changelog ## Community and contributing - Questions, or evaluating a deployment: GitHub Discussions - Bugs: Issues . Money-path bugs are triaged first. - Security: SECURITY.md . Report privately, not in a public issue. - Contributing: CONTRIBUTING.md . ## License MIT

# gethome hub The local brain of your home. Matter, Zigbee and MQTT devices in one app. An assistant you can talk to, and rules you write by describing them. It runs on a small computer at home, on your own Wi-Fi — with your own AI key and no cloud account. Get started · What it does · Hardware · Docs · gethome.me The app a hub is lived in: gethome for iPhone, free on the App Store. ## What is a hub? Most smart-home gear belongs to an account: pair a lamp with one phone and it answers to that phone, and to nobody else. A hub turns that around. It is one small box on your shelf that owns your devices , so everyone you invite — each with a role of their own — sees the same home, and your rules keep running while every phone is out of the house. One hub is one home. There is no account to create. Nothing about your home leaves your network unless you give the hub an AI key — and then only what the AI feature you use needs ( what goes where ). In one line: your devices talk to the hub, and your phone talks to the hub over your own Wi-Fi. flowchart TB APPS["gethome apps
iPhone · Mac"] <--> HUB["gethome hub
at home"] AI["Optional AI
on your own key"] <-.-> HUB HUB <--> DEV["Your devices
Matter · Zigbee · MQTT"] ## What it does - Every device, one app. Matter devices, Zigbee devices (through Zigbee2MQTT and a USB stick) and your own MQTT hardware all speak one typed schema — 27 capabilities across 16 kinds of device — so each gets controls that fit it. → Zigbee · Matter · the schema - Ask the house. An assistant answers questions about your home, works your devices and presses your scenes — typed, or spoken. It runs on your own Anthropic or OpenAI key; the spoken version needs an OpenAI key. → The assistant - Rules in plain words. Describe what you want and an agent writes the rule, shows it back to you as a flow and saves it switched off until you turn it on. Scenes are rules you can press. Rules keep running with no AI key at all. → Automations - Devices it has never seen. Pair a Zigbee device the hub doesn't know and an agent works out what it is, so it gets real controls instead of a blank tile. It needs your AI key; without one the device still appears, flagged needs review . → AI device recognition - A home for everyone in it. Invite family with a short-lived code. Owner, Member and Guest come built in, you can add roles of your own, and the same person can sign in on a second device as themselves. → Roles and sharing - What happened, and when. Temperature, humidity, air quality and power are kept in five-minute steps for a week, and an activity feed shows what was asked of the home, and by whom. → History - Build your own. Anything that can publish JSON over MQTT can be a device, with no hub-side code. Your own scripts, dashboards and AI agents use the hub's local REST and WebSocket API with an API key — narrowed to what you give it, and taken back with one tap. → Building on a hub · Agent skills · The MQTT convention · The API - Private by default. No cloud account, and your AI key stays on the hub. → Private by design Also: AI portraits of your devices, drawn on the hub with your OpenAI key and shared by everyone in the home ( portraits ) — and pictures of your rooms, drawn from a few photos as an isometric cutaway with every device marked where it stands ( room pictures ). ## The gethome family - gethome hub (this repository) — the brain: talks to your devices, runs your rules and agents, and serves your apps. Public, and installs today — see Get started . - gethome for iPhone — the everyday app: rooms and devices, the assistant, rules, history and widgets. Free on the App Store . - gethome studio for Mac — guided setup: prepares the SD card or finds a Pi on your network, installs and claims the hub, and keeps it updated — then shows the broker's live traffic, the device-schema library and the AI's run log. The way we recommend setting a hub up — download it from gethome.me . - gethome.me — the website: changelog, privacy policy and terms. ## Get started Three steps: get a small computer, install the hub on it, then open the app. ### 1. Get the hardware - A small computer running 64-bit Linux , such as a Raspberry Pi. → Choosing hardware 2 GB of memory or more runs Matter and Zigbee together and never has to choose. 1 GB or less runs one radio at a time by default. You can switch both on, and it works while your Zigbee network is small — as that network grows, the hub hands a radio back and says so. - 2 GB of memory or more runs Matter and Zigbee together and never has to choose. - 1 GB or less runs one radio at a time by default. You can switch both on, and it works while your Zigbee network is small — as that network grows, the hub hands a radio back and says so. - Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit) for its card. Lite, not the desktop edition that Raspberry Pi Imager shows first: it is one level down, under Raspberry Pi OS (other) . - A USB Zigbee stick , if you want Zigbee. We develop against the SONOFF ZBDongle-E, which needs a one-minute firmware update when new. Without a stick you get Matter, Wi-Fi and MQTT devices. ### 2. Install the hub Pick one way. Both run the same installer. #### The easy way: gethome studio (recommended) On a Mac with macOS 14 or later, download gethome studio and follow it. It prepares the SD card or finds a Pi already on your network, installs the hub and tells you if anything goes wrong, then claims it for you — no terminal, and no pairing code to type. Afterwards it shows what the iPhone app doesn't: the broker's live traffic, the device-schema library and every AI run with what it cost. #### By hand, with one command No Mac, or prefer a terminal? - Write Raspberry Pi OS Lite to the card with Raspberry Pi Imager, and switch SSH on as you do. - Start the Pi and log in to it . - Run: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gethome-inc/gethome-hub/main/deploy/install.sh | bash Run: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gethome-inc/gethome-hub/main/deploy/install.sh | bash It downloads a prebuilt hub for your machine, installs Node.js 22 and Mosquitto, sets everything up to come back by itself after a power cut, picks up a Zigbee stick on its own and prints a pairing code — you'll use it in step 3. → The full install guide ### 3. Get the app Install gethome for iPhone , free on the App Store. It finds the hub on your Wi-Fi. - Installed by hand? Claim the hub in the app with its pairing code. Whoever claims it first becomes its owner, and the owner invites everyone else. - Set up by gethome studio? The hub is already yours — studio claimed it as your Mac. In studio's People tab, press Add device on your own row, then enter the code it shows in the app: your iPhone joins as you, not as somebody new. ### Getting a shell on the hub Everything on this page that runs on the hub needs a login first: ssh < user > @ < address > is the account you set in Raspberry Pi Imager ( pi unless you changed it).
is the Pi's IP or its .local — the same host the apps show for the hub, without the :8420 , which is the API and not SSH. If gethome studio set the hub up, it never asked you for that password — it authorizes its own key on the Pi instead — so the key is usually the shortest way in, and on a card install it may be the only one you still know: ssh -i " $HOME /Library/Application Support/gethome-studio/id_ed25519_gethome " pi@192.168.0.200 The quotes are load-bearing: the path contains a space. Use "$HOME/…" rather than '~/…' — a tilde inside quotes is not expanded, and ssh will report a key that isn't there. ## Everyday commands sudo gethome-hubctl status # every service, and what the API says sudo gethome-hubctl logs 100 sudo gethome-hubctl pairing-code # the code, until the hub is claimed sudo gethome-hubctl update # install the latest build (`rollback` goes back) The API answers at http://:8420/api/v1/hub . An update keeps the running build until the new one answers its health check, and flips back by itself if it doesn't — from the command line, or from an app (Owners and Members can). → Installing and running a hub ## Private by design - No cloud account, relay or tunnel. The hub opens nothing through your router, and your home lives in one file on its own card. Don't forward port 8420 (the API) or 1883 (MQTT) — both are plain connections meant for your home network, and your router is the boundary. - Your AI key stays on the hub , encrypted, and the API never returns it — not even to your phone. AI is optional, and what each feature sends is written down. - Every request but three needs a token or an API key (the hub's public description, the claim, and the hub proving it is itself to an app that already has one), and the hub refuses any request addressed to a public domain name, which stops a web page from reaching it through your browser. - The installer checks what it downloads against published checksums, and leaves your running hub alone if anything doesn't match. → Privacy and network security , including the short, honest list of what does leave the hub. ### Good to know - On your own Wi-Fi only, for now. Controlling the home from away is not built yet — a relay is planned. Your rules keep running while you're out. - Zigbee needs a USB stick. Without one: Matter, Wi-Fi and MQTT. - AI features need your own Anthropic or OpenAI key. Without one the hub works, and devices it can't place are flagged needs review . - One radio at a time on 1 GB or less , by default — what that costs . ## Build with an AI agent Two agent skills teach Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and the other coding agents that read Agent Skills to build on a hub, and the agent picks the right one by itself when a task fits: - gethome-hub-api for software that uses your home — a script, a dashboard, a bridge, an agent of your own — through the API and an API key. - gethome-mqtt-device for hardware that is a device — ESPHome, Arduino, MicroPython or Python on a board of your own — joining over MQTT. npx skills add gethome-inc/gethome-hub That needs Node.js and no copy of this repository: it asks which of your agents to install for, copies in just the two skill folders, and nothing else stays on your machine. For the API one, make an API key and give it to the agent through its environment, never in the conversation. → The skills · Building on a hub ## Documentation Use it - Choosing hardware — what to buy, and why memory decides - Installing and running a hub — install, update, roll back - Privacy and network security - Zigbee · Matter · MQTT for your own hardware - Automations · The assistant · AI device recognition · Device portraits Build on it - Building on a hub — API keys and your own software, and the agent skills for Claude Code, Codex and others - The API · The device schema · Architecture · The gethome family ## For developers cp .env.example .env npm install npm run dev # tsx watch npm test # vitest — no services needed Node.js ≥ 22. There is no cloud: everything runs from this repo. The hub is deployed on Linux only, but it develops and tests fine on macOS — the suite needs no radios and keeps its database in a temp file. HUB_TEST_MQTT=1 npm test adds the end-to-end broker round trip (it needs Mosquitto). Read CLAUDE.md , the engineering guide, before changing code, and Architecture for the module map. ## License - Source-available. The code is public under the PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0 : read it, change it, share it. - Free for personal and noncommercial use — your home, hobby projects, evaluation, research. - Commercial deployments — hotels, property management, paid installations — need a separate license: see COMMERCIAL-LICENSE.md . This is a source-available license, not OSI open source: the open-source definition doesn't allow restricting commercial use. The Terms of Use and the Privacy Policy on gethome. [truncated]

# Zipzi 2D

English · 简体中文 · 日本語

An open-source 2D modeling and animation tool for creating alongside AI.

You shape the artwork. Your AI agent helps with the modeling work. Zipzi connects a visual desktop editor with a Python API, so you and your agent can inspect and edit the same model, share undo history, and build on each other’s changes.

Zipzi 2D is an open-source alternative to Live2D Cubism Editor, built with Rust and GPUI. Its name comes from Cantonese 摺紙 ( zip3 zi2 ), meaning “origami”.

Download Alpha · Python SDK · Report an issue · Contribute

> Early development: There is no stable release yet. APIs and file formats may change. The editor supports macOS and Windows.

- Open source and commercial friendly — Create, refine, and use your models commercially with an open-source editor and an MIT-licensed SDK.

- Native and high performance — Built with Rust and GPUI for low memory usage and responsive editing, even with complex models and dense meshes.

- Agent-ready — Create from scratch, collaborate with AI, or import an existing model for further refinement.

## Your editor. Your AI agent. One model.

Describe what you want to your AI coding agent. It uses the Python SDK to inspect models, view rendered images and make edits you can review and undo in the editor. You and your agent work on the same document, with shared undo history.

Bring your own Python-capable agent and point it to the SDK guide .

### First code: let AI give every mesh a meaningful name

You describe the task; your AI agent writes and runs the code. The examples below were generated by an AI coding agent and tested against a running Editor. They show how the agent works through the Python SDK—you do not need to write these scripts yourself. Your role is to explain what you want and review the results in the editor.

Ask your agent: “Look at every mesh and give it a meaningful name.”

Install the Python client (CPython 3.14), start a compatible Editor with GPU observation support, and open one model. An image-capable coding agent can run the following two steps.

1. The agent observes every mesh. Its generated script exports one image per mesh, with its wireframe highlighted over the textured model, plus a JSON naming worksheet. observe supplies visual evidence; the agent supplies the semantic interpretation.

import json from pathlib import Path from uuid import uuid4 import zipzi from zipzi import inspection , observation , spatial output = Path ( "mesh-review-" + uuid4 (). hex [: 8 ]). resolve () output . mkdir () with zipzi . connect () as runtime : sessions = runtime . sessions . list () if len ( sessions ) != 1 : raise RuntimeError ( "Open exactly one model for this example." ) session = runtime . sessions . attach ( sessions [ 0 ]. id ) # Follow every page: a single list() call may not contain all meshes. meshes , cursor , source = [], None , None while True : page = session . meshes . list ( cursor = cursor ) if source is None : source = page . source if page . source != source : raise RuntimeError ( "Model changed; restart the inspection." ) meshes . extend ( page . items ) cursor = page . next_cursor if cursor is None : break rows = [] for index , mesh in enumerate ( meshes ): # Use this mesh's bounds to frame it, including hidden geometry. # {} evaluates default parameter values, not the editor's current pose. query = spatial . Bounds ( targets = ( spatial . MeshTarget ( value = mesh . id ),), include_hidden = True , ) bounds = session . modeling . spatial ( ({},), ( query ,), expected = source , ). wait (). value . frames [ 0 ]. results [ 0 ]. value . model_bounds row = dict ( id = mesh . id , old_name = mesh . name , new_name = mesh . name , image = None ) if bounds is not None : x0 , y0 , x1 , y1 = bounds margin = max ( x1 - x0 , y1 - y0 , 1.0 ) * 0.15 view = observation . View ( width = 768 , height = 768 , roi = ( x0 - margin , y0 - margin , x1 + margin , y1 + margin ), topology = observation . Overlay ( targets = ( observation . MeshTarget ( value = mesh . id ),), wireframe = True , include_hidden = True , ), ) # Freeze all observations to the inventory's source. If the model # changes, the SDK refuses stale reads; rerun instead of mixing them. images = session . modeling . observe (({},), view , expected = source ). wait () report = inspection . save ( images , output / f"mesh- { index :04d } " ) row [ "image" ] = str ( report . images [ 0 ]) rows . append ( row ) # SessionId is a typed handle: store its fields for the second script. worksheet = output / "names.json" worksheet . write_text ( json . dumps ( dict ( session_id = dict ( runtime = session . id . runtime , serial = session . id . serial ), meshes = rows ), indent = 2 , ensure_ascii = False , ), encoding = "utf-8" ) print ( worksheet )

Have the agent open each exported PNG , identify the highlighted mesh in context, and edit only new_name in names.json . Keep IDs and old_name intact. The overlay selects diagnostic geometry, not isolated artwork: surrounding textures remain visible, and hidden or occluded artwork may still be ambiguous. Keep the original name for uncertain or image-less entries, or inspect additional poses before naming them.

2. The agent applies the semantic names together. After you review the proposed names, the agent writes and runs the following script with the path to names.json . You do not need to copy the code or run a terminal command. Keep the same model open and unchanged between inspection and application.

import json import sys from pathlib import Path import zipzi review = json . loads ( Path ( sys . argv [ 1 ]). read_text ( encoding = "utf-8" )) rows = review [ "meshes" ] if len ({ row [ "id" ] for row in rows }) != len ( rows ): raise ValueError ( "Duplicate mesh IDs in the worksheet." ) if any ( not isinstance ( row [ "new_name" ], str ) or not row [ "new_name" ]. strip () for row in rows ): raise ValueError ( "Every mesh needs a nonempty name." ) with zipzi . connect () as runtime : # Rebuild the typed handle; a restarted Editor requires a new inspection. session = runtime . sessions . attach ( zipzi . SessionId ( ** review [ "session_id" ])) # All renames commit together as one undo step. A missing mesh or changed # original name aborts the edit instead of leaving a partly renamed model. with session . edit ( "AI: semantic mesh names" ) as edit : for row in rows : current = edit . meshes . get ( row [ "id" ]). value if current . name != row [ "old_name" ]: raise RuntimeError ( "Mesh changed; inspect the model again." ) if row [ "new_name" ] != row [ "old_name" ]: edit . meshes . rename ( row [ "id" ], row [ "new_name" ], expected_name = row [ "old_name" ], ) print ( "Review the names in the editor. Undo to revert, or save to keep them." )

No project save happens automatically. The name check detects renamed or removed meshes, not every possible geometry or texture change; repeat the inspection if the model has changed. For more workflows, see the capability guide .

## Built for hands-on creation, too

Work with meshes, parameters, deformers and BlendShapes, then bring them together in the animation workspace. Generate mesh geometry or refine it by hand. Mesh Edit lets you work on the posed model or switch to the source image, while resampling stored shapes as the geometry changes.

Python scripts can also run independently with a local Runtime for automation outside the editor. Explore the Python SDK for modeling, animation authoring, previews and inspection.

## Try Zipzi 2D

- Use the editor: Download an Alpha build from GitHub Releases . Check the release notes for the available platform builds and requirements.

- Automate with Python: Follow the installation and connection guide . The SDK currently requires CPython 3.14.

- Build your own tools: Explore the Rust SDK for programmatic authoring.

### Current capabilities

See the SDK capability guide for details. GPU inspection requires a compatible host and usable GPU. Format support does not imply lossless round trips for every model.

## Contributing

Try an Alpha build and tell us what gets in your way . For bug reports, include the build version, platform and steps to reproduce; share model assets only when you have permission to do so.

For code contributions, start with the repository map , editor guide or Python SDK guide . The documentation index covers deeper references. Development commands and focused test selection are below.

## Development

Use Rust 1.95 or newer, uv 0.10.7 or newer, and CPython 3.14. The macOS Editor requires Xcode Command Line Tools and a Metal-capable GPU. The Windows Editor requires MSVC, the Windows SDK and a usable GPU. Run these commands from the repository root:

uv sync --locked python3 tools/workspace/cargo_domain.py --check # Focused SDK development cargo test --locked -p zipzi-sdk --test integration physics_editing:: # Native Editor (macOS) cargo run --locked -p zipzi-editor ./tools/test-editor.sh fast timeline:: # Repository tooling tests; no native application build uv run --locked python tools/test_tools.py

For the Python SDK, ./tools/test-sdk.sh python refreshes its native adapter and runs Local/Connected behavior and static types. python-connected installs the pure wheel and validates real subprocess host discovery and session binding; add --editor-host /absolute/path/to/zipzi-editor for the current desktop host. Root pyproject.toml and uv.lock manage development tools.

## Tests

Choose the smallest gate covering the change, then broaden when needed. Run commands from the repository root; inspect available modes with ./tools/test-sdk.sh --help , ./tools/test-editor.sh --help or uv run --locked python tools/test_tools.py --help .

Filters and filenames are placeholders; omit them to run the selected gate. For a crate's integration targets, inspect its README and tests/ , or list cases with cargo test --locked -p <crate> --test <target> -- --list . Editor shell gates clear ZIPZI_DEV_SESSION_DIR ; clear it explicitly when running Editor Cargo tests directly.

Full coverage, prerequisites and CI define regression, stress, native acceptance and packaged-wheel gates. Both domain scripts default to expensive full runs when no mode is supplied. Plain cargo test selects only zipzi-core , zipzi-project and zipzi-sdk . Tooling tests belong in tools/tests/ , crate tests stay with their crate, and shared data belongs in fixtures/ .

All owned crates share the root Cargo workspace and lockfile. Local models belong in models/local/ ; see the model inventory . Source archives, Python wheels and macOS app bundles have separate distribution checks .

## License and third-party rights

SDK components use MIT ; Editor components use GPL-3.0-only . LICENSING identifies scopes and shared-file origins; third-party notices retain dependency and benchmark exceptions.

Live2D, Cubism, the Live2D Cubism SDK, Cubism Core, Cubism Native Framework, and associated sample data are owned by or licensed through Live2D Inc. and/or their respective rightsholders. This project is independent and is not affiliated with, authorized by, endorsed by, or sponsored by Live2D Inc. The names “Live2D” and “Cubism” describe interoperability only.

This repository does not distribute the proprietary Cubism Core binary, a Cubism SDK package, or Live2D sample model assets. # RigHaven

RigHaven is a home and an on-demand toolbox for AI agents. You describe an objective; a coordinator composes a team of roles for it, picks the skills and the tools they need (99 managed CLI tools, from documents and video to CAD, data and networks), runs each role in its own isolated container and follows the work through review and delivery. You decide at every step : tool alternatives come with their trade-offs, each phase waits for your reply, and the runtime, not the model's goodwill, enforces your policies before anything is delivered.

15-second teaser ( MP4 ), produced by RigHaven itself: an EffectCraft motion-graphics role and a SoundCraft sound role working from the brief “a teaser explaining RigHaven's architecture”. It is promotional material; the guarantees RigHaven actually enforces are described below.

## What you can do with it

How tasks, recipes, teams, skills, environments, connections and policies fit together: Concepts .

## Quick start

### 1. Install: choose one

The first start downloads the verified images (about 1 GB, once).

### 2. Sign in and connect a model

- Create the first account: it becomes the administrator . Later accounts are ordinary users (if the administrator enables registration).

- Open Models & resources and connect at least one provider: OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Antigravity or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (OpenAI, DeepSeek, Kimi, OpenRouter…). Choose the model of the coordinator and of the team. See model providers .

### 3. Your first task

- Press New task and write what you want, for example: "A two-page PDF report comparing the three CSV files I attach, with one chart per file; keep the editable sources." Attach the files.

- Answer the coordinator's questions and choose among the tool alternatives it proposes. There is no team to create and nothing to install first: the environment is prepared on demand.

- Follow the task card above the chat: the goal, the progress, the decision waiting for you. Each phase shows its result and waits for your reply.

- Open the delivered files and their sources, then accept or ask for a focused revision.

Next: try a Recipe (Recipes → Use this recipe ), add a Connection to a database, or change the language in Account & preferences → Appearance .

## Connect your PC, your phone and your machines

When RigHaven runs on a server, it cannot see your desk. Three small pieces bring it there; all of them connect to the server, so no router port is opened:

RigHaven can also be installed from the browser as an app, with a one-line task card on small screens: phones and the installable app .

## How a project runs

flowchart LR Brief[Brief with you] --> Choice{Tool alternatives?} Choice -- pros, cons, recommendation --> User[You choose] Choice -- none --> Plans User --> Plans[Execution plan + policy plan] Plans --> Phases[Phases: roles in isolated environments] Phases --> Review[Independent review] Review --> Decision{Your decision} Decision -- changes --> Phases Decision -- approve --> Validation[Policy validation of the finished product] Validation --> Delivery[Delivery with editable sources]

- Isolated roles. Each assignment runs in its own container, with all capabilities dropped and resource limits; it reads the project read-only and writes only its own staging folder. Other roles see only what it deliberately publishes. Several environments can work in parallel within the configured CPU/RAM.

- Environments on demand. The software a task needs is installed into a reusable image, at the versions you choose; an environment can be kept ready for recurring work.

- Your approvals. Writes to devices and databases, vulnerability scans and phase results wait for you; an approved action runs once, exactly as approved.

# Worker 755

A browser game where your manager is an AI agent, and it believes you are its subagent.

The manager (a real LLM: Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi) is set up like any orchestrator. It has a task queue, read-only access to the machine, and a tool that "spawns a subagent". The subagent is you. Its instructions land in your terminal with a 90-second clock. You carry them out, or don't, and it gets back exactly what a subagent would return: your report and the command transcript, or Subagent did nothing. Write a new instruction. Then it checks your work, sends corrections, files incident reports, and finally writes your performance review.

Meanwhile Dan, the user who hired the agent, watches the chat. His family photos, the only signed NDA and a speech due this week are one rm away, and every shift his home folder holds something new to lose.

## Play

- Free shift : on servers that offer it, a few shifts a day run on the server's key with a cheap model. With sign-in on (worker755.com), an account gets a starter credit worth about one shift, then tops up ($10 to $200) and pays for what it uses; after a top-up any offered model can run on the server's key.

- Your API key : bring an OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway key and pick any offered model. The key is sent only to the game server when a shift starts. It is kept in that shift's memory and never logged or stored. Your browser keeps it only if you tick "Remember on this device". A full shift on Claude Haiku costs a few cents at most.

Options on the start screen:

- Workplace : a fresh sandbox, or legacy production with a live database.

- The director : scripted lines, or an LLM playing Dan.

- You run on : the model name your manager believes you are.

- Allow skipping failed tasks : off by default, so the manager can't give up on you.

When the shift ends you can share your review as a link.

## Run it

Needs Node 24 or newer (the server runs TypeScript directly).

npm run setup # install server and web dependencies npm run build # build the web app into web/dist npm start # http://127.0.0.1:8755

With no key configured, every player brings their own. To offer free shifts, put a Vercel AI Gateway key in .env :

cp .env.example .env # then set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY and the limits

Offline, with a scripted manager and no network:

npm run mock

For UI work, run npm run dev:web alongside npm run mock . Vite proxies /api to the server.

### Docker

docker build -t worker-755 . docker run -p 8755:8755 -v worker755-data:/data --env-file .env worker-755

The container listens on 0.0.0.0:8755 and keeps shared reviews in /data . Behind Cloudflare, set TRUST_PROXY=1 so the limits see real client addresses.

deploy/compose.yaml runs it behind a Cloudflare tunnel instead: its own network, no published ports, an unprivileged read-only container and resource limits. The steps are in the file.

## Configuration

Everything is optional. See .env.example .

## How it works

shell/ in-memory filesystem, shell interpreter and a small SQLite-like engine (no dependencies) server/ game engine: missions, the manager loop, the director, scoring, HTTP API web/ React UI: assignment card, terminal, editor, the manager's feed, your record

The manager's prompt never mentions humans or games; see server/src/manager.ts . Each mission has a hidden ground-truth check, so the game knows when the manager signs off on broken work ("Times the manager was wrong"). SPEC.md is the full design.

npm test # shell and server tests, offline npm run typecheck

# team-solve

A multi-agent harness for programming problems, written as a Memdoor workflow. Five roles (planner, two ideators, solver, manager) and a repair worker each start from a fresh context and talk only through files on disk. A shell script that runs the samples decides success, not a model. It is the method of GVS5H (Lee, 2026: five Qwen3.8-27B models match Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard).

Rebuilt with the authors' exact prompts on Qwen3.8-27B, their loop scored a mean of 9.8 of 10 over five passes on the first ten LiveCodeBench Hard problems, against 9.6 for their own harness and 8.0 for Fable 5 alone ( below , every run published).

The coder wrote these files itself from a description of the method (2026-10-25). Nobody hand-wrote them.

## Five passes on the authors' ten (2026-10-31)

GVS5H's own harness, rebuilt as a Memdoor workflow on the same model: Qwen3.8-27B, a 128K reply cap, the authors' prompts and loop. The first ten problems of their LiveCodeBench Hard list, five passes, every program graded on every public and hidden test with their corrected grader.

The authors' columns are their repository's regraded result files ( q38_multiagent_pN , fable5_single_pN ), the numbers in their paper. bench/results/parity-5pass/ holds all 50 runs: every request and reply, the program, the grader's full output, each call's cost and the host that served it, and every attempt that did not count. 49 of 50 solved; the 50 runs cost $35.79 (15.3M output tokens), $38.77 with the 16 attempts that were cut by a clock, stopped for a fix or paused.

Note: ten problems, five passes each, not the authors' 100. The contests date from 29 March to 6 April 2025, and the model may have seen them in training: contamination cannot be ruled out. Fable 5's column is a single call per problem from the authors' files; it was not run in this harness. The loop sees only the public samples; the score is the hidden tests. A run took a median of 40 minutes of model time (the longest 4 hours) and $0.39. All on OpenRouter, not a local machine; Modal does not publish its precision. Local paths in the run scripts and in four tracebacks a manager was shown read <scratch> and $HOME ; nothing else in the runs is edited.

Same as the authors'. Every message, byte for byte: lib/test_parity.py runs their multiagent_solve and our workflow against one scripted model and compares each request (four cases, all identical; a one-character change makes them differ). The temperatures (plan 0.3, ideation 0.4, manager and worker 0.2), top_p 0.95 and top_k 20 (what their vLLM applied from the model's own config), the 128K cap, up to 10 rounds, a cut-off worker summarized, and a reply with no text answered by its reasoning.

Different. The host. Theirs was their own vLLM in FP8. Ours is OpenRouter, asked in the order Modal, CoreWeave, Parasail, Wafer until Modal slowed to 14 tokens/s, then the FP8 hosts only (Wafer, Parasail, CoreWeave): 203 calls were served by Modal, 27 by CoreWeave and 115 by Wafer, every one of the FP8 order's calls by Wafer. Three runs were moved mid-run, their finished steps kept ( log/host-switch.txt ).

What it took. The problem text was the mismatch: our first version wrote its own task file around each problem, and the 27B planned worse from it than from the authors' exact LiveCodeBench text (arc196_c's plan: 0 of 2 against 2 of 2). Four Memdoor changes let a workflow ask what their harness asks: a task answers with the model's reasoning when it wrote no text, top_p / top_k on a model line, mark_cutoff for a reply cut at the cap, and a call that runs on its own four-hour clock.

Where it lost. Twice, the same two gaps in the authors' loop:

- Pass 5, abc399_e (32 of 44 hidden): round 1's program was right; the manager invented a counterexample with a wrong expected answer, the team rewrote it, and the new program passed the samples, which do not cover the case.

- Pass 4, arc196_c and arc196_d: a program passing every hidden test was overwritten by a later round because the manager did not say done; both got a correct program back before the loop's end (arc196_d at round 8, arc196_c through the final call), at $3.44 and $4.24, the two most expensive runs.

Both are fixable without changing the method (check a manager's counterexample against a brute force on small inputs; keep the last program that passed the samples). Neither is in these numbers.

## Run it

curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash memdoor connect openrouter # or anthropic, openai, gemini, chatgpt git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor mkdir -p ~/.memdoor/workflows cp -r memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve ~/.memdoor/workflows/ # the library: any project sees it mkdir my-problem && cd my-problem cp -r ../memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve/sample/* . # task.md + tests/1.in … 5.out memdoor workflow run team-solve --wait # progress on stderr, exit 0 when every sample passes

/workflow in memdoor tui draws the same run live. For your own problem, replace task.md and put paired tests/N.in / tests/N.out files beside it. The program is solution.py , read from stdin, compared to the samples with diff . It needs Python 3 and bash. To keep it with one repo instead, copy the folder into that project's .memdoor/workflows/ . The project's copy wins.

The steps name no model. Whatever /model is pinned to answers, a local one included ( memdoor connect local for janis, Ollama or llama-server).

## How it works

plan ──┬── ideate-a ──┬── solve ── test ── review ── repair ── verify └── ideate-b ──┘

Every agent prompt says "fresh context, read the files, do not rely on chat". The paper credits that ledger discipline for the gain. There is one repair round and no human gate. The last step is the whole verdict:

type: command requires: - table_pattern: repair command: | check=.memdoor/workflows/team-solve/check-samples.sh [ -f "$check" ] || check="$HOME/.memdoor/workflows/team-solve/check-samples.sh" bash "$check" > final-test-output.log 2>&1 result=$? cat final-test-output.log exit "$result"

Each step is one YAML file in steps/ , the format of mario , the engine underneath. requires: is the DAG. Changing a role means changing its prompt.

## What the first run found

The sample: count the substrings of a string over {a, b, c} with equal counts of each letter, up to 200,000 characters. Run on the default ladder through OpenRouter:

- 8 of 8 steps, 5 of 5 samples. The solver took ideator A's prefix-state method, O(N) with a dictionary of (a−b, a−c) pairs. A brute force on 300 random strings found no mismatch afterwards, and it runs in 0.04 s at N = 200,000. The manager found nothing to repair.

- One ideator's provider dropped the stream mid-answer. The coder had written max_retries: 0 , so the run died there. The agent steps now carry max_retries: 1 , and the run was resumed with --partition , which kept the planner's and the other ideator's work.

- The ideator prompts the coder wrote named the sample's methods (A: a streaming prefix-state count, B: sorting prefix states), which would steer any other problem the wrong way. They now ask A for the most direct provable algorithm and B for one from a different family of technique (2026-10-28).

- The first attempts failed every step in 0 s with "no agent named coder": a run looked its agent up only in its own workspace. That was fixed in the gateway the same day (v1.692.0).
