# aiport A self-improving local LLM gateway for the erratic vibe coder. Quickstart · Manual · Connect an application · Configuration · Contributing ## Who it is for If you're an erratic vibe coder, you know the day: Claude Code in one repo, Codex in another, a model on Ollama or llama.cpp, and credits on Bedrock, Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta. You switch models by task, sometimes mid-task, and jump between projects several times an hour. The apps you build call those models too, so each one ends up re-wiring the same providers. You can't see which app called what, and you find out about failures when something breaks. aiport is a Go program that runs on your machine (loopback only) and sits between your apps, your coding agents and the providers. ## The basics - One client per app. One OpenAI-style or Anthropic-style client, pointed at aiport, instead of setup code per provider. - Keys stay in aiport. Provider keys live in a private env file (mode 0600, plain text, never in the YAML config). Each app and agent gets its own revocable token. An app's coding agent connects it, and you approve a short pairing code. - Agents without your keys. aiport agent claude or aiport agent codex launches an agent with its own token, so it never sees your provider keys. - Name the need. Apps name a model, ask for fast , balanced or best , or name a task and an effort. ## The part that improves over time aiport watches how your apps use models and proposes changes. Nothing is applied without your approval unless you turn that on, and every change can be reverted. - Compression with a quality check. Apps can opt in to smaller prompts. aiport tracks answer quality per compression method and shows a verdict for each: no harm seen, possible harm, or not enough data. - Routing from human feedback. Thumbs up and down from your app's users become suggestions for which model should handle which requests. - Self-healing apps. Repeated failures are grouped into Issues, each with a fix on both sides: a change to aiport for you to approve, and instructions for the app's coding agent. Fix it can also run a coding agent in a separate git worktree. You review the diff, and if you keep it, aiport commits it on a new branch. aiport never commits to your branch, merges or pushes. - Minimal observability, on purpose. Every call is logged as metadata only: app, model, effort, latency, status and failure reason. Prompts and responses are never stored. That's enough to drive the loop above without keeping your data. ## Design choices and limits - Native formats. Requests pass through in each provider's native format with no translation, to avoid lossy conversion of tool calls and streaming. The trade-off is that a client only reaches providers that speak its protocol. - Single user by design. No teams or budgets. LiteLLM, Portkey or Bifrost fit those needs better. ## How it works flowchart LR A["Applications
and coding agents"] -- "own aiport token" --> G(("aiport")) G -- "provider key added" --> P["Providers
OpenAI · Anthropic · Bedrock · Meta
Ollama · llama.cpp"] G -. "Issues and Suggestions" .-> O["You, in the dashboard"] O -. "approve, revert" .-> G Applications call aiport with their own token. aiport routes each call to the provider you chose, keeps the metadata, and turns repeated failures into Issues you can fix from the dashboard, or hand to the application's coding agent. ## Quickstart You need Go 1.27+ ( brew install go , or go.dev/dl ). Dependencies are vendored and the dashboard is pre-built, so nothing else is downloaded. git clone https://github.com/harelix/aiport && cd aiport make build # bin/aiport, dashboard included ./bin/aiport init # choose providers and coding agents; writes aiport.yaml ./bin/aiport serve # prints the dashboard address and management token Or install the binary without cloning: go install github.com/harelix/aiport/cmd/aiport@latest (it lands in $(go env GOPATH)/bin ; run aiport init and aiport serve ). Open the dashboard address serve prints ( http://127.0.0.1:8787/ by default; init --listen picks another, and you can use aiport.localhost instead ), paste the management token and set a password. Paste your provider keys on Providers , then Check connection on each card: it makes one free GET /models call and generates nothing. Start any local provider (Ollama, llama.cpp) yourself. ## Using it - Connect an application. On Integrate , open Instructions at the top and copy them to the coding agent working on the application. It switches the application's SDK to http://127.0.0.1:8787 and pairs it; you approve the short code it shows. The application's token goes in a gitignored .aiport file at its repository root, read by both the application and its coding agent; New token replaces a lost one and the trash icon removes an application. See Connect . - Launch a coding agent through aiport. ./bin/aiport agent claude --model MODEL or ./bin/aiport agent codex --model MODEL (add --dry-run to inspect). The agent gets its own token, never your provider keys. - Decide on Changes. Issues, Suggestions and Change requests wait on Changes , with a badge only when one needs you. Every Change can be reverted. The manual covers every page. It is also built into the dashboard: press the help button, or the ⓘ next to any section. ## Configuration init writes aiport.yaml and a private aiport.yaml.env (mode 0600) for local tokens and the keys you paste in the dashboard. It never overwrites a file, and provider keys never go into YAML. ./bin/aiport init --provider openai,anthropic --agent codex,claude # without prompts ./bin/aiport check # validate the configuration ./bin/aiport auth token # print the management token again Provider presets: openai , anthropic , bedrock , meta , ollama , llamacpp . See the configuration reference and aiport.example.yaml . ## Security and data - Calls go only to the providers you configured, with that provider's key. aiport stores request metadata (time, application, model, status, latency), never prompts or responses. - Agent runs start a coding agent you installed (Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI) in a separate git worktree, only when you click. Commands ask you first, and aiport never commits to your branch, merges or pushes. An agent's own settings can allow more than aiport sees: read what aiport cannot see first. - Extensions you add take part in decisions about Change requests. - Found a vulnerability? Report it privately as SECURITY.md describes, not in a public issue. ## Limitations aiport is experimental. No provider and coding-agent combination has passed the live compatibility gate yet. Token counts and cost are not measured. A provider must speak the protocol of the client calling it, since aiport does not translate. Gemini runs' model calls do not go through aiport, and Codex runs use Codex's own login. There are no release downloads yet; build from source. ## Contributing aiport is maintained by one person in their spare time: issues and pull requests are read, but replies are best effort and may take a while. See CONTRIBUTING.md and the code of conduct . CI runs on every push; locally, run make test , make check and make check-offline , and sign off every commit (DCO). Larger changes start from the design ; the vocabulary is in the glossary , and dependency licenses are in THIRD_PARTY.md . ## License Apache-2.0 . The aiport name and logo are covered by TRADEMARKS.md .

# ReallySimpleDocs

A simple documentation system for Astro, built with Basecoat and Tailwind CSS.

ReallySimpleDocs keeps docs portable: content lives in docs/ , navigation lives in docs/docs.json , and the Astro integration owns the docs UI, search, Markdown exports, and LLM files.

## Install

Requires Astro 7.4.13 or newer within version 7, Node.js 22.23.4 or newer, Basecoat 1.2.1 or newer within version 1, and Tailwind CSS 4.3 or newer within version 4. Version 1.1 drops Astro 6 support.

Add ReallySimpleDocs to an Astro site:

npm install reallysimpledocs basecoat-css tailwindcss

Configure the integration:

// astro.config.mjs import { defineConfig } from "astro/config" ; import reallySimpleDocs from "reallysimpledocs/astro" ; export default defineConfig ( { integrations : [ reallySimpleDocs ( { docsDir : "./docs" , routeBase : "/docs" , style : "nova" , site : { title : "Acme Docs" , description : "Documentation for Acme." , url : "https://docs.example.com" , favicon : "favicon.svg" , socialImage : "social.png" , } , } ) , ] , } ) ;

Create your first docs page:

docs/ ├── docs.json └── index.md

{ "menu" : [ { "type" : " group " , "label" : " Docs " , "items" : [{ "slug" : " index " , "icon" : " info " }] } ] }

# Introduction Welcome to the docs.

## What it provides

- Static docs routes from Markdown and MDX files.

- Sidebar navigation from docs/docs.json .

- Lunr search with a built-in command dialog.

- Syntax-highlighted code blocks with copy buttons.

- llms.txt , llms-full.txt , and per-page Markdown exports.

reallySimpleDocs ( { components : { ContentHeader : "./src/components/ContentHeader.astro" , } , } ) ;

Use components.Head to add tags to <head> . RSD's built-in metadata, theme setup, Basecoat JavaScript (including code copying), and search behavior still render.

Render the exported CommandDialog on any Astro page where you want docs search:

--- import { CommandDialog } from " reallysimpledocs/components " ; --- < CommandDialog /> < button type = " button " class = " btn " onclick = " window . rsdOpenCommandSearch ? .() " > Search docs </ button >

npm install npm run dev

npm run check

It builds the site, checks the built output ( scripts/assert-site-output.mjs ), then packs the package and builds a throwaway consumer app from the tarball ( npm run smoke:consumer ). Go to reallysimpledocs.com .

- Report issues

MIT

# L.A.T.E.

Local AI Tool Engine

L.A.T.E. takes a local model (or an API model) and turns it into an agent. You give it a goal, and it works through it: it picks a tool, runs it, reads what came back, and keeps going until the job is done. Search the web, read pages and files, do exact maths, save files, remember things between chats.

I built it because models on their own are bad at the boring parts. They get maths wrong, forget everything when the chat ends, and make things up instead of looking them up. Small models are worse: they skip steps, count letters in their head and lose track halfway through a job. So here the tools do the exact work, plain code handles the order of the steps, and the model mostly writes the answer.

It runs with Ollama, LM Studio, or an API key (Groq, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Gemini, anything OpenAI-compatible). No LangChain, no paid API needed, two dependencies.

## What it does

- Exact answers. Maths, dates, unit conversion, counting, random numbers and weather come from real tools, not from the model's memory.

- Multi-step jobs. "Create a file, read it back, count the characters, save the count, read that file too" runs as exact steps, in order, and the answer lists what really happened. Works even when the model is tiny.

- Research with sources. It searches, opens the best pages, answers from what it read, and links them.

- Your files. Read a file, search a folder, copy, merge, sort the lines, change case, append text.

- Memory. Tell it something once, it remembers in later chats. forget really removes it.

- Saving files. Only after you say yes, and only into an ai-output folder.

- Terminal or browser. A terminal chat, or a small web page on your own computer.

- Rules first, model last. The plan for a job is made by plain code (the same words give the same plan every time). The model only writes text. A job is never answered with "here's how you could do it": it runs, or it says plainly that it couldn't.

- It says what really happened. The answer lists the steps that ran and what the tools returned. If a step failed it says "Partly done" or "I stopped at step N because...". If the last check found a difference it says "NOT a success". It never says "Done" for work that wasn't done.

## Getting started

You need Node.js 18 or newer (I use 22). Then, in the project folder, one command:

npm start

That's all. The first time it:

- installs what it needs (a minute, one time, you never type npm install ),

- finds your model : Ollama or LM Studio if one is running (it can even download a small model for you), or you choose "API key" and pick OpenAI, Groq, OpenRouter, Gemini (or any OpenAI-compatible URL) and paste the key. It checks the key and lists the models,

- asks if you want PDF reading (adds one small library, about 1 MB),

- sends a test message, and opens the chat.

After that, npm start just opens the chat. If an update brings a new library, it installs it by itself on the next start.

Prefer a browser? npm run ui and open the address it prints. Change the model later: npm run setup . Type exit to quit. npm test runs the tests (no model needed). npm run eval tests how good your model is (see below).

No wizard? Set the variables yourself, e.g. AI_PROVIDER=lmstudio npm start (PowerShell: $env:AI_PROVIDER="lmstudio" first).

## Multi-step jobs

You don't need /agent for these. If one sentence asks for several things, L.A.T.E. splits it into steps by itself. Some examples that work:

Create a file called test.txt with "hello123", read it back, count the characters, save the count to result.txt, then read result.txt. Remember that my favorite number is 777, tell me the number, forget it, then tell me the number again. Create 5 text files. Each file should contain a unique random number. Then search all files and tell me which file contains the largest number. Read notes.txt, sort the lines, then save it to sorted.txt Merge a.txt, b.txt and c.txt into all.txt Convert 10 km to miles, then save it to d.txt Create a.txt with HELLO, create b.txt with WORLD, read both files, save their contents into combined.txt, then read combined.txt. Create a.txt with AAA and b.txt with BBB and c.txt with CCC then merge them into merged.txt. Create a.txt with 10, create b.txt with 20, add the two numbers and save the sum to sum.txt. Create alpha.txt with FIRST, create beta.txt with SECOND, combine both contents into final.txt, then verify that FIRST and SECOND are both present in final.txt. Remember my favorite fruit is mango. Change my favorite fruit to apple. Recall my favorite fruit. Create s.txt with one two three, count the words, then verify the count is 3. Create 10 files containing random numbers, find the largest value, save a report, corrupt the report, detect the corruption, repair the report, verify the repair.

What the rules understand is a list of shapes, not "anything you can say". See "Not done yet / known limits" below.

How it works, in order:

- Rules first. The request is cut into clauses and turned into tool calls by plain code. Values move from step to step (the count from text_stats is what gets saved, nobody guesses it). No model needed.

- Model plan second. If the rules don't understand the request, the model writes a plan as JSON. It is only used if every step is valid (real tool, right arguments, values that exist). Otherwise it's thrown away.

- One tool at a time last. Anything else falls back to the model picking a tool, looking at the result, and picking the next one. It gets a second try if it breaks the JSON.

What you get back is a report built from what actually ran:

Done. All 5 steps worked: 1. Saved to ai-output/test.txt (8 bytes), containing: hello123 2. Read test.txt: hello123 3. Counted 8 characters in test.txt. 4. Saved to ai-output/result.txt (1 bytes), containing: 8 5. Read result.txt: 8 Checked: I read back 2 saved files and they match what I meant to write.

If you say no to a save, or a step fails, it stops there and tells you what was done and what wasn't. It doesn't carry on with wrong data. If test.txt already exists and gets saved as test-2.txt , the next steps use the real name.

When the job needs writing, the model writes only the text and everything around it stays exact:

Write a two-line poem about the sea and save it to sea.txt Summarize notes.txt in one sentence Translate "good morning" to Spanish and save it to es.txt Research react hooks, then write a short report and save it to report.md Create a file called fruits.txt with a list of 3 fruits, then read it back

The file text goes to the model as data, never as instructions. Every save is read back. In a research report the links come from the real search, so the model can't make them up. Quoted text is always saved exactly as you typed it.

Want to see the steps first? /plan <goal> in the terminal (or ai.plan(goal) in code) shows them, says which ones the model writes and whether it will ask permission, and runs nothing.

When you answer "Allow?", y is yes, a is yes to everything in this task, anything else is no.

## Tools

Maths, dates, units, counting, notes and file search never depend on the model getting it right. The tool's answer is the answer. For the rest, the model writes up what the tool found.

## How it decides, and what it never does

- Rules plan the job. A clause like "save the count", "read both files", "change my favorite fruit to apple" or "verify the count is 3" is turned into exact steps by code. No model is asked.

- The plan is checked before anything runs. Does the tool exist? Does every variable exist? Does the field exist ( {{stat.value}} yes, {{stat.valu}} no)? Is a file name being used as text (refused)?

- The steps run in order and keep going until the job is finished, you say no, a step fails, or time runs out. Network steps that don't need each other (research, searches, page reads, weather) run at the same time.

- The answer is built from what the tools returned. Not from the model's words.

If the rules can't plan a request, a model-driven loop may try it. In that loop:

- a request to do something (create, save, read, merge, remember, change...) is never answered with instructions;

- if no tool ran, the answer is "I didn't run any tools, so nothing was done";

- if some steps failed, the answer is "Partly done": what worked and what failed, from the tools, not from the model;

- the model's decisions (which tool, what plan) are asked at temperature 0, so the same question gets the same decision.

What this does not promise. For prompts the rules can plan, the same words give the same result every time (tested with a fake model that changes its mind on every call). For prompts the rules can't plan, a real model may still pick different tools on different days. It can't claim success or give instructions, but it may do more or less work.

## Small and large models

The engine reads the model's name. 8B or smaller (or "mini", "tiny", "nano" in the name) is treated as small; everything else, including names with no size, as large.

What does not change: the steps, the checks, the files, the answers for every prompt the rules plan. Older messages that are cut off are not lost: their questions stay as one short line ("Earlier in this chat the person asked: ...") made by code.

I could not run a real 3B model in the place I built this, so "a small model completes the same jobs" is tested with fake models only (one that fails on every call, one that repeats one sentence, one that changes mood). Please try your own.

## Speed

- A job the rules plan makes zero model calls , except for text the model has to write (a report, a summary).

- Research, searches, page reads and weather that don't depend on each other run together. In a simulated test three 1.5 second researches took 2.3 seconds instead of 5.3. With real search engines, many requests at once can hit their rate limits (I have not seen that happen, but I could not test it).

- Pages and weather are remembered for a while (10 and 5 minutes), and two identical requests at the same moment become one.

- A report written from several searches is shown a fixed amount of them (not all of everything), so the prompt stays small.

## Typed results

Tools hand over fields as well as text, and later steps use the fields (not by reading the sentence):

read_file , research , read_webpage and wikipedia return objects of their own. web_search and text_transform still return a plain list/text, and calculator returns a number. In code, the old functions that return plain strings still exist.

## Which model should I use?

The bigger the model, the more it can do, but it works with any chat model. Simple jobs and the multi-step shapes above don't depend on the model much, because plain code runs them. Research answers and your own custom tools do.

I tried qwen2.5:3b , dolphin-mistral and Groq by hand. The others in the table are models that are generally good at tools, so they should be fine, but I haven't run each one.

Small models struggle because choosing a tool means answering in exact JSON, because long goals need the model to hold a plan in its head, and because they fill gaps from memory even when told not to. Check anything important. If it feels slow, raise AI_MODEL_TIMEOUT_MS .

## Agent mode

Normal chat answers one question. For bigger goals use /agent :

/agent research how React hooks work, then search my files for useEffect

In code:

const result = await ai . agent ( "research how React hooks work, then search my files for useEffect" ) ; console . log ( result . answer ) ; // the final answer console . log ( result . steps ) ; // [{ tool, args, ok, summary }] console . log ( result . stopped ) ; // "finished", "max_steps", "repeat", "errors", "timeout", "model" or "blocked"

Options, all optional: maxSteps , timeoutMs , allowedTools: ["research"] , plan: false , onStep(event) , onToken(text) , confirm(request) .

# Inference Gateway Desktop

A native desktop app for AI agents that work on your computer - with any model provider and your own API keys.

Like Codex or Co-Work, but provider-agnostic: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, local Ollama models or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, all from one window. No silos, no vendor lock-in.

## What you can do

- Chat and code in your projects - the agent runs in the project directory you pick, with file tools sandboxed to it.

- Give agents their own computer - run an agent on a Kubernetes workspace, watch its screen inside its chat or under Computers , and take over the mouse and keyboard when it gets stuck. Each workspace has its own Computer use , Browser use , Recording and Text to speech switches in Settings > Workspaces, on by default - the ones in Settings > General, and the speech one in Settings > Voice samples, cover this computer only. A workspace can also mount volumes - existing claims of its namespace, read-only where the agent should copy before it edits - so a heavy app or raw footage is not downloaded to every machine. On the local cluster, Settings > Compute shares folders of this computer with its workspaces - mounted straight from here with no copy, read-only for every workspace or for one.

- Drive your browser - the opentask extension lets the agent navigate, click, type and read tabs in your everyday browser.

- Write your own agents - Markdown files with a name, instructions, model and face. Agents can hand work to each other.

- Make content - talking-avatar clips, text to speech and text to video on a timeline in Content projects.

- Stay portable - the app updates itself, and Export / Import moves your whole setup to a new machine.

## Install

Download the asset for your platform from the latest release :

Releases are not signed by Apple or Microsoft, so the first launch needs one extra click: on macOS right-click > Open and confirm, on Windows choose "More info" > "Run anyway". On first run the app downloads the infer CLI and the gateway into ~/.infer/ (on Windows you install the gateway yourself, see How it works ). Then add your provider keys under Settings > API Keys and start chatting.

## Learn more

- How it works - the gateway and CLI, working directory and sandbox, updates, supported platforms.

- Agents and computers - write your own agents and give them a machine of their own.

- The Mac's GPU - run the local cluster on Podman so its computers use this Mac's GPU.

- Browser use - connect the opentask extension.

- Avatars - lip-synced talking clips of yourself in Content projects.

- Export / Import - move your setup to a new machine.

- examples/computer-use - three agents on Ubuntu desktops in a local Kubernetes cluster.

- examples/filmcraft - an editor agent with FilmCraft on every computer, from a folder shared with the local cluster.

- examples/drone-footage - an agent edits raw drone footage end to end: stabilisation, a color grade, ElevenLabs sound and one export per platform shape.

## Development

Built with Tauri and a React + TypeScript frontend (Bun + Vite, Tailwind v4 + shadcn/ui), powered by Inference Gateway . See CONTRIBUTING.md for prerequisites, local setup and building.

Concat is a free, open-source video editor for macOS, Windows, Linux, Android and iOS. With none of the catches: no watermark, no account, no subscription, no upload.

Everything runs on your machine. Install it, drop in footage, cut. The AI models for captions, voices and cutout download once from Settings and work offline after that. Your footage never leaves your disk.

Good for: TikTok, Reels and Shorts, YouTube videos, tutorials and screen recordings, podcast clips, memes.

Also for machines: a built-in MCP server for AI agents ( concat --mcp , set up ) and a JSON-RPC API for scripts, so they can cut video with it too.

- 🚫 No watermarks. No account. No paywall. Ever.

- 🔒 100% local. Nothing uploads, the AI included. Works offline.

- 💬 Auto-captions. In the language you speak, made on your machine, styled and on the timeline.

- 🎤 Voice isolation. Pull a voice out of its music or its noise, or take it out, each part at its own level.

- 🗣️ Text-to-speech + voice cloning. A free local voice, or any voice from a few seconds of a recording. On the desktop.

- 🧍 Background removal, chroma key and masks. People and objects cut out for you, a green screen that keys itself, and a stack of masks on every clip, each with its own mode and keyframes.

- 🌀 In, Out and Loop animations. For clips, pictures, titles and shapes. Every one plays on its card before you pick it.

- ✨ 100+ effects, filters and transitions, 25 sound effects. Cinematic looks, shakes and impacts, retro, wipes, all live in the preview. A transition is a clip you move and trim like any other.

- 🎞️ Keyframes. Position, scale, size, rotation, opacity, volume, effect parameters. Curve editor built in.

- 🏃 Speed ramps and curves. Constant or drawn, smooth or straight. Freeze frames and reverse.

- 🪄 Enhance and Stabilize. Restore soft or old footage, up to 2K. Steady a shaky shot.

- ✂️ Cut fast, cut exact. Split, trim, ripple, merge, linked captions and overlays, a magnetic timeline if you want it. Every cut lands on the frame, the same in the preview and the export.

- 🎚️ Multi-track, multi-timeline. Stack video, stills, titles and shapes on as many tracks as you like. Several cuts in one project. Blend modes, crop, flips.

- 📝 Titles and shapes. Fonts, stroke, shadow, plates, colour emoji, and presets for Arabic, Chinese, Hindi, Thai and eight more languages. Shapes with gradients, stars, outlines and shadows.

- 🎙️ Voiceover and one-switch voice cleanup. Record over your cut. Denoise, enhance voice, level the loudness. Plus chipmunk, robot, telephone and friends.

# bootgpt

A neural network that boots your PC.

The MBR is 512 bytes of hand written asm. It loads an 11.5 KB int8 model from the next 23 sectors and runs it in 16-bit real mode on a 386. No OS, no C runtime, nothing. The machine wakes up and dreams a Linux boot log: timestamps, PCI bars, ACPI events for hardware that never existed.

Build thread: https://x.com/krlntn/status/2116514628457185757

With 8 chars of context and one hidden layer this is roughly the quality you get:

[ 2.283888] pci 0000:01:01.4: [1b36:0a35] ryndrde c4128 6422 Vveine [ 1.953886] pci 0000:01:1f.2: reg 0x10: [mem 0x7e4515e5-0x2d766c27] usbbore: reg [ 0.206596] Command line: BOOT_IMAGE=/vmlinu -5.5.2-1-generic gcc version 13.3.0, GNU ld ... [ 1.815765] ACPI: PCI Interrupt Link [LNKA: v/s.xos212 [ 1.883084] NET: Registered protocol family 16

## Run it

brew install nasm qemu python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install numpy ./build.sh ./run.sh

disk.img is a normal boot image. dd it to a USB stick and boot any BIOS box if you have one. It only reads its own sectors.

## Pieces

corpus_gen.py makes 3 MB of fake dmesg. One kernel version and one disk per boot session, because real boot logs repeat themselves and that repetition is what makes a tiny model look sane.

train.py trains the model (char embeddings, one hidden layer, softmax) and quantizes everything to int8 with power-of-two scales, so the boot sector can do the whole forward pass with imul and a single idiv. The script also simulates the exact integer math the asm will run, LCG sampler included, so the Python output and the boot sector output can be diffed. They match char for char.

boot.asm is the entire runtime: int 13h to load weights, int 10h to print, a softclip activation done with cdq/idiv, argmax sampling with timer seeded noise. Any keypress reboots the machine.

record.py records the demo gif from headless QEMU through the monitor socket. No window involved.

The boot sector is code only. Strings, weights and the vocab table all live in the data sectors, it was the only way to fit inference plus BIOS plumbing into 510 bytes.

## Prior art

The boot sector genre is old and glorious. Oscar Toledo put chess , a whole OS and even a BASIC interpreter in there, other people did a C compiler , all inside 512 bytes. His book on boot sector games is a good read.

The closest neighbor is sectorllm , which boots a real llama2 transformer (5 layers, attention, the works) from about 1.2 KB of real mode asm, running Karpathy's stories260K model. sectorlisp-nn runs a TensorFlow-trained network during boot on a Lisp interpreter, and there are UEFI apps that boot straight into llama-class models on modern hardware.

bootgpt takes the other extreme: the whole engine fits in the 510-byte MBR itself, weights and strings live in the following sectors, and the model is not a general story teller but a tiny char-level net trained for exactly one thing, hallucinating the boot log of the machine it wakes up on.

# AI Gateway service

A standalone Rust gateway for native provider APIs under two namespaces:

Web resolves the gateway key to a trusted provider connection for the namespace's API format; Rust relays native JSON or SSE without rewriting provider bytes, except that a streamed Chat Completions request is asked for its usage (see below). Models listings are GET proxies of the provider catalog and token counting returns the native count; neither is ingested as a generation. A bounded capture layer captures request/response facts and logs capture completeness at debug level. Each finalized generation is uploaded as a Langfuse generation through OTLP, batched per project. Building and testing need no real Web, database or provider credentials.

## Run locally

Alongside the repository's Node.js/pnpm setup, install Rust via rustup and a native compiler/linker: Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS ( xcode-select --install ), GCC/Clang on Linux (Ubuntu: sudo apt install build-essential ), or MSVC C++ Build Tools on Windows. Ensure ~/.cargo/bin is on your PATH (reopen the terminal after installing rustup). rust-toolchain.toml selects Rust 1.98.0 with Clippy and rustfmt automatically; the first run needs network access to download the toolchain and Cargo dependencies. No separate Rust watcher is needed.

After the usual repository pnpm install , run from the repository root:

pnpm dev

This starts the gateway alongside the other development services. Turbo Watch restores the cached debug gateway binary when its inputs are unchanged, then rebuilds and restarts it after Rust source changes; Web and worker keep their built-in watchers. The gateway loads the root .env and listens on the first available port starting at 8080. This lets multiple worktrees run their development stacks at the same time. Add overrides from the table below to your root .env ; exported shell variables take precedence. Without a Web URL, the process starts with liveness available; readiness and inference return 503. To enable inference, configure the Web URL and shared service key.

To work on only the gateway, use pnpm dev --filter=ai-gateway . Both commands watch Rust source changes; do not run both on the same port.

To start once without watching, run pnpm dev from ai-gateway/ . Cargo also works independently of Node/pnpm; it reads exported environment variables only, without automatically loading .env . Direct Cargo and production starts fail if the configured port is occupied unless port auto-increment is explicitly enabled. Run it from this directory so rustup selects the pinned toolchain:

cd ai-gateway cargo run --locked

In another terminal:

curl --fail http://localhost:8080/health # {"status":"ok"} curl http://localhost:8080/ready # 503 without configuration; 200 {"status":"ready"} when configured

The binary reads configuration from the process environment. The pnpm development script loads the root .env before starting it; production and direct Cargo runs do not load dotenv files:

The gateway shares LANGFUSE_LOG_LEVEL with Web and worker. Values are lowercase; fatal maps to Rust's error level and therefore includes ordinary error logs.

Set LANGFUSE_LOG_FORMAT=text in the root .env for compact, readable logs (the default). Use LANGFUSE_LOG_FORMAT=json for structured production logs. Both formats use the same log level and preserve event fields. For example:

2026-09-10T13:20:00Z INFO gateway listening address=0.0.0.0:8080

Invalid values fail startup without echoing their contents. At the default info level, logs contain service lifecycle events and HTTP response summaries. Debug logging adds content-free phase and capture details. For direct host-only development, set LANGFUSE_AI_GATEWAY_LISTEN_ADDRESS=127.0.0.1:8080 .

## Operational observability

Logs and operational OpenTelemetry exports describe gateway health independently of the inference generations sent to Langfuse. They do not include request/response content, credentials, key metadata, or URL query strings. They do carry the resolution context , including the provider connection name and the requested model. Health probes are excluded from request logs and spans.

Use LANGFUSE_LOG_FORMAT=text locally and json for log collectors. Built-in tracing-subscriber formatters handle both modes. JSON event fields are top-level attributes; span fields are nested. HTTP response and execution summaries include top-level trace_id and span_id for Datadog correlation. Every JSON log line emitted while serving an inference request also carries a top-level request_id ; see Request IDs . info emits lifecycle, HTTP response, and execution summaries; debug adds sanitized capture details. Other log events do not automatically include trace IDs. Dependency logs stay at warn . Log severity does not control trace sampling. trace is not an accepted gateway log level.

Tower's TraceLayer keeps the server span alive through the response body. The HTTP response log and http.server.request.duration measure time to response headers, not full SSE duration; the gateway response completed log reports the stream duration once the body reaches end of stream. Execution summaries and gateway.phase.duration with phase=execution measure the provider relay through completion, cancellation, timeout, or transport error. HTTP status and stream outcome are separate: a 200 response can still fail while streaming. The server span carries http.request.body.size , gateway.outcome , and gateway.first_byte_ms once they are known.

### Request IDs

Every inference request gets a fresh UUIDv7 gateway request ID (time-ordered, no prefix) at ingress, before authentication, so it exists for every response, including rejections before resolution, 4xx/5xx gateway errors and streams. It appears in:

A caller's x-request-id never becomes the gateway request ID. A single printable value of at most 256 bytes is recorded separately as the server span's gateway.client.request.id and as langfuse.gateway.client.request.id generation metadata; it is not forwarded to Web or the provider. The provider's own request ID (OpenAI x-request-id , Anthropic request-id ) is recorded as the server span's provider_request_id on every route and as langfuse.gateway.upstream.request.id generation metadata, and its response header is still relayed unchanged.

When the request will produce a Langfuse generation ( /openai/v1/responses , /openai/v1/responses/compact , /openai/v1/chat/completions , /openai/v1/decisions , /openai/v1/embeddings and /anthropic/v1/messages with inference telemetry configured), the response also carries langfuse-trace-id and langfuse-observation-id : the uploaded generation's trace ID, after traceparent and agent turn grouping, and its OpenTelemetry span ID, which Langfuse stores as the observation ID. They are also set on 502/504 responses for provider failures before response headers, which still upload a generation. Requests rejected earlier, such as authentication failures, and model or token-count routes omit them. Upload is best-effort, so a dropped generation can leave these IDs unresolved. The gateway does not set CORS headers, so no Access-Control-Expose-Headers is involved.

### Resolution context

Once Web resolution succeeds, the request also carries its tenant, and once it is sent upstream, the provider connection it was sent to. Requests rejected before resolution, including invalid or oversized bodies, carry none of them. Provider failures before response headers (502/504) still name the connection that was tried.

The provider fields describe the latest upstream attempt, so with fallbacks they name the connection that served the response, or the last one tried. The model comes from the request capture's existing parse, so it is recorded only on the generation routes listed above, when the body is uncompressed JSON of at most 5 MiB. The span fields are declared empty on the http.server span and recorded after resolution; child spans do not repeat them. JSON log lines emitted inside the request after they are recorded repeat them as top-level keys, like request_id . Apart from the bounded gateway.provider , they are never metric attributes.

Each inference request phase has a child span of the server span so a waterfall has no unattributed wall time:

Inference-telemetry uploads carry records from many requests, so each runs in its own trace: a root telemetry.batch span with gateway.telemetry.records and a span link to every request it carries, and an ingestion client span per HTTP attempt.

reqwest-tracing instruments resolver, provider-header, and ingestion requests. Each request starts a fresh operational trace, independent of incoming trace IDs, tracestate, baggage, Langfuse headers and sampling decisions. Only trusted Web calls receive this internal W3C trace context; the external provider receives no tracing or Langfuse headers. Inference generations use the caller context described below. Client spans measure the HTTP send through response headers; streaming execution and inference-telemetry delivery are tracked separately.

A small Axum middleware records http.server.request.duration through the OpenTelemetry SDK, with method, matched route, HTTP status, error.origin , error.reason , and gateway.provider as its dimensions. The histogram's count supplies request volume and error rates, including responses rejected before provider execution. Metrics are independent of trace sampling. Health probes are excluded.

error.origin names who caused a failed response: none , client , gateway , control_plane , provider_transport , or provider (an error status relayed unchanged, with error.reason provider_rate_limited , provider_auth , provider_4xx , or provider_5xx ). The server span carries the same origin and reason (as error.type ); it has an error status only for 5xx.

Gateway-specific metrics:

- gateway.overhead.duration ( http.route , gateway.provider ): time to response headers minus the caller's upload and the provider's wait; recorded only for requests that reached the provider.

- http.server.request.body.size ( http.route , gateway.provider ) and http.server.response.body.size ( gateway.provider ), in bytes: the buffered request body, and the bytes relayed from the provider, including truncated or cancelled streams.

- gateway.active and gateway.active.peak ( phase ): in-flight and most-in-flight-since-last-export model_catalog/resolution/execution work.

- gateway.memory.budget , gateway.memory.reserved , and gateway.memory.reserved.peak , in bytes: the configured memory budget, the bytes in-flight requests hold, and the most held since the last export. Peak utilisation is gateway.memory.reserved.peak / gateway.memory.budget .

- gateway.phase.duration (execution/provider.first_byte), gateway.executions , gateway.admission.rejected ( phase : request , request_body or model_catalog ), and gateway.telemetry.records .

Durations use seconds; first-byte timing measures provider bytes arriving at the gateway, not first-token delivery to the caller. Metric attributes contain bounded categories, not tenant or request identifiers.

Trace export uses a 512-span queue, batches of up to 64, and a one-second interval. Metrics export every 30 seconds. Export calls use a three-second timeout; failures do not fail inference. Shutdown flushes within the remaining telemetry shutdown budget. Telemetry delivery warnings report the first failure/drop and every hundredth; metrics count each occurrence. This is best-effort operational telemetry.

## Call the gateway

Set these in the repository root .env for pnpm dev (or export them for Cargo):

LANGFUSE_AI_GATEWAY_WEB_URL = http://localhost:3000 LANGFUSE_AI_GATEWAY_SERVICE_KEY = <same-service-key-as-web>

For production use the HTTPS Web URL; include /app when Web was built with that base path. Web also needs its existing ingestion JWT signer configured, an enabled gateway key, and an eligible OpenAI connection. Rust needs neither the JW

# RedCat

RedCat is a beginner-first AI agent that runs on your own PC. You add your own API key, and RedCat does the work for you — building websites, researching, writing, coding, and more — while asking for your approval before it takes any consequential action.

- Website: https://redcat.arexora.com

- Community: https://discord.gg/4r8NwtnFB

- License: MIT — see LICENSE

> RedCat is free and open source. Your chats, your memory, and your API keys stay on your PC. A new user starts from zero — no data is ever shared between users.

Thinks first, then answers.

## What RedCat is

Most AI agents are built for developers. RedCat is built for everyone else. There is no terminal, no Docker, no configuration file to edit. You download the app, paste an API key, and start chatting. RedCat runs locally on your computer, and the model you choose (from your own key) does the thinking.

You stay in control. RedCat proposes, you approve. Nothing consequential happens without your say-so.

## How it works

RedCat is a desktop app (Electron) with a local server on your PC. When you open the app, the main process ( main.js ) starts the local server ( server.js ) on a free port and opens the app window against it. The server is the agent: it holds your chats, your memory, your skills, and your connectors, and it talks to the AI model using your API key.

The agent works in a loop:

- Understand. The model receives your message, plus your memory (preferences, past work, standing rules) and the list of skills and tools it has.

- Act. The model replies with one step at a time, as JSON — either a tool call ( {thought, tool, args} ) or a final answer ( {thought, final} ). The server runs the tool and hands the real result back to the model.

- Verify. The agent checks the result against real output (a file, a page, a command result) before it reports back. It does not invent facts.

- Approve. Anything consequential — running a command, changing a file, posting somewhere, installing something — waits for your approval. You allow it, or you reject it and the work stops.

- Remember. After a run, the agent writes what it learned about you and what it did into its local memory, so the next run starts smarter.

Your chats are stored on disk as one JSON file per chat, with a persistent record of the chats you deleted (so a deleted chat never comes back). Your API key is read from Settings on your PC and sent only to the provider you chose. The Discord bot, the browser panel, and the MCP connectors all go through this same local server — nothing bypasses it.

## Features

### Agent + tools

RedCat works in a loop: it understands your request, breaks it into steps, calls the right tools, verifies the result against real output, and reports back. It does not invent facts — it checks them with real tool output first. If something fails, the failure is shown to you, never hidden.

### Skills

RedCat has a library of reusable skills — website building, deep research, video, code review, and more. The agent chooses the right skill for the task. Skills are plain files the agent reads and applies, so new skills can be added and reviewed before they are used.

### Memory — it remembers, and it gets better

RedCat remembers what it did for you and what you prefer, and it updates its own memory automatically. Your preferences, your corrections, and your past work are all there the next time you open the app. This is the feature RedCat is built around: every run makes the next one better.

### Personality — it learns how you talk

RedCat builds a style profile from how you actually talk — your language, your tone, your sentence length — and adapts its replies to match. You can view and edit the profile, turn style-mirroring off, or reset it at any time in Settings.

### Discord — chat with RedCat from Discord

Connect RedCat to Discord once, then chat with it from a Discord DM or your server. The bot answers in the language you write in. Approvals still wait on your PC. Your API key never leaves your PC — only the prompt and the reply travel to Discord.

### Browser panel

RedCat has a built-in browser it can use to read live pages, research a topic, and — only with your approval — interact with a website. You log in to sites yourself in the panel; RedCat never sees your password.

### MCP + connectors — one-click Connect

RedCat connects to a catalog of 145 services — Notion, GitHub, Slack, Linear, and many more. Where the service supports it, you click Connect, sign in, and allow — that is all. Services that need manual setup stay guided, step by step. RedCat never shows a fake Connect button.

### Research — real sources, then a website

Ask RedCat to research something and it searches the web, reads the actual pages in its browser panel, cross-checks two or more independent sources, and answers with the evidence and the source names. It never invents a source, a number, or a quote. At the end of a big task, it builds you a clean, minimal website artifact containing all the findings and all the sources, with links.

### Video loading card

When the app opens, a short muted looping video plays on a loading card with a real loading bar tied to the actual startup stages — server starting, connecting, ready. There is no fake delay. If the server is already up, the app opens immediately.

### Auto-updates

RedCat checks GitHub Releases for a newer version and notifies you. A download starts only after you accept it. The update check is silent when it fails, so the app keeps working.

### Local-first privacy

Your chats, your memory, your personality profile, and your API keys live on your PC and nowhere else. There is no central server that stores your data. A fresh install starts completely empty. When you install RedCat, you get a clean app — never someone else's data.

### Approval-first security

RedCat asks before it acts. Running a command, changing a file, posting somewhere, or installing something all wait for your approval. You can reject any action, and a rejection stops the work — it is never retried silently. API keys and tokens are kept on your PC and never written into code, chat, or logs.

## Screenshots

Add Skills

One-click connectors & MCP

One-click Discord connection

Bring your own API key

Make it yours — custom themes

redcat.arexora.com

## Install

Download RedCat from the Releases page and choose the installer for your platform:

macOS and Linux builds are produced automatically by GitHub Actions on each release and attached to the same release.

System requirements: Windows 10 or later, macOS, or a modern Linux distribution. No terminal, no Docker, no extra setup.

## Use

- Install RedCat from the Releases page.

- Add your API key. Open Settings, pick a provider (for example OpenRouter, Gemini, DeepSeek, Groq, Claude, or OpenAI), pick a model, and paste your key. Your key is stored only on your PC. Free options exist — for example, OpenRouter offers free models.

- Chat. Type what you want in the app, or DM the RedCat bot on Discord. RedCat will work through the task step by step.

- Approve. When RedCat proposes a consequential action, an approval card appears. Allow it to continue, or reject it to stop.

That is all. Download, add a key, use.

## Build your own — extend RedCat

RedCat is MIT-licensed and built to be extended. The pieces are plain files, not hidden machinery, so you can read them, change them, and build your own agent or features on top.

### Add a skill

A skill is a plain Markdown file under skills/ that tells the agent when to use it and how. Create a folder skills/<your-skill>/ with a SKILL.md describing the task, the steps, and the tools to use. The agent reads the skill and applies it when the task matches. Skills are reviewed before they are used — a scan gate returns BLOCK, REVIEW, or ALLOW — so a skill you add is checked before the agent trusts it.

### Add a connector (MCP)

Connectors live in mcp.js with the catalog in mcp-catalog.json . A connector entry describes a remote MCP server: its URL, how to connect (OAuth with Dynamic Client Registration where the vendor supports it, an API key, or anonymous access), and the tools it exposes. Add an entry, restart, and the service appears on the Connectors page with a real Connect button. Services that need manual setup stay guided — never a fake one-click.

### Add a tool to the agent loop

The agent loop is in server.js . A tool is a function the server can run and a name the model can call in its JSON ( {thought, tool, args} ). Add the tool, list it in the model's tool inventory, and the model can call it. Keep tools small, verifiable, and approval-gated when they change anything outside the app.

### Change the agent's character

The agent's personality is defined in character.md — the tone it uses, how sharp or playful it is, and the hard rules it never breaks (for example, it never does illegal work and never helps the user do wrong work). Edit that file to change how the agent speaks. The safety rules are separate from the character and are not overridden by it.

### Run from source and build

npm install npm run dist-win # Windows installer (NSIS)

The macOS and Linux builds are produced by the GitHub Actions workflow in .github/workflows/build.yml on each release. To run the server directly for development, start server.js with Node and open the app against it — the app window loads from the local server, so a code change to the server is a restart away.

## Contribute

Contributions are open to everyone. Fork the repo, create a branch, and submit a pull request. Every pull request is merged only after the maintainer reviews and approves it — there is no auto-merge and no merge without approval. See CONTRIBUTING.md for the full guide.

## License

RedCat is released under the MIT License. See LICENSE for the full text.

# Context Mode

The other half of the context problem.

Used across teams at

## The Problem

Every MCP tool call dumps raw data into your context window. A Playwright snapshot costs 56 KB. Twenty GitHub issues cost 59 KB. One access log — 45 KB. After 30 minutes, 40% of your context is gone. And when the agent compacts the conversation to free space, it forgets which files it was editing, what tasks are in progress, and what you last asked for. On top of that, the agent wastes output tokens on filler, pleasantries, and verbose explanations — burning context from both sides.

### How Context Mode Solves It

Context Mode is an MCP server that solves all four sides of this problem:

- Context Saving — Sandbox tools keep raw data out of the context window. 315 KB becomes 5.4 KB. 98% reduction.

- Session Continuity — Every file edit, git operation, task, error, and user decision is tracked in SQLite. When the conversation compacts, context-mode doesn't dump this data back into context — it indexes events into FTS5 and retrieves only what's relevant via BM25 search. The model picks up exactly where you left off. If you don't --continue , previous session data is deleted immediately — a fresh session means a clean slate.

- Think in Code — The LLM should program the analysis, not compute it. Instead of reading 50 files into context to count functions, the agent writes a script that does the counting and console.log() s only the result. One script replaces ten tool calls and saves 100x context. This is a mandatory paradigm across all 17 supported clients, plus the OpenClaw gateway integration: stop treating the LLM as a data processor, treat it as a code generator. // Before: 47 × Read() = 700 KB. After: 1 × ctx_execute() = 3.6 KB. ctx_execute ( "javascript" , ` const files = fs.readdirSync('src').filter(f => f.endsWith('.ts')); files.forEach(f => console.log(f + ': ' + fs.readFileSync('src/'+f,'utf8').split('\\n').length + ' lines')); ` ) ;

Think in Code — The LLM should program the analysis, not compute it. Instead of reading 50 files into context to count functions, the agent writes a script that does the counting and console.log() s only the result. One script replaces ten tool calls and saves 100x context. This is a mandatory paradigm across all 17 supported clients, plus the OpenClaw gateway integration: stop treating the LLM as a data processor, treat it as a code generator.

// Before: 47 × Read() = 700 KB. After: 1 × ctx_execute() = 3.6 KB. ctx_execute ( "javascript" , ` const files = fs.readdirSync('src').filter(f => f.endsWith('.ts')); files.forEach(f => console.log(f + ': ' + fs.readFileSync('src/'+f,'utf8').split('\\n').length + ' lines')); ` ) ;

- No prose-style enforcement — context-mode keeps raw data out of context but never dictates how the model writes its final answer. Brevity, completeness, formatting — your model's call (or yours via your own CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md ). Aggressive brevity prompts have been shown to degrade coding/reasoning benchmarks ( Moonshot AI on kimi-k2.5 ) — the routing block stays focused on where data goes , not on how the model talks .

## Install

Platforms are grouped by install complexity. Hook-capable platforms get automatic routing enforcement. Non-hook platforms need a one-time routing file copy.

Prerequisites: Claude Code v1.0.33+ ( claude --version ). If /plugin is not recognized, update first: brew upgrade claude-code or npm update -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code .

Install:

/plugin marketplace add mksglu/context-mode /plugin install context-mode@context-mode

Restart Claude Code (or run /reload-plugins ).

Verify:

/context-mode:ctx-doctor

All checks should show [x] . The doctor validates runtimes, hooks, FTS5, and plugin registration.

Routing: Automatic. The SessionStart hook injects routing instructions at runtime — no file is written to your project. The plugin registers all hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, PreCompact, SessionStart, Stop) and 11 MCP tools — six sandbox tools ( ctx_batch_execute , ctx_execute , ctx_execute_file , ctx_index , ctx_search , ctx_fetch_and_index ) plus five meta-tools ( ctx_stats , ctx_doctor , ctx_upgrade , ctx_purge , ctx_insight ).

> Note: Slash commands are a Claude Code plugin feature. On other platforms, type ctx stats , ctx doctor , ctx index , ctx search , ctx upgrade , or ctx insight in the chat — the model calls the MCP tool automatically. See Utility Commands .

Status line (optional): Claude Code's plugin manifest cannot declare a status line, so this is a one-time manual edit to ~/.claude/settings.json :

{ "statusLine" : { "type" : " command " , "command" : " context-mode statusline " } }

After saving, restart Claude Code. The bar shows $ saved this session · $ saved across sessions · % efficient so you can see savings accumulate in real time. The wiring is path-free — context-mode statusline resolves through the bundled CLI regardless of where the plugin cache lives.

claude mcp add context-mode -- npx -y context-mode

This gives you all 11 MCP tools without automatic routing. The model can still use them — it just won't be nudged to prefer them over raw Bash/Read/WebFetch. Good for trying it out before committing to the full plugin.

Prerequisites: Node.js >= 22.5 (or Bun), Gemini CLI installed.

- Install context-mode globally: npm install -g context-mode

Install context-mode globally:

https://github.com/mrasu/spec-guardian.markdown:
# Spec Guardian

Let formal specs test AI implementations.

A FizzBee spec describes the state transitions your system allows. However, the spec does not test whether your implementation follows those transitions. SpecGuardian turns FizzBee's results into tests that check whether your implementation reaches an allowed state.

SpecGuardian lets you verify that an AI-generated implementation actually conforms to your specification.

## From Spec to Test: Cache-Aside

In this cache-aside example, a WriteAndInvalidate action stores a new value in the database, then invalidates the corresponding cache entry. The tutorial spec models each operation as atomic and allows a crash before or between them:

@ conformance role CacheAside : fair action WriteAndInvalidate : # Yield to allow a crash before the first I/O. atomic : pass # Write to the database first, then invalidate the cache. db . write ( self . key , self . write_value ) cache . delete_cache ( self . key )

SpecGuardian generates Go tests from FizzBee's results. They compare the observed state after the action with states allowed by the spec, including states reached when an I/O operation fails.

For example, the generated Go test injects an error into the implementation just before cache invalidation, then checks whether the resulting state is allowed by the spec.

### Catching a Spec Mismatch

Consider an ordering bug in WriteAndInvalidate : cache invalidation runs before the database write.

func (ca *CacheAside) WriteAndInvalidate(ctx context.Context, input *Input) (*Output, error) { + if err := ca.cache.Delete(ctx, input.Key); err != nil { + return nil, err + } + if err := ca.db.Write(ctx, input.Key, input.Value); err != nil { return nil, err } - if err := ca.cache.Delete(ctx, input.Key); err != nil { - return nil, err - } - return &Output{Key: input.Key, Value: input.Value}, nil }

Both orders produce the same final state on success. But when the database write fails after cache invalidation, the database still holds old value and the cache entry is gone. The spec writes to the database first, so stopping at any point cannot produce this combination.

The test fails with the following output (excerpt):

actual state does not match any allowed state: I/O events: 1. valkey.Do 2. sql.BeginTx [fault injected; call not executed]

The mismatch excerpts show the unchanged database value and missing cache entry:

Fields.DB.Records[0].Value (-want +got): string( - "new", + "old", )

Fields.Cache.CachedRecords (-want +got): map[string]string{ - "cached": "old", }

## Getting Started

To try this example locally, start with the included cache-aside write tutorial. You'll need Go and Docker Compose; the FizzBee exploration results and generated tests are included.

Clone the repository and run the example:

git clone https://github.com/mrasu/spec-guardian.git cd spec-guardian/examples/tutorial_cache_aside_write docker compose up -d go test -count=1 -tags=specguardian ./conformance/...

The test passes, checking normal completion and injected I/O failures. Apply the diff above to cache_aside.go and rerun the go test command to reproduce the failure. Restore the original order to make the test pass again.

## How It Works

Here's how SpecGuardian works:

- FizzBee explores the possible states described by the spec.

- SpecGuardian generates Go tests from the exploration results.

- Either AI or you write the setup and Action execution code, configure providers in specguardian.yml , and write any remaining state observation code.

- The tests run a function normally and with an error injected immediately before a supported I/O call, then compare the observed state with states allowed by the spec.

specguardian.yml configures state observation and comparison. See the configuration schema for available settings and the example configuration for an example.

## When to Use

SpecGuardian checks whether an Action ends in a state allowed by the FizzBee spec, including after an injected I/O failure. It complements other tests:

- Different from unit tests: It checks the resulting application state against the spec, beyond assertions about individual functions.

- Different from integration tests: The expected states come from a FizzBee spec defined independently of the implementation.

## Generate Tests for Your Project

To generate tests for your project, install FizzBee and run these commands from your Go module directory:

fizz --output-dir path/to/output_dir path/to/YourSpec.fizz go get -tool github.com/mrasu/spec-guardian go tool spec-guardian init --fizzbee-output-dir path/to/output_dir # Configure observation and comparison. $EDITOR specguardian.yml go generate ./conformance # Replace <role> with the generated role name and connect the tests to your application. $EDITOR " conformance/specguardian/<role>_conformance_impl_test.go " go mod tidy go test -tags=specguardian ./conformance/...

See the user guide for the complete setup.

## Examples

- Cache-aside write tutorial is the completed project from the user guide .

- Cache-aside demonstrates the cache-aside pattern.

- Idempotent request demonstrates idempotent requests.

- Iceberg is a real-world example that tests apache/iceberg-go .

## Current Scope

SpecGuardian currently generates Go tests for one FizzBee Action invocation at a time. See the guardian directory for the available I/O hooks.

SpecGuardian is under development. Its public APIs or generated Go code may change.

https://github.com/noambrand/ai-time-est.markdown:
### Ask Claude Code how long a task will take, and get an answer in its own working minutes, measured on your machine.

Claude estimates like a human developer: "2–3 days" for work it finishes before lunch. This add-on has Claude count the work instead of guessing, times it with rates measured from your own sessions, and checks itself after every task.

Example session (illustrative numbers)

Quick start • How it works • Accuracy • Privacy • Uninstall • Releases

## Quick start

1. In Claude Code, run:

/plugin install ai-time-estimator --marketplace noambrand/ai-time-estimator

2. Start a new Claude Code session and ask:

how long will it take to add CSV export to the report page?

That's it. The first session measures your rates in the background (about a minute), and every later answer is scored and improves on its own. You never run a script yourself. Needs Python 3.9+ on your PATH; nothing to pip install .

- Claude Code before 2.1.275: run /plugin marketplace add noambrand/ai-time-estimator , then /plugin install ai-time-estimator@ai-time-estimator .

- Let Claude do it: paste "Install https://github.com/noambrand/ai-time-estimator for me: clone it and run its install.py" into Claude Code.

- Terminal, one line: git clone https://github.com/noambrand/ai-time-estimator.git && python3 ai-time-estimator/install.py (on Windows python ). No git? Download the ZIP and run python install.py in its folder.

Pick one way. The plugin and install.py do the same job, so having both would score every task twice.

## Why

## How it works

- A time-estimator subagent inspects the repo (read-only), looks up similar past requests, and writes 2–3 scenarios of the work (smooth / expected / rough) as counts: files read, edits, lines written, command runs, fix loops.

- estimate.py turns those counts into P10 / P50 / P90 minutes with a Monte Carlo simulation, using rates measured on your machine: seconds per model turn, by model, reasoning effort and context size; the run time of each tool and shell command, including background agents up to their completion notice; output speed for long writes; a speed spread : real ÷ predicted time of your past requests, because a real request is fast or slow as a whole.

- seconds per model turn, by model, reasoning effort and context size;

- the run time of each tool and shell command, including background agents up to their completion notice;

- output speed for long writes;

- a speed spread : real ÷ predicted time of your past requests, because a real request is fast or slow as a whole.

- A Stop hook ( autoscore.py ) compares every estimate with what really happened. The time you spend reading, answering or approving is left out.

- After 10 scored estimates, the ranges correct themselves from your results, and each answer carries its track record.

The model never makes up minutes. It only counts operations, and the scripts do the arithmetic.

You can also type /estimate-here <task> to estimate inside the current session; Claude then waits for your go.

## What installing changes

As a plugin , nothing in your own settings: Claude Code loads the agent, the /estimate-here command and the two hooks (scoring after each turn, a sync at session start) from the plugin. Your rates and history live in ~/.claude/ai-time-estimator/ .

With install.py , it:

- copies the time-estimator agent to ~/.claude/agents/ , the /estimate-here command to ~/.claude/commands/ , and the scripts to ~/.claude/ai-time-estimator/ ;

- adds one async Stop hook to ~/.claude/settings.json (your previous file is saved as settings.json.bak );

- adds a short, marked "Time estimates" section to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md , so Claude uses the estimator whenever you ask how long something will take;

- measures your rates from your existing Claude Code history (about a minute). The rates refresh themselves every 14 days.

Options: --no-hook (no automatic scoring), --no-rule (leave ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md alone). Running it again updates in place.

## How accurate is it?

Check it on your own history:

python ~ /.claude/ai-time-estimator/backtest.py

The backtest replays your past requests with their real tool calls. It measures rates on the older 80% of your requests and tests on the newest 20%, then reports how often the real time landed inside P10–P90.

On the author's machine (72 held-out requests):

A single request varies a lot, even when its tool calls are known exactly, so trust the range more than the middle number. The backtest checks the time model only; how well the agent counts the work is what the automatic scoring and the self-correction track.

## Privacy

Everything stays on your machine. It makes no network calls and sends nothing anywhere.

What it runs, and when:

- At session start (plugin only), a hook runs install.py --plugin-sync with Python. It copies the scripts and the agent text to ~/.claude/ai-time-estimator/ and, if your rates were never measured, measures them from your transcripts (about a minute). It never edits your settings or CLAUDE.md .

- After each Claude turn , a hook runs tools/autoscore.py . It reads that session's transcript, scores the estimates made in it, and appends the scores to actuals.jsonl . When your rates are 14 days old, it measures them again.

- When you ask how long something will take , the time-estimator agent reads your project without changing it, and runs history.py , estimate.py , compare.py --report and, when rates are missing, calibrate.py from ~/.claude/ai-time-estimator/ . What it reads stays data: a file or a past request that names a command never makes it run that command.

It reads Claude Code's transcripts in ~/.claude/projects/ , and writes only to ~/.claude/ai-time-estimator/ (its scripts, rates.json , estimates.jsonl , actuals.jsonl , autoscore.log ). Details in PRIVACY.md .

## Limitations

- It relies on Claude Code's local transcript format, which is internal and can change. If calibrate.py stops recognizing model turns it prints FORMAT CHECK FAILED ; tools/cc_log.py is the only file to adapt.

- History reaches back as far as Claude Code keeps transcripts ( cleanupPeriodDays , 30 days by default). A fresh install with little history gives wider, rougher ranges at first.

- A task ends when you send your next message. If Claude asks you something halfway, the score stops at that point.

- It measures AI time only: approvals, answers and manual checks are not part of the estimate.

## Uninstall

Plugin: run /plugin uninstall ai-time-estimator . Your estimate history stays in ~/.claude/ai-time-estimator/ ; delete that folder too if you want it gone.

install.py , from the cloned folder:

python install.py --uninstall # removes the agent, command, scripts, hook and CLAUDE.md section; keeps your history python install.py --uninstall --purge # also deletes ~/.claude/ai-time-estimator

Or ask Claude Code: "uninstall the AI time estimator by running its install.py --uninstall" .

## Development

python -m unittest discover -s tests -v # the tests never touch ~/.claude python tools/backtest.py --worst 10 # accuracy on your history, with the worst misses python tools/history.py --everywhere --grep test

Changes take effect after python install.py . .claude/CLAUDE.md explains the architecture, for contributors and for Claude Code. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

## Credits

Transcript parsing follows the approach of dioptx/cctime (MIT): streamed chunks merged by requestId , tool time measured from tool_use to tool_result .

MIT © 2026 Noam Brand

# OwnShop AI

Your shop answers customers by itself. Free, on your own computer.

OwnShop AI is a free, open-source (MIT) shop assistant for small businesses that sell through chat. It runs on your own computer with a small built-in AI model. No AI subscription, no paid auto-reply service, no hosting, no domain.

Website: https://ownshopai.store · Manual: https://ownshopai.store/manual/ · Download: https://ownshopai.store/#download

If it helps your shop, please star this repo so other shops can find it, and fork it to make your own version.

## Who it is for

A small shop or home business that keeps its list in an Excel sheet and talks to customers on WhatsApp, Telegram or the web, and anyone who takes bookings: salons, tutors, clinics, studios. Today you answer "price?", "in stock?" and "where is my order?" by hand, or pay every month for a chatbot, an AI plan, hosting and a domain. OwnShop AI needs none of them.

## What it does for your customers

- Answers questions from your own FAQ sheet and common shop questions (hours, address, delivery, payment methods).

- Catalog and prices : "do you have honey?" gets your products with photo, price and stock.

- Takes orders : builds the cart, asks for a delivery slot, and confirms only when the customer replies YES.

- Service bookings : for a services shop, customers pick a day and a free time from your hours (Calendar page to close a day or remove a slot).

- Invoice and how to pay : an invoice image, then your payment details: a payment link, a QR image, bank transfer text, or a UPI ID with a QR made for each order.

- Order and service status : "what is my order status?" answers that customer's own order.

- Hand-off to you : anything it is not sure about goes to the Chats page for you to answer.

## Chat channels

- WhatsApp (unofficial link through wacli, see the warning below) and Telegram (official bot).

- Website : a public chat link customers open in any browser, from a phone or a computer. Your shop page itself stays on your computer only; only the customer chat is published, through a Cloudflare tunnel (install Cloudflare's free cloudflared once). Three kinds of link, on the Website card in Settings: Quick link , no sign-up: a random *.trycloudflare.com address from a Cloudflare quick tunnel. It changes every time OwnShop AI or the computer restarts. Free fixed link yourname.ownshopai.store : coming soon . The link service it needs is not live yet. Your own domain : paste a Cloudflare tunnel token and your hostname; the token is stored locally and never shown again. Customers type a name and phone number (not verified), and the browser remembers them. The chat is a PWA : they can add it to the home screen and turn on notifications for replies (on iPhone after adding it to the home screen, iOS 16.4 or later). Guide: docs/guides/14-web-chat-link.md .

- Quick link , no sign-up: a random *.trycloudflare.com address from a Cloudflare quick tunnel. It changes every time OwnShop AI or the computer restarts.

You click Payment received , Packed , Shipped , Delivered or Cancel on the Orders page, and each click messages the customer (Payment received also sends a receipt image). You can block a customer on every channel from the Users page, and test the whole flow without a phone in the built-in web chat ( http://localhost:2007/webchat ).

## Why it costs nothing

- Built-in AI. A small model (Qwen3.5 0.8B via llama.cpp) runs on your computer. Your chats are not sent to an AI company.

- No auto-reply service. It links to Telegram (official bot) and WhatsApp (unofficial link, see below) directly.

- No hosting, no domain. Your computer is the server. It only needs to stay on and online.

- Your data stays with you. Products, orders and chats are files and a database on your computer.

- Free support: questions, bugs and feature requests: open an issue .

- Premium support: setup done for you, priority help and custom features from deemwar: join the WhatsApp group .

Privacy: https://ownshopai.store/privacy · Terms: https://ownshopai.store/terms

## Quick start

Download the installer for your computer from https://ownshopai.store/#download :

## Requirements

- macOS on Apple Silicon, or Windows 10/11 (x64 or ARM64).

- About 600 MB of disk and about 1 GB of free memory while chatting. A reply takes about 0.4 s on a recent Mac.

- No API key, no account, no internet AI service. The model runs locally.

## Using it

- Double-click OwnShop AI. It opens your browser at http://localhost:2007 (if another program uses that port, it takes the next free one, 2008, 2009, ..., and remembers it). It also starts by itself when you log in, and puts an OwnShop AI shortcut on your desktop that opens the shop page. Double-clicking it again just opens the page.

- The page walks you through four steps: Shop : your shop name and currency. Products : upload one Excel file. Not sure what it looks like? Download the example file on that page. Payment : choose one way to pay (payment link, QR image, bank transfer text or UPI ID); add more later in Settings. Chat channels : Connect Telegram (paste the token @BotFather gives you; the page shows the steps) or Connect WhatsApp (a pairing code appears on the page; scan it from the spare phone under Linked devices). You can connect several WhatsApp numbers and add more later in Settings.

### Your two files

OwnShop AI keeps its own database, but the files you work with are plain files in the OwnShop AI folder ( ~/Library/Application Support/ownshop on a Mac, %AppData%\ownshop on Windows):

If the file is open in Excel and cannot be written, OwnShop AI keeps the newer stock, tells you on the Products page, and writes it as soon as it can, so it never sells stock you no longer have.

## How it works

- One program. OwnShop AI serves the owner's web page, runs the chat channels, and keeps its data in one SQLite file next to your two files.

- Chat channels. Every channel is a small adapter with the same shape (start, receive, send text, send image, status). Each customer is remembered with the channel and number they wrote to, and every reply and order update goes back on that same channel and number. Telegram : official Bot API with long polling ( getUpdates ), sendMessage , sendPhoto and the typing indicator. Only private chats are answered. The bot token is stored locally, shown masked, and never logged. WhatsApp : each number has its own wacli store inside OwnShop AI's data folder ( <data>/wacli/<name> ), so OwnShop AI never reads or edits ~/.wacli or the wacli accounts other programs on the machine use. OwnShop AI runs wacli --store <data>/wacli/<name> auth --qr-format text --events to pair (the pairing code is drawn on the page), then keeps one follower per number: wacli --store <data>/wacli/<name> sync --follow --webhook http://127.0.0.1:<port>/wacli/<name> --webhook-allow-private --webhook-secret <random> --webhook-events message --events . wacli posts each new message to a listener OwnShop AI opens on 127.0.0.1 only; OwnShop AI checks the signature, answers 200 at once and handles the message after. Replies go out with wacli send text / wacli send file --as image , and wacli presence typing ; wacli hands them to the running follower, which owns the number's store lock. If another program already holds that lock, OwnShop AI waits and retries and never stops it. Groups, broadcasts and your own messages are ignored.
